chapters.title: The Overturning
chapters.html:
Genesis 19

1And the two messengers came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom. And Lot saw, and rose to meet them, and bowed, face to the ground.

2And he said, "Look now, my lords — turn aside, please, to your servant's house, and spend the night, and wash your feet. And you shall rise early and go on your way." And they said, "No. We will spend the night in the square."

3And he pressed them greatly, and they turned aside to him and came into his house. And he made them a feast, and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.

4They had not yet lain down, and the men of the city — the men of Sodom — surrounded the house, from young to old, all the people, from every quarter.

5And they called to Lot and said to him, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, and let us know them."

6And Lot went out to them, to the doorway, and shut the door behind him.

7And he said, "Please, my brothers, do not do evil.

8Look now — I have two daughters who have not known a man. Let me bring them out to you, and do to them what is good in your eyes. Only to these men do nothing, for this is why they have come under the shadow of my roof-beam."

9And they said, "Step aside!" And they said, "This one came to sojourn, and he judges, judging! Now we will do worse to you than to them." And they pressed hard against the man, against Lot, and drew near to break the door.

10And the men put out their hand and brought Lot in to them, into the house, and they shut the door.

11And the men who were at the opening of the house they struck with blindings, from small to great, and they wore themselves out trying to find the opening.

Get Out

12And the men said to Lot, "Who else do you have here — a son-in-law, and your sons, and your daughters, and everyone you have in the city? Bring them out from the place.

13For we are ruining this place, because their outcry has grown great before the face of the LORD, and the LORD has sent us to ruin it."

14And Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, the takers of his daughters, and said, "Rise, get out from this place, for the LORD is ruining the city." And he was like one making a joke in the eyes of his sons-in-law.

15And as the dawn came up, the messengers urged Lot, saying, "Rise, take your wife and your two daughters who are found here, or you will be swept away in the guilt of the city."

16And he lingered. And the men seized his hand, and the hand of his wife, and the hand of his two daughters — in the LORD's pity on him — and they brought him out and set him down outside the city.

17And it came to pass, as they brought them outside, that he said, "Escape, for your life! Do not look behind you, and do not stand still anywhere in the plain. Escape to the hill country, or you will be swept away."

18And Lot said to them, "Not so, please, my lord.

19Look now — your servant has found favor in your eyes, and you have made great your kindness that you did with me, to keep my soul alive. But I cannot escape to the hill country — the evil will overtake me and I will die.

20Look now — this city is near, to flee there, and it is a little thing. Let me escape there, please — is it not a little thing? — and my soul will live."

21And He said to him, "Look, I have lifted your face in this matter also: I will not overturn the city of which you have spoken.

22Hurry, escape there, for I cannot do anything until you arrive there." Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.

23The sun had gone out over the earth, and Lot came to Zoar.

24And the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah sulfur and fire, from the LORD, from the heavens.

25And He overturned those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew from the ground.

26And his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.

27And Abraham rose early in the morning, to the place where he had stood before the face of the LORD.

28And he looked down over the face of Sodom and Gomorrah, and over all the face of the land of the plain, and he saw — and here, the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a kiln.

29And it came to pass, when God ruined the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham, and He sent Lot out from the midst of the overturning, when He overturned the cities in which Lot had settled.

The Cave

30And Lot went up from Zoar and settled in the hill country, and his two daughters with him, for he was afraid to settle in Zoar. And he settled in the cave, he and his two daughters.

31And the firstborn said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is no man in the earth to come to us according to the way of all the earth.

32Come, let us give our father wine to drink, and let us lie with him, and let us keep seed alive from our father."

33And they gave their father wine to drink that night, and the firstborn came and lay with her father. And he did not know when she lay down or when she rose.

34And it came to pass on the next day that the firstborn said to the younger, "Look — I lay last night with my father. Let us give him wine to drink tonight also, and you go in, lie with him, and let us keep seed alive from our father."

35And they gave their father wine to drink that night also, and the younger rose and lay with him. And he did not know when she lay down or when she rose.

36And the two daughters of Lot conceived by their father.

37And the firstborn bore a son, and she called his name Moab. He is the father of Moab to this day.

38And the younger, she also bore a son, and she called his name Ben-ammi. He is the father of the sons of Ammon to this day.

Notes

  • v1 "the two messengers" — three men came to Abraham's tent in chapter 18; two arrive here. The third is not accounted for, and the text does not remark on it.

  • vv1–3 against 18:1–8 — read the two receptions side by side. Abraham ran; Lot rose. Abraham bowed to the ground; Lot bowed face to the ground. Abraham's guests accepted at once; Lot's refuse, and he has to press them. Abraham killed a calf and baked leavened loaves; Lot bakes matsot, flat bread, the quick kind. The scene is the same scene, one degree colder at every step, and Lot is sitting in the city gate rather than at a tent door.

  • v5 "let us know them" — ve-ned'ah otam. Everywhere else in this book, yada is the word for intimacy that produces a child and a name — Adam and Eve, Cain and his wife (see the note at 4:1) — while shakhav, to lie with, is the word for the act when it is coerced or illicit. Here a mob demanding to assault two strangers uses the knowing word. Lot's answer in v8, daughters who have not known a man, uses it in its ordinary sense and settles what they meant. Whether the mob's choice of word is the narrator's irony or simply the idiom is not something the verse says; what can be said is that it is the wrong word for what they are asking.

  • v8 — Lot offers his two virgin daughters to a mob to protect two guests. The text reports it without a word of comment, as it reported Abraham handing Sarai to Pharaoh. Judgment is withheld here in the same way, and the chapter's last scene is what his daughters do to him.

  • v9 "he judges, judging" — va-yishpot shaphot, the doubled verb for emphasis. They are mocking him for playing judge, and the reader has just come from chapter 18, where Abraham asked whether the Judge of all the earth would do justice. The same root, in a sneer, one chapter later.

  • v11 "blindings" — sanverim, a rare word that appears only here and in one other episode in the Hebrew Bible. Not the ordinary word for blind. Whatever it names, the men keep groping for the door, so they are not simply sightless — they cannot find what is in front of them.

  • vv13, 14, 29 "ruining" — shachat, four times in this chapter. It is the flood verb from 6:11–13, where the earth was ruined and God said I am ruining them. Sodom is the second time the word is used at full strength, and 13:10 warned the reader with it before Lot ever moved there.

  • v14 "like one making a joke" — ki-metsacheq, from tsachaq, to laugh. The same root as Abraham's laugh in 17:17, Sarah's in 18:12, and the name Isaac. Here the laughter is at a man warning of death, and the sons-in-law stay.

  • v16 "And he lingered" — va-yitmahmah, one word, and it is the whole character. Then the messengers take him by the hand and carry him out. He is rescued while resisting.

  • v17, 15 "swept away" — tissapheh, the same verb Abraham used in 18:23: will you really sweep away the righteous with the wicked? The word from the bargain comes back as a warning to the one man the bargain saved.

  • v20 "it is a little thing… is it not a little thing?" — mits'ar, twice, and the city is then named Tso'ar, Little, in v22. He is given the mountain and negotiates his way down to a town, and the town is named for his argument.

  • vv24–25 "rained… overturned" — himtir, the rain verb from the flood, and haphakh, to overturn, turn upside down. Haphakh and its noun haphekhah run through vv21, 25, 29 — four times. This is not burning; it is inversion. The word will become the standing biblical name for what happened to these cities.

  • v26 "his wife looked back" — va-tabbet, the verb for gazing, looking intently — the same one used in 15:5 when Abram was told to look at the stars. She is not named, here or anywhere.

  • v29 "God remembered Abraham" — va-yizkor Elohim et Avraham, the identical construction as 8:1, and God remembered Noah. Both come at the turn of a catastrophe, and both mean that something is now going to happen. Note who is remembered: not Lot. Lot is saved because of a conversation he was not present for.

  • v30 "for he was afraid to settle in Zoar" — he argued for the town in v20 and will not live in it. Three verses of negotiation, and then he goes up the mountain he had refused.

  • vv31–36 the wine and the cave — the last man to be made drunk and uncovered in this book was Noah in 9:21, also after a world was destroyed, also with children involved and a curse following. The pattern repeats with the roles reversed: there the son saw the father's nakedness, here the daughters take it.

  • v33, 35 "he did not know" — the two verbs of this chapter arrive in one sentence. Va-tishkav, she lay with her father — the word Genesis reserves for the act when it is a violation. And ve-lo yada, he did not know — the word Genesis reserves for the act when it makes a family. Lot lay and did not know. The verse puts the two side by side and negates the second one.

  • v33 "when she lay down or when she rose" — the Masoretes placed a dot over a letter in u-ve-qumah, "and when she rose," in this verse — and not in v35, where the identical phrase describes the younger daughter. Both verses sit four lines apart with the same words, and the mark is on only one of them. As with the other dotted words, the scribes flagged it and changed nothing.

  • vv37–38 "Moab… Ben-ammi" — the names are given plainly: Mo-av sounds like from father, and Ben-ammi means son of my people. Two nations that will spend centuries at war with Israel are introduced here, with their origins stated and no verdict attached. The chapter ends to this day.

speech.text: Genesis 19
And the two messengers came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom. And Lot saw, and rose to meet them, and bowed, face to the ground.

And he said, "Look now, my lords — turn aside, please, to your servant's house, and spend the night, and wash your feet. And you shall rise early and go on your way." And they said, "No. We will spend the night in the square."
And he pressed them greatly, and they turned aside to him and came into his house. And he made them a feast, and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.
They had not yet lain down, and the men of the city — the men of Sodom — surrounded the house, from young to old, all the people, from every quarter.
And they called to Lot and said to him, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, and let us know them."
And Lot went out to them, to the doorway, and shut the door behind him.
And he said, "Please, my brothers, do not do evil.

Look now — I have two daughters who have not known a man. Let me bring them out to you, and do to them what is good in your eyes. Only to these men do nothing, for this is why they have come under the shadow of my roof-beam."

And they said, "Step aside!" And they said, "This one came to sojourn, and he judges, judging! Now we will do worse to you than to them." And they pressed hard against the man, against Lot, and drew near to break the door.
And the men put out their hand and brought Lot in to them, into the house, and they shut the door.
And the men who were at the opening of the house they struck with blindings, from small to great, and they wore themselves out trying to find the opening.
Get Out
And the men said to Lot, "Who else do you have here — a son-in-law, and your sons, and your daughters, and everyone you have in the city? Bring them out from the place.
For we are ruining this place, because their outcry has grown great before the face of the LORD, and the LORD has sent us to ruin it."

And Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, the takers of his daughters, and said, "Rise, get out from this place, for the LORD is ruining the city." And he was like one making a joke in the eyes of his sons-in-law.
And as the dawn came up, the messengers urged Lot, saying, "Rise, take your wife and your two daughters who are found here, or you will be swept away in the guilt of the city."
And he lingered. And the men seized his hand, and the hand of his wife, and the hand of his two daughters — in the LORD's pity on him — and they brought him out and set him down outside the city.

And it came to pass, as they brought them outside, that he said, "Escape, for your life! Do not look behind you, and do not stand still anywhere in the plain. Escape to the hill country, or you will be swept away."
And Lot said to them, "Not so, please, my lord.

Look now — your servant has found favor in your eyes, and you have made great your kindness that you did with me, to keep my soul alive. But I cannot escape to the hill country — the evil will overtake me and I will die.
Look now — this city is near, to flee there, and it is a little thing. Let me escape there, please — is it not a little thing? — and my soul will live."
And He said to him, "Look, I have lifted your face in this matter also: I will not overturn the city of which you have spoken.
Hurry, escape there, for I cannot do anything until you arrive there." Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.
The sun had gone out over the earth, and Lot came to Zoar.
And the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah sulfur and fire, from the LORD, from the heavens.
And He overturned those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew from the ground.
And his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
And Abraham rose early in the morning, to the place where he had stood before the face of the LORD.
And he looked down over the face of Sodom and Gomorrah, and over all the face of the land of the plain, and he saw — and here, the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a kiln.

And it came to pass, when God ruined the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham, and He sent Lot out from the midst of the overturning, when He overturned the cities in which Lot had settled.
The Cave
And Lot went up from Zoar and settled in the hill country, and his two daughters with him, for he was afraid to settle in Zoar. And he settled in the cave, he and his two daughters.
And the firstborn said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is no man in the earth to come to us according to the way of all the earth.
Come, let us give our father wine to drink, and let us lie with him, and let us keep seed alive from our father."
And they gave their father wine to drink that night, and the firstborn came and lay with her father. And he did not know when she lay down or when she rose.

And it came to pass on the next day that the firstborn said to the younger, "Look — I lay last night with my father. Let us give him wine to drink tonight also, and you go in, lie with him, and let us keep seed alive from our father."
And they gave their father wine to drink that night also, and the younger rose and lay with him. And he did not know when she lay down or when she rose.
And the two daughters of Lot conceived by their father.
And the firstborn bore a son, and she called his name Moab. He is the father of Moab to this day.
And the younger, she also bore a son, and she called his name Ben-ammi. He is the father of the sons of Ammon to this day.

chapters.title: Abimelech, and the Integrity of a Heart
chapters.html:
Genesis 20

1And Abraham journeyed from there to the land of the Negev, and he settled between Kadesh and Shur, and he sojourned in Gerar.

2And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, "She is my sister." And Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took Sarah.

3And God came to Abimelech in a dream of the night, and said to him, "Here, you are a dead man, over the woman you have taken — and she is owned by an owner."

4And Abimelech had not come near her. And he said, "My Lord, will You kill even a righteous nation?

5Did he not say to me, 'She is my sister'? And she — she herself also said, 'He is my brother.' In the integrity of my heart and in the cleanness of my hands I have done this."

6And God said to him in the dream, "I also know that in the integrity of your heart you did this. And I also held you back from sinning against Me. Therefore I did not let you touch her.

7And now, return the man's wife, for he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and live. And if you do not return her, know that dying you shall die — you and all that is yours."

8And Abimelech rose early in the morning and called all his servants, and spoke all these words in their ears, and the men were very afraid.

9And Abimelech called Abraham and said to him, "What have you done to us? And how have I sinned against you, that you have brought upon me and upon my kingdom a great sin? Deeds that are not done, you have done with me."

10And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What did you see, that you did this thing?"

11And Abraham said, "Because I said, 'Surely there is no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me over the matter of my wife.'

12And also, truly, she is my sister — the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother — and she became my wife.

13And it came to pass, when God made me wander from my father's house, that I said to her, 'This is your kindness that you shall do with me: at every place where we come, say of me, He is my brother.'"

14And Abimelech took flocks and cattle and male servants and female servants, and gave them to Abraham, and he returned to him Sarah his wife.

15And Abimelech said, "Here is my land before you. Settle where it is good in your eyes."

16And to Sarah he said, "Here — I have given a thousand of silver to your brother. Here, it is for you a covering of eyes, for all who are with you; and with everyone, you are cleared."

17And Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, and his wife, and his slave women, and they bore children.

18For the LORD had closed up, closing up, every womb of the house of Abimelech, over the matter of Sarah, Abraham's wife.

Notes

  • v3 "you are a dead man" — hinnekha met, literally here-you-are dead. Not a threat about the future; a statement of present condition, using the participle. And it is said to a man who has done nothing yet.

  • v3 "owned by an owner" — be'ulat ba'al. Ba'al is the ordinary Hebrew word for a husband, and it is also the word for an owner, a master, a possessor. The phrase doubles it — she is ba'al-ed by a ba'al. English has no way to say that a wife is described with the vocabulary of property, because our word for husband does not carry it.

  • v4 "will You kill even a righteous nation?" — ha-goy gam tsaddiq taharog. Two chapters ago Abraham stood before the LORD and asked whether the Judge of all the earth would sweep away the righteous with the wicked. Here a foreign king, with no covenant and no promise, makes the same objection in the same words — tsaddiq, righteous — and he is the one who has been wronged.

  • v5 "in the integrity of my heart and in the cleanness of my hands" — be-tom levavi u-ve-niqyon kappai. Tom is the noun behind tamim, the word God used to Abraham in 17:1: be whole. The pagan king claims the quality Abraham was commanded to have, and God confirms it in v6.

  • v7 "he is a prophet" — navi, the first occurrence of the word in the Bible. It is applied to Abraham, by God, in a conversation with a foreigner, to explain why the foreigner should ask Abraham to pray. A word that will carry Isaiah and Jeremiah arrives here as a reason to trust a man who has just lied.

  • v7 "dying you shall die" — mot tamut, the formula from 2:17, the death sentence phrasing. It is spoken to Abimelech, not to Abraham.

  • v9 "Deeds that are not done" — ma'asim asher lo ye'asu, a passive with no agent. Not you should not have; rather, things one does not do. It is the language of a shared standard, spoken by the man supposed to have no standards.

  • v11 "there is no fear of God in this place" — Abraham's explanation, delivered to a man who has just risen early, assembled his household, feared greatly, returned the woman, and paid compensation. The chapter has spent ten verses establishing that he was wrong, and then lets him say it.

  • v13 "when God made me wander" — hit'u oti Elohim, and the verb is plural, agreeing with Elohim as a plural form, which Hebrew usually does not do when the word means the one God. Abraham is speaking to a foreign king and his grammar bends toward the way that king would hear it. The verb itself, ta'ah, means to wander or go astray — it is what a lost animal does.

  • v16 "a covering of eyes" — kesut einayim, and nobody knows what it means. A veil? Compensation that covers the offense in the sight of others? The second half of the verse, ve-et kol ve-nokhachat, is harder still and its grammar does not resolve. Rendered word for word; the obscurity is in the Hebrew and should not be smoothed away.

  • v16 "to your brother" — Abimelech says it to her face, about her husband, after being told the truth. It is the one barbed word in a speech that is otherwise generous.

  • v17 "And Abraham prayed" — va-yitpallel, the first prayer of intercession in the Bible. The man who deceived Abimelech is the one who has to ask God to heal him.

  • v18 "the LORD had closed up, closing up, every womb" — atsor atsar, the doubled verb. This is the same verb Sarai used in 16:2 — the LORD has held me back from bearing. The chapter closes on wombs being shut and then opened, immediately before the chapter in which Sarah's is opened.

  • The shape — this is the second time Abraham has passed his wife off as his sister, and the second time a foreign king has been struck for it and has paid him to leave. The first was Pharaoh in 12:10–20. The narrator does not compare them or comment; the story simply happens again, twenty-five years later, after the covenant, after the name change, after the circumcision.

chapters.title: Laughter, and the Sending Away
chapters.html:
Genesis 21

1And the LORD attended to Sarah as He had said, and the LORD did for Sarah as He had spoken.

2And Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the appointed time of which God had spoken to him.

3And Abraham called the name of his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore to him, Isaac.

4And Abraham circumcised Isaac his son at eight days old, as God had commanded him.

5And Abraham was a hundred years old when Isaac his son was born to him.

6And Sarah said, "Laughter God has made for me. Everyone who hears will laugh for me."

7And she said, "Who would have spoken it to Abraham — Sarah has nursed sons? For I have borne a son in his old age."

The Sending Away

8And the child grew and was weaned, and Abraham made a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned.

9And Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham — laughing.

10And she said to Abraham, "Drive out this slave woman and her son, for the son of this slave woman shall not inherit with my son, with Isaac."

11And the thing was very evil in Abraham's eyes, on account of his son.

12And God said to Abraham, "Let it not be evil in your eyes over the boy and over your slave woman. All that Sarah says to you — listen to her voice, for through Isaac shall seed be called for you.

13And also the son of the slave woman I will make into a nation, for he is your seed."

14And Abraham rose early in the morning and took bread and a skin of water, and gave them to Hagar — setting them on her shoulder — and the child, and he sent her away. And she went, and she wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.

15And the water was finished from the skin, and she cast the child under one of the bushes.

16And she went and sat down opposite him, far off, about a bowshot, for she said, "Let me not see the child die." And she sat opposite, and she lifted her voice and wept.

17And God heard the voice of the boy, and the messenger of God called to Hagar from the heavens and said to her, "What is it with you, Hagar? Do not fear, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.

18Rise, lift up the boy, and hold your hand strong on him, for I will make him into a great nation."

19And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. And she went and filled the skin with water, and gave the boy drink.

20And God was with the boy, and he grew, and he settled in the wilderness, and he became an archer.

21And he settled in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.

The Well of the Oath

22And it came to pass at that time that Abimelech, and Phicol the commander of his army, said to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do.

23And now, swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me, nor with my offspring, nor with my posterity. According to the kindness I have done with you, you shall do with me, and with the land in which you have sojourned."

24And Abraham said, "I will swear."

25And Abraham reproved Abimelech over the matter of a well of water that Abimelech's servants had seized.

26And Abimelech said, "I do not know who did this thing. And you also did not tell me, and I also have not heard of it until today."

27And Abraham took flocks and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two of them cut a covenant.

28And Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock by themselves.

29And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What are these seven ewe lambs that you have set by themselves?"

30And he said, "For you shall take the seven ewe lambs from my hand, so that it may be a witness for me that I dug this well."

31Therefore that place was called Beersheba, for there the two of them swore.

32And they cut a covenant at Beersheba. And Abimelech rose, and Phicol the commander of his army, and they returned to the land of the Philistines.

33And he planted a tamarisk at Beersheba, and there he called on the name of the LORD, God of Everlasting.

34And Abraham sojourned in the land of the Philistines many days.

Notes

  • v1 "attended to" — paqad, a wide verb: to visit, to muster, to number, to take account of, to appoint an overseer. It is what a commander does when he counts his troops and what a creditor does when he calls in what is owed. Rendered "attended to" because "visited" has gone soft in English, and the verb means action was taken.

  • vv6–7 "Laughter… will laugh" — tsechoq and yitschaq. The second of those is the boy's name, written out as an ordinary verb. She says God has made laughter for me, and everyone who hears will Isaac for me — and the preposition li can mean for me, with me, or at me. Whether the neighbors are laughing with her or at her is left open in the Hebrew, from a woman who denied laughing in 18:15.

  • v7 "Sarah has nursed sons" — she quotes a sentence nobody ever said, as the thing nobody could have said. And banim is plural: sons, not a son.

  • v9 "laughing" — metsacheq, the participle of the same root as Isaac's name. What Ishmael was doing is one word, and it can mean laughing, playing, joking, mocking, or fondling — and this verse gives no context at all. English Bibles supply one: "mocking," "playing," "laughing." The Hebrew says he was Isaac-ing, and the whole chapter turns on a sentence that does not say what he did.

    The book uses the same form twice more, and both are worth setting beside this one. In 19:14, Lot warning his sons-in-law of the city's destruction seems to them ki-metsacheq, like a man making a joke. In 26:8, Abimelech looks through a window and sees Isaac metsacheq with Rebekah his wife — and concludes at once that they are married, not siblings. There the word plainly means something between a husband and a wife.

    So the range is real and wide, and the text itself demonstrates it: a joke in one place, intimacy in another, and here, whatever Sarah saw. What cannot be said is that the word means mocking. That is a translator's decision about a boy's guilt, and it is the decision on which his expulsion is usually justified.

  • v10 "Drive out" — garesh, the verb used in 3:24 when God drove out the man from the garden, and in 4:14 when Cain says you have driven me out. It is expulsion, not dismissal.

  • v11 "very evil in Abraham's eyes" — va-yera… me'od. The only time in these chapters that something is said to grieve him. Not when Sarai afflicted Hagar in 16:6; not when he was asked for Isaac in the next chapter. Here.

  • v12 "listen to her voice" — shema be-qolah. In 3:17 the man was condemned because you listened to the voice of your wife; in 16:2 Abram listened to the voice of Sarai and it produced this crisis. Here God commands the same phrase. The book uses the identical expression for the fall, for the error, and for the instruction, and does not explain the difference.

  • v14 "bread and a skin of water" — he had just been given flocks, cattle, and servants by Abimelech in 20:14, and had a household large enough to arm 318 men in 14:14. She leaves with what she can carry on one shoulder.

  • v14 "she wandered" — va-teta, the verb Abraham used of himself in 20:13, when God made me wander. He was made to wander and came out rich; she is sent to wander with a waterskin.

  • v16 "she lifted her voice and wept" — and then in v17 God heard the voice of the boy. She is the one weeping; the voice that is heard is his. The text does not say the boy made a sound.

  • v17 "where he is" — ba-asher hu sham, three words, no explanation. Heard in the place he is in, as he is.

  • v17 Ishmael, again — the name means God hears, and the verse says God heard twice without ever using the boy's name. The same wordplay was made to Hagar in 16:11 and to Abraham in 17:20. Three times, always about hearing, always about this son.

  • v19 "God opened her eyes, and she saw a well" — the well was there. Nothing is created; her eyes are opened. This is the second time she has been met at water in a wilderness (16:7), and the second time she is the one who sees — she is the woman who named God El Ro'i, God of my seeing.

  • v25–30 "a well… seven ewe lambs" — the naming turns on a pun that works only in Hebrew: sheva is seven, and shava is to swear an oath; be'er is a well. Be'er-sheva is therefore Well of Seven and Well of the Oath at the same time, and v31 gives the oath explanation while vv28–30 give the seven. Both are in the text, and they do not compete.

  • v33 "a tamarisk" — eshel. He plants a tree in a land he does not own, at a well he had to prove he dug, having just sworn not to deal falsely with the people who took it.

  • v33 "God of Everlasting" — El Olam. Olam is not eternity as a philosophical category; it is the vanishing point — the farthest back and the farthest ahead that anyone can see. Another El title, like El Elyon from Melchizedek and El Shaddai in 17:1 and El Ro'i from Hagar. Four of them now, each given at a particular place by a particular person.

speech.text: Genesis 21
And the LORD attended to Sarah as He had said, and the LORD did for Sarah as He had spoken.
And Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the appointed time of which God had spoken to him.
And Abraham called the name of his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore to him, Isaac.
And Abraham circumcised Isaac his son at eight days old, as God had commanded him.
And Abraham was a hundred years old when Isaac his son was born to him.
And Sarah said, "Laughter God has made for me. Everyone who hears will laugh for me."
And she said, "Who would have spoken it to Abraham — Sarah has nursed sons? For I have borne a son in his old age."
The Sending Away
And the child grew and was weaned, and Abraham made a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned.
And Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham — laughing.
And she said to Abraham, "Drive out this slave woman and her son, for the son of this slave woman shall not inherit with my son, with Isaac."
And the thing was very evil in Abraham's eyes, on account of his son.
And God said to Abraham, "Let it not be evil in your eyes over the boy and over your slave woman. All that Sarah says to you — listen to her voice, for through Isaac shall seed be called for you.
And also the son of the slave woman I will make into a nation, for he is your seed."

And Abraham rose early in the morning and took bread and a skin of water, and gave them to Hagar — setting them on her shoulder — and the child, and he sent her away. And she went, and she wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.
And the water was finished from the skin, and she cast the child under one of the bushes.
And she went and sat down opposite him, far off, about a bowshot, for she said, "Let me not see the child die." And she sat opposite, and she lifted her voice and wept.

And God heard the voice of the boy, and the messenger of God called to Hagar from the heavens and said to her, "What is it with you, Hagar? Do not fear, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.
Rise, lift up the boy, and hold your hand strong on him, for I will make him into a great nation."
And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. And she went and filled the skin with water, and gave the boy drink.
And God was with the boy, and he grew, and he settled in the wilderness, and he became an archer.
And he settled in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.
The Well of the Oath
And it came to pass at that time that Abimelech, and Phicol the commander of his army, said to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do.

And now, swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me, nor with my offspring, nor with my posterity. According to the kindness I have done with you, you shall do with me, and with the land in which you have sojourned."
And Abraham said, "I will swear."
And Abraham reproved Abimelech over the matter of a well of water that Abimelech's servants had seized.
And Abimelech said, "I do not know who did this thing. And you also did not tell me, and I also have not heard of it until today."
And Abraham took flocks and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two of them cut a covenant.
And Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock by themselves.
And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What are these seven ewe lambs that you have set by themselves?"
And he said, "For you shall take the seven ewe lambs from my hand, so that it may be a witness for me that I dug this well."
Therefore that place was called Beersheba, for there the two of them swore.
And they cut a covenant at Beersheba. And Abimelech rose, and Phicol the commander of his army, and they returned to the land of the Philistines.
And he planted a tamarisk at Beersheba, and there he called on the name of the LORD, God of Everlasting.
And Abraham sojourned in the land of the Philistines many days.

chapters.title: The Binding
chapters.html:
Genesis 22

1And it came to pass after these things that God tested Abraham. And He said to him, "Abraham." And he said, "Here I am."

2And He said, "Take, please, your son — your only one — whom you have loved — Isaac. And go, for yourself, to the land of Moriah, and bring him up there as a going-up, upon one of the mountains that I will say to you."

3And Abraham rose early in the morning and saddled his donkey, and took his two young men with him, and Isaac his son. And he split the wood for the going-up, and he rose and went to the place that God had said to him.

4On the third day Abraham lifted his eyes and saw the place from far off.

5And Abraham said to his young men, "Sit yourselves here with the donkey, and I and the boy will go over there. And we will bow down, and we will return to you."

6And Abraham took the wood of the going-up and set it on Isaac his son, and he took in his hand the fire and the knife. And the two of them went together.

7And Isaac said to Abraham his father, and he said, "My father." And he said, "Here I am, my son." And he said, "Here is the fire and the wood — and where is the lamb for a going-up?"

8And Abraham said, "God will see to the lamb for a going-up for Himself, my son." And the two of them went together.

9And they came to the place that God had said to him, and Abraham built there the altar and arranged the wood. And he bound Isaac his son and set him on the altar, on top of the wood.

10And Abraham put out his hand and took the knife, to slaughter his son.

11And the messenger of the LORD called to him from the heavens and said, "Abraham! Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am."

12And He said, "Do not put out your hand toward the boy, and do not do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God, and you have not withheld your son, your only one, from Me."

13And Abraham lifted his eyes and saw — and here, a ram, behind, caught in the thicket by its horns. And Abraham went and took the ram and brought it up as a going-up in place of his son.

14And Abraham called the name of that place "The LORD Will See," of which it is said today, "On the mountain of the LORD it will be seen."

15And the messenger of the LORD called to Abraham a second time from the heavens,

16and said, "By Myself I have sworn — the utterance of the LORD — that because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only one,

17that blessing, I will bless you; and multiplying, I will multiply your seed as the stars of the heavens and as the sand that is on the lip of the sea. And your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies.

18And in your seed all the nations of the earth shall bless themselves — because you listened to My voice."

19And Abraham returned to his young men, and they rose and went together to Beersheba. And Abraham settled in Beersheba. ## News from Home

20And it came to pass after these things that it was told to Abraham, saying, "Here — Milcah has borne sons, she also, to Nahor your brother:

21Uz his firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel father of Aram,

22and Chesed and Hazo and Pildash and Jidlaph, and Bethuel."

23And Bethuel fathered Rebekah. These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother.

24And his concubine, whose name was Reumah — she also bore Tebah and Gaham and Tahash and Maacah.

Notes

  • v1 "Here I am" — hinneni, one word. It is said three times in this chapter and nowhere else in it: to God in v1, to Isaac in v7, to the messenger in v11. The same word to the one commanding, to the one being taken, and to the one who stops it. The chapter is built on those three.

  • v2 "Take, please, your son — your only one — whom you have loved — Isaac" — four phrases, each introduced by the object marker, and they narrow exactly as 12:1 narrowed: your land, your kindred, your father's house. Same technique, same speaker, same man. The tightening ends on the name.

  • v2 "And go, for yourself" — lekh lekha. These two words occur together only twice in the Hebrew Bible, and both times God says them to Abraham: here, and in 12:1. Both times he is sent to a place that is not named — the land that I will show you, one of the mountains that I will say to you. The call and the test are written as the same sentence.

  • v2 "whom you have loved" — ahavta. This is the first occurrence of the word love in the Bible. Not between man and woman, not between God and anyone: it appears for the first time in the sentence commanding a father to give up the son he loves.

  • v2 "a going-up" — olah, the burnt offering, named for the smoke that rises (see 8:20). The verb in the same verse, ha'alehu, is bring him up. He is told to bring his son up as a bringing-up, on a mountain — three motions upward in one command.

  • v3 "And he split the wood" — he does this before setting out, at home, in the dark, for a fire three days away. Nothing required it then. The verse lists the saddling, the men, the son, and the wood in one breath and does not pause on any of them.

  • v4 "on the third day" — the text gives no word for those three days. Whatever was said on the road is not recorded.

  • v5 "we will bow down, and we will return to you" — both verbs are first person plural. He tells the servants that two will come back.

  • vv6, 8 "And the two of them went together" — va-yelekhu shneihem yachdav, identical, twice, framing the only conversation between father and son in the Bible. It is said once before the question and once after the answer, and the second time it means something different.

  • v7 "Here is the fire and the wood — and where is the lamb?" — Isaac carries the wood; his father carries the fire and the knife, the two things that could hurt him. The boy counts what is present and names what is missing.

  • v8 "God will see to the lamb" — Elohim yir'eh lo ha-seh. The verb is ra'ah, to see. Hebrew says see to it where English says provide, and this chapter runs on that verb: Abraham saw the place from far off (v4), God will see the lamb (v8), Abraham lifted his eyes and saw the ram (v13), and the place is named for it twice in v14. The word for the whole chapter's mercy is an eye.

  • v9 "And he bound" — va-ya'aqod. This verb, in this sense, occurs once in the entire Hebrew Bible. The same three letters appear elsewhere, but as an adjective for streaked animals (30:35–31:12) and in a place name (2 Kings 10:12). The act has no other name. This is why Jewish tradition calls the chapter the Akedah, the Binding — the whole episode is known by the one word that exists only inside it.

  • v12 "you have not withheld" — lo chasakhta. Two chapters back, God said to Abimelech I also held you back from sinning against Me — va-echsokh, the same verb. God withheld a pagan king from a sin; Abraham did not withhold his son.

  • v13 "a ram, behind" — ayil achar, and the second word is a problem. Achar means behind or after; some readers take it as echad, one, differing by a single letter. As it stands the ram is behind — which is why Abraham has to lift his eyes and turn.

  • v14 "The LORD Will See… it will be seen" — YHWH yir'eh, then be-har YHWH yera'eh. The same verb, active and then passive. He names the place the LORD sees; the saying that survives is on the mountain, He is seen. One letter separates being the one who looks from being the one who is looked at.

  • v16 "By Myself I have sworn" — the only time God swears by Himself to Abraham. In 15:17 He passed alone between the pieces; here there is nothing left to swear by that is not Himself.

  • v17 "as the stars… and as the sand" — the promise has been made three times with three images: dust of the earth (13:16), stars of the heavens (15:5), and now both stars and sand together. Each time it is given after Abraham has let something go.

  • v19 "And Abraham returned to his young men" — Abraham returns. Isaac is not mentioned. Two went up together, twice; one is named coming down. The text does not say Isaac stayed, and it does not say he came. It simply stops counting him, and the next time he appears is in 24:62, arriving from the well called Lahai-roi — Hagar's well.

  • vv20–24 twelve sons, and Abraham has one — the knife comes down off Isaac, Abraham walks back to Beersheba, and the very next sentence is news from home: his brother Nahor has eight sons by his wife and four more by a concubine. The list is dropped in without comment, immediately after a chapter in which Abraham nearly lost the only son he has. Twelve is also the number Jacob's household will end up with, three generations later, and it is Nahor's line that gets there first.

  • v23 "And Bethuel fathered Rebekah" — the point of the whole list, and the only woman named in it. She arrives here, in a genealogy, two chapters before Abraham's servant is sent north to find a wife for Isaac and finds her at a well. The reader is given her before the servant is.

  • vv21–22 Uz and Chesed — two of these names go somewhere. Uts is the land Job lives in: a man was in the land of Uz, Job his name (Job 1:1). And Kesed is the singular behind Kasdim, the Chaldeans — the people of Ur of the Chaldees, where this family started and where Haran died (11:28). The genealogy quietly ties Abraham's relatives to the country he left and to the one book of the Bible set outside Israel altogether.

chapters.title: A Holding for a Grave
chapters.html:
Genesis 23

1And the lives of Sarah were a hundred years and twenty years and seven years — the years of the lives of Sarah.

2And Sarah died in Kiriath-arba — that is Hebron — in the land of Canaan. And Abraham came to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.

3And Abraham rose from before the face of his dead, and he spoke to the sons of Heth, saying,

4"A sojourner and a settler I am with you. Give me a holding for a grave with you, and let me bury my dead from before my face."

5And the sons of Heth answered Abraham, saying to him,

6"Hear us, my lord. A prince of God you are among us. In the choicest of our graves, bury your dead. No man among us will withhold his grave from you, from burying your dead."

7And Abraham rose and bowed to the people of the land, to the sons of Heth.

8And he spoke with them, saying, "If it is with your soul to bury my dead from before my face, hear me, and press for me with Ephron son of Zohar,

9and let him give me the cave of Machpelah that is his, which is at the end of his field. For full silver let him give it to me, in your midst, as a holding for a grave."

10And Ephron was sitting among the sons of Heth. And Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the ears of the sons of Heth, before all who came in at the gate of his city, saying,

11"No, my lord — hear me. The field I have given to you, and the cave that is in it, to you I have given it. Before the eyes of the sons of my people I have given it to you. Bury your dead."

12And Abraham bowed before the people of the land.

13And he spoke to Ephron in the ears of the people of the land, saying, "Only — if you would only hear me. I have given the silver of the field. Take it from me, and let me bury my dead there."

14And Ephron answered Abraham, saying to him,

15"My lord, hear me. Land of four hundred shekels of silver — between me and you, what is that? So bury your dead."

16And Abraham heard Ephron, and Abraham weighed out to Ephron the silver that he had spoken of in the ears of the sons of Heth: four hundred shekels of silver, passing to the merchant.

17And the field of Ephron that is in Machpelah, which faces Mamre — the field and the cave that is in it, and every tree that is in the field, that is in all its border round about —

18was raised up to Abraham as a purchase, before the eyes of the sons of Heth, before all who came in at the gate of his city.

19And after that, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah, facing Mamre — that is Hebron — in the land of Canaan.

20And the field was raised up, and the cave that is in it, to Abraham, as a holding for a grave, from the sons of Heth.

Notes

  • v1 "the lives of Sarah… the years of the lives of Sarah" — chayyei Sarah, the plural of life, twice, opening and closing the verse. Hebrew habitually speaks of a lifespan in the plural, and the verse spends its whole length saying her age and then naming her again. She is the only woman in the Hebrew Bible whose age at death is recorded.

  • v2 "to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her" — lispod is formal, public lament, the wailing of a funeral; livkot is simply to cry. The verse gives him both, in that order, and the next verse has him rising and getting to work.

  • v4 "A sojourner and a settler I am with you" — ger ve-toshav. Two words that sit awkwardly together: a ger is a resident foreigner with no land rights, a toshav is a dweller. Abraham has been promised this entire country four times by now, and he opens negotiations by stating that he owns none of it.

  • v4, 9, 20 "a holding" — achuzzah, from a root meaning to grasp or seize — a possession you have hold of. It is the same word used in 17:8, where God promised him all the land of Canaan as an everlasting achuzzah. The only achuzzah he ever gets is a grave, and he pays cash for it.

  • v6 "A prince of God you are among us" — nesi Elohim attah be-tokhenu. High courtesy, and possibly more: nasi is a chieftain, and the phrase could be read as a mighty prince, Hebrew sometimes using Elohim as an intensifier. They honor him and then sell him a field at a stiff price.

  • vv6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 16 "hear me" — shema'eni and its variants run through the chapter six times, and the negotiation is conducted entirely in the language of courtesy. Every party bows, every party defers, and nobody says a direct thing until v15.

  • v11 "The field I have given to you" — Abraham asked for the cave at the end of the field (v9). Ephron offers the field — with the cave thrown in. This is not generosity; it is how you turn a sale of a burial plot into a sale of real estate, and it is why the price lands where it does. Abraham's next words go straight past the gift and name the silver.

  • v15 "between me and you, what is that?" — the whole transaction in one sentence. He names a price, calls it nothing, and does not lower it. Four hundred shekels is a great deal of silver; when Jeremiah buys a field it costs seventeen.

  • v16 "passing to the merchant" — over la-socher, silver at the standard current among traders — weighed, not counted, because coinage does not yet exist. He pays in public, by weight, at merchant standard, in front of witnesses at the city gate. Nothing about this can later be disputed.

  • vv17, 20 "was raised up" — va-yaqom, the verb for standing or rising, used here in the legal sense of a transfer being made to stand — confirmed, established. The same verb that describes Abraham rising from beside his dead in v3 is used of the deed.

  • vv17–18 — the boundary description is a legal one: the field, the cave, every tree, all its border round about, before the eyes of the sons of Heth, before all who came in at the gate. It reads like a contract because it is one, and the narrator slows down to record every clause.

  • The shape of the chapter — Abraham spends twenty verses and four hundred shekels acquiring a grave. It is the only piece of the promised land he ever owns, the promise is not mentioned once, and the chapter ends with the word Heth. Everything he was told he would be given, he buys, from the people who already live there.

chapters.title: The Servant at the Well
chapters.html:
Genesis 24

1And Abraham was old, coming on in days, and the LORD had blessed Abraham in everything.

2And Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his house, the one ruling over all that was his, "Put, please, your hand under my thigh.

3And I will make you swear by the LORD, God of the heavens and God of the earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanite, among whom I am dwelling.

4But to my land and to my kindred you shall go, and take a wife for my son, for Isaac."

5And the servant said to him, "Perhaps the woman will not be willing to go after me to this land. Shall I bring your son back, bringing him back to the land you came out from?"

6And Abraham said to him, "Guard yourself — do not bring my son back there.

7The LORD, God of the heavens, who took me from my father's house and from the land of my kindred, and who spoke to me and who swore to me, saying, 'To your seed I will give this land' — He will send His messenger before you, and you shall take a wife for my son from there.

8And if the woman is not willing to go after you, then you are clear from this oath of mine. Only do not bring my son back there."

9And the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master, and swore to him concerning this matter.

The Sign

10And the servant took ten camels from his master's camels and went, and all his master's good things in his hand. And he rose and went to Aram-naharaim, to the city of Nahor.

11And he made the camels kneel outside the city, by the well of water, at evening time, at the time the water-drawers go out.

12And he said, "LORD, God of my master Abraham — let it happen, please, before me today, and do kindness with my master Abraham.

13Here I am, standing by the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water.

14Let it be that the girl to whom I say, 'Tip, please, your jar, and let me drink,' and she says, 'Drink — and your camels also I will water' — her You have appointed for Your servant, for Isaac. And by her I shall know that You have done kindness with my master."

15And it came to pass, before he had finished speaking, that here — Rebekah was coming out, who was born to Bethuel son of Milcah, wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother — and her jar on her shoulder.

16And the girl was very good to look at, a virgin, and no man had known her. And she went down to the spring and filled her jar and came up.

17And the servant ran to meet her and said, "Let me sip, please, a little water from your jar."

18And she said, "Drink, my lord." And she hurried and lowered her jar onto her hand and gave him drink.

19And she finished giving him drink, and she said, "For your camels also I will draw, until they have finished drinking."

20And she hurried and emptied her jar into the trough, and ran again to the well to draw, and drew for all his camels.

21And the man was gazing at her, silent, to know whether the LORD had made his way succeed or not.

22And it came to pass, when the camels had finished drinking, that the man took a gold ring, a beka in weight, and two bracelets for her hands, ten of gold in weight,

23and said, "Whose daughter are you? Tell me, please. Is there room in your father's house for us to spend the night?"

24And she said to him, "I am the daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor."

25And she said to him, "There is both straw and much fodder with us, and also room to spend the night."

26And the man bowed low and bowed down to the LORD.

27And he said, "Blessed be the LORD, God of my master Abraham, who has not forsaken His kindness and His truth from my master. I — on the way the LORD has led me — to the house of my master's brothers."

Laban

28And the girl ran and told her mother's household these things.

29And Rebekah had a brother, and his name was Laban. And Laban ran out to the man, to the spring.

30And it came to pass, when he saw the ring and the bracelets on his sister's hands, and when he heard the words of Rebekah his sister, saying, "Thus the man spoke to me" — that he came to the man, and here he was, standing by the camels at the spring.

31And he said, "Come, blessed of the LORD. Why do you stand outside? And I have cleared the house, and a place for the camels."

32And the man came to the house, and he unharnessed the camels, and gave straw and fodder to the camels, and water to wash his feet and the feet of the men who were with him.

33And food was set before him to eat. And he said, "I will not eat until I have spoken my words." And he said, "Speak."

34And he said, "I am Abraham's servant.

35And the LORD has blessed my master greatly, and he has become great. And He has given him flocks and cattle, and silver and gold, and male servants and female servants, and camels and donkeys.

36And Sarah, my master's wife, bore a son to my master after her old age, and he has given him all that is his.

37And my master made me swear, saying, 'You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanite, in whose land I am dwelling.

38But to my father's house you shall go, and to my family, and take a wife for my son.'

39And I said to my master, 'Perhaps the woman will not go after me.'

40And he said to me, 'The LORD, before whom I have walked about, will send His messenger with you and make your way succeed. And you shall take a wife for my son from my family and from my father's house.

41Then you will be clear from my oath, when you come to my family. And if they do not give her to you, then you are clear from my oath.'

42And I came today to the spring, and I said, 'LORD, God of my master Abraham — if now You are making my way succeed, the way on which I am going:

43here I am, standing by the spring of water. Let it be that the young woman who comes out to draw, and I say to her, Give me a little water to drink, please, from your jar —

44and she says to me, You drink, and for your camels also I will draw — she is the woman the LORD has appointed for my master's son.'

45I had not yet finished speaking to my heart, and here — Rebekah was coming out, with her jar on her shoulder. And she went down to the spring and drew, and I said to her, 'Give me drink, please.'

46And she hurried and lowered her jar from upon her, and said, 'Drink — and your camels also I will water.' And I drank, and she watered the camels also.

47And I asked her and said, 'Whose daughter are you?' And she said, 'The daughter of Bethuel son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.' And I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her hands.

48And I bowed low and bowed down to the LORD, and I blessed the LORD, God of my master Abraham, who led me in a true way to take the daughter of my master's brother for his son.

49And now, if you are doing kindness and truth with my master, tell me. And if not, tell me, and I will turn to the right or to the left."

50And Laban and Bethuel answered and said, "The matter has come out from the LORD. We cannot speak to you evil or good.

51Here is Rebekah before you. Take her and go, and let her be a wife for your master's son, as the LORD has spoken."

52And it came to pass, when Abraham's servant heard their words, that he bowed to the ground to the LORD.

53And the servant brought out objects of silver and objects of gold, and garments, and gave them to Rebekah. And he gave precious things to her brother and to her mother.

54And they ate and drank, he and the men who were with him, and they spent the night. And they rose in the morning, and he said, "Send me off to my master."

55And her brother and her mother said, "Let the girl stay with us days, or ten. After that she may go."

56And he said to them, "Do not delay me, and the LORD has made my way succeed. Send me off, and let me go to my master."

57And they said, "Let us call the girl and ask her mouth."

58And they called Rebekah and said to her, "Will you go with this man?" And she said, "I will go."

59And they sent off Rebekah their sister, and her nurse, and Abraham's servant, and his men.

60And they blessed Rebekah and said to her,
"Our sister, may you become thousands of ten thousands,
and may your seed possess the gate of those who hate him."

61And Rebekah rose, and her young women, and they rode on the camels and went after the man. And the servant took Rebekah and went.

The Field at Evening

62And Isaac had come from coming to Beer-lahai-roi, and he was dwelling in the land of the Negev.

63And Isaac went out to walk in the field toward evening. And he lifted his eyes and saw — and here, camels coming.

64And Rebekah lifted her eyes and saw Isaac, and she fell from upon the camel.

65And she said to the servant, "Who is that man, walking in the field to meet us?" And the servant said, "He is my master." And she took the veil and covered herself.

66And the servant recounted to Isaac all the things he had done.

67And Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother, and he took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. And Isaac was comforted after his mother.

Notes

  • The servant has no name. Sixty-seven verses, the longest chapter in Genesis, and the man at the center of it is called ha-eved, the servant, throughout. He is the most reliable character in the book so far and the text never says who he is.

  • v2 "under my thigh" — tachat yerekhi. The yarekh is the upper thigh and loin, and Hebrew uses it as the place offspring come from — "those who came out of his yarekh." An oath about a man's descendants is sworn with a hand on the part of the body they come from. English "thigh" preserves the word and loses the reason.

  • v7 "He will send His messenger before you" — Abraham says this. The messenger is never mentioned again, never appears, and is never credited. Whatever happens at the well happens through a young woman's ordinary decency.

  • v12 "let it happen, please, before me" — haqreh na, from qarah, to happen, to befall, to chance upon. He is asking God to arrange a coincidence, and the word he uses is the word for accident.

  • vv12, 14, 27, 49 "kindness" — chesed, four times. There is no good English word: it is loyalty inside a relationship, the thing you do because of who you are to someone, not because you are obliged. Not mercy, not love, not kindness quite. In v27 and v49 it is paired with emet, truth or faithfulness, and the pair means something like steady, reliable good faith.

  • v14 "your camels also I will water" — the servant's test. It is worth understanding what he is asking for. Ten camels, at the end of a long desert journey, drink an enormous quantity of water, and it comes up a jar at a time, by hand, from a well a woman has to walk down into and back up out of. The sign he chooses is not a word or a gesture. It is hours of heavy labor, offered freely by someone who has no reason to.

  • vv18–20 "she hurried… she hurried… ran" — three verbs of speed in three verses, matching Abraham's four in 18:6–7 when he fed the three men. Hospitality in this book is measured in how fast someone moves.

  • v21 "gazing at her, silent" — mishta'eh… macharish. The first word is rare and means staring in astonishment; the second is the ordinary word for keeping quiet. He watches her do it and says nothing until the last camel finishes.

  • v22 "a gold ring… two bracelets" — he gives the jewelry before he asks who she is. He has decided.

  • vv30, 31 "when he saw the ring and the bracelets… Come, blessed of the LORD" — the narrator puts Laban's running and Laban's piety in that order, after the gold. Nothing is said about it. This is the reader's first look at a man Jacob will spend twenty years working for.

  • v33 "And food was set before him" — the Masoretes record two forms here: the text as written, and the text as it is to be read. The written consonants and the pronounced word differ, and the scribes preserved both rather than choosing. It is a small thing about eating, and they kept the discrepancy anyway.

  • vv34–49 — the servant retells the whole story, at length, to the family. Hebrew narrative rarely repeats itself like this, and the repetition is not identical: in v45 he says I had not yet finished speaking to my heart, which tells the reader that his prayer in v12 was silent. He also drops the detail that he gave the jewelry before asking her name, and reverses the order so that it comes after.

  • vv50–51 "And Laban and Bethuel answered" — the brother is named before the father, and the father says nothing afterward. In v55 it is again her brother and her mother who negotiate. Whatever the household arrangement is, the text shows it rather than explaining it.

  • vv57–58 "Let us call the girl and ask her mouth" — ve-nishalah et piha. After sixty verses of men swearing oaths and arranging a marriage, someone asks her. And her answer is one word in Hebrew — elekh, I will go — which is the same verb Abram was given in 12:1, lekh lekha. She does what he did, without being told to, and nobody has promised her anything.

  • v60 "may your seed possess the gate of those who hate him" — her family's blessing is nearly word for word God's oath to Abraham in 22:17, your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies. They have never heard that oath. The same promise arrives twice from opposite directions.

  • v62 "from coming to Beer-lahai-roi" — Isaac's first appearance since the mountain in chapter 22, and he is arriving from Hagar's well — the place she named the Living One who sees me in 16:14. The text does not say why he was there.

  • v63 "to walk in the field" — lasuach, a verb that occurs only here in this form, and its meaning is not established. To meditate, to complain, to wander, to talk to oneself. Something a man does alone in a field at dusk, and Hebrew has one word for it that it never uses again.

  • v64 "she fell from upon the camel" — va-tippol, the plain verb for falling. Most English versions print "alighted" or "dismounted." The Hebrew says she fell.

  • v67 "and he loved her" — va-ye'ehaveha. This is the second occurrence of love in the Bible. The first was 22:2, the son Abraham loved, on the way to the mountain. The word appears in this book first as what is asked for and then as what is found.

  • v67 "And Isaac was comforted after his mother" — va-yinnachem, from nacham, the root of Noah's name and of God's relenting in 6:6. The chapter that begins with an old man arranging his succession ends with his son being consoled for a death the reader was told about a chapter ago and that Isaac was never shown being told.

chapters.title: Gathered to His People, and Two Nations
chapters.html:
Genesis 25

1And Abraham went on and took a wife, and her name was Keturah.

2And she bore him Zimran and Jokshan and Medan and Midian and Ishbak and Shuah.

3And Jokshan fathered Sheba and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were Asshurim and Letushim and Leummim.

4And the sons of Midian: Ephah and Epher and Hanoch and Abida and Eldaah. All these were the sons of Keturah.

5And Abraham gave all that was his to Isaac.

6And to the sons of the concubines that Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and he sent them away from Isaac his son, while he was still alive, eastward, to the land of the east.

7And these are the days of the years of Abraham's life that he lived: a hundred years and seventy years and five years.

8And Abraham expired and died at a good gray age, old and satisfied, and he was gathered to his people.

9And Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, which faces Mamre,

10the field that Abraham bought from the sons of Heth. There Abraham was buried, and Sarah his wife.

11And it came to pass after Abraham's death that God blessed Isaac his son. And Isaac settled by Beer-lahai-roi.

The Begettings of Ishmael

12And these are the begettings of Ishmael son of Abraham, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's servant girl, bore to Abraham.

13And these are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, by their begettings: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth; and Kedar and Adbeel and Mibsam,

14and Mishma and Dumah and Massa,

15Hadad and Tema, Jetur, Naphish and Kedemah.

16These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their villages and by their encampments — twelve chieftains by their peoples.

17And these are the years of Ishmael's life: a hundred years and thirty years and seven years. And he expired and died, and was gathered to his people.

18And they settled from Havilah as far as Shur, which faces Egypt, as you come toward Asshur. In the face of all his brothers he fell.

The Begettings of Isaac

19And these are the begettings of Isaac son of Abraham. Abraham fathered Isaac.

20And Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram, sister of Laban the Aramean, for himself as a wife.

21And Isaac pleaded with the LORD opposite his wife, for she was barren. And the LORD let Himself be pleaded with, and Rebekah his wife conceived.

22And the sons crushed each other inside her, and she said, "If so, why am I this?" And she went to inquire of the LORD.

23And the LORD said to her,
"Two nations are in your belly,
and two peoples from your inward parts shall be separated.
And people shall be stronger than people,
and the great shall serve the small."

24And her days were filled to give birth, and here — twins in her belly.

25And the first came out ruddy, all of him like a hairy mantle, and they called his name Esau.

26And after that his brother came out, and his hand holding the heel of Esau, and he called his name Jacob. And Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.

27And the boys grew, and Esau was a man who knew hunting, a man of the field; and Jacob was a whole man, dwelling in tents.

28And Isaac loved Esau, because hunted game was in his mouth. And Rebekah loves Jacob.

The Red Stuff

29And Jacob boiled a boiling, and Esau came in from the field, and he was weary.

30And Esau said to Jacob, "Let me gulp, please, some of the red — this red stuff — for I am weary." Therefore his name was called Edom.

31And Jacob said, "Sell me, as of today, your birthright."

32And Esau said, "Here I am, going to die. And what is this to me, a birthright?"

33And Jacob said, "Swear to me as of today." And he swore to him, and he sold his birthright to Jacob.

34And Jacob gave Esau bread and a boiling of lentils, and he ate and drank and rose and went. And Esau despised the birthright.

Notes

  • v6 "eastward, to the land of the east" — the direction of leaving in this book, as at 3:24, 4:16, 11:2 and 13:11. Every son who is not the chosen one goes east, and the text says it plainly each time.

  • v8 "old and satisfied" — zaqen ve-savea, the word for having eaten enough. He dies full. It is not a stock phrase; only a handful of people in the Hebrew Bible get it.

  • v8 "gathered to his people" — va-ye'asef el ammav, an idiom distinct from both dying and being buried — the verse names all three separately, in order. Whatever it pictures, it is not the cave, since his people are not in it.

  • v9 "Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him" — the last time these two were in the same sentence, one was being sent into the wilderness with a waterskin because of the other. They meet again at their father's grave, in that order, and nothing is said about the years between.

  • v11 "Isaac settled by Beer-lahai-roi" — Hagar's well again (16:14), where Isaac was also coming from in 24:62. The son who stayed lives at the place named by the woman who was driven out.

  • v17 "and was gathered to his people" — Ishmael gets the same formula as Abraham, and his twelve sons are called nesi'im, chieftains, exactly as God promised in 17:20. The blessing given to the son who was sent away is recorded as kept.

  • v18 "In the face of all his brothers he fell" — al penei kol echav naphal. The same phrase was used of him before he was born, in 16:12, where it was he shall dwell. Here the verb is naphal, fell — which can mean to settle, to encamp, or to fall upon. The Hebrew closes his story with the same words it opened it with, and one of them has changed.

  • v21 "pleaded… let Himself be pleaded with" — va-ye'tar… va-ye'ater, the same rare verb, active then passive, in one verse. Isaac entreats and God is entreated. And the whole of Isaac's twenty childless years is in that single verse; his wife is barren like his mother, and the text spends nine words on it.

  • v22 "the sons crushed each other inside her" — va-yitrotsatsu, a violent reciprocal verb from a root meaning to crush or smash. Not "struggled." And her response — im ken lamah zeh anokhi — is broken Hebrew: if so, why this I? Something like if it is like this, why am I? Translations complete the sentence for her. The Hebrew does not.

  • v23 "the great shall serve the small" — ve-rav ya'avod tsa'ir. The line has no preposition and no object marker, which in Hebrew poetry means the word order alone decides who serves whom — and word order in poetry is flexible. It can be read the elder shall serve the younger or, with equal grammar, the younger shall serve the elder. The oracle that governs the rest of Genesis is, strictly, reversible.

  • v25 "ruddy… like a hairy mantle" — admoni and se'ar. The first chimes with Edom, red, which v30 will make explicit; the second chimes with Se'ir, the country Esau settles. His body is a map of the nations he will father.

  • v26 "holding the heel… Jacob" — aqev, heel, and Ya'aqov. The name is the heel made into a verb: heel-grabber, and by extension one who supplants or trips. It is a name given by what he was doing when he arrived, and he spends the rest of the book doing it.

  • v27 "a whole man" — ish tam. This is the word used of Noah in 6:9 and commanded to Abraham in 17:1: be whole, unblemished, sound, entire. English prints "quiet," "plain," "mild," none of which is what the word means anywhere else. The book calls the deceiver by the same adjective it uses for the man who walked with God, and does not explain itself.

  • v28 "And Rebekah loves Jacob" — the verbs change tense. Isaac loved Esau — a completed statement with a reason attached, and the reason is food. Rebekah loves Jacob, participle, ongoing, no reason given. Two kinds of love in one verse, and the Hebrew marks the difference by grammar alone.

  • v29 "boiled a boiling" — va-yazed nazid, verb and its own noun, the construction from 11:3. Deliberately flat: he cooked a cooked-thing.

  • v30 "Let me gulp, please, some of the red — this red stuff" — hal'iteni na min ha-adom ha-adom ha-zeh. Hal'it is a coarse verb used of stuffing food into an animal, and it occurs only here. He does not name the food. He says the red, the red, twice, because he is too spent to find the word for lentils, and the narrator turns his grunt into the name of a nation.

  • v34 "he ate and drank and rose and went" — four verbs, no objects, no pause. Then one more clause: and Esau despised the birthright. It is the only judgment the narrator passes in the chapter, and it falls on him rather than on the brother who asked for an oath before handing over soup.
