And these are the days of the years of Abraham's life that he lived: a hundred years and seventy years and five years.
And Abraham expired and died at a good gray age, old and satisfied, and he was gathered to his people.
And Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, which faces Mamre,
the field that Abraham bought from the sons of Heth. There Abraham was buried, and Sarah his wife.
And it came to pass after Abraham's death that God blessed Isaac his son. And Isaac settled by Beer-lahai-roi.
The Begettings of Ishmael
And these are the begettings of Ishmael son of Abraham, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's servant girl, bore to Abraham.
And these are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, by their begettings: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth; and Kedar and Adbeel and Mibsam,
and Mishma and Dumah and Massa,
Hadad and Tema, Jetur, Naphish and Kedemah.
These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their villages and by their encampments — twelve chieftains by their peoples.
And these are the years of Ishmael's life: a hundred years and thirty years and seven years. And he expired and died, and was gathered to his people.
And they settled from Havilah as far as Shur, which faces Egypt, as you come toward Asshur. In the face of all his brothers he fell.
The Begettings of Isaac
And these are the begettings of Isaac son of Abraham. Abraham fathered Isaac.
And Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram, sister of Laban the Aramean, for himself as a wife.
And Isaac pleaded with the LORD opposite his wife, for she was barren. And the LORD let Himself be pleaded with, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
And the sons crushed each other inside her, and she said, "If so, why am I this?" And she went to inquire of the LORD.
And the LORD said to her, "Two nations are in your belly, and two peoples from your inward parts shall be separated. And people shall be stronger than people, and the great shall serve the small."
And her days were filled to give birth, and here — twins in her belly.
And the first came out ruddy, all of him like a hairy mantle, and they called his name Esau.
And after that his brother came out, and his hand holding the heel of Esau, and he called his name Jacob. And Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.
And the boys grew, and Esau was a man who knew hunting, a man of the field; and Jacob was a whole man, dwelling in tents.
And Isaac loved Esau, because hunted game was in his mouth. And Rebekah loves Jacob.
The Red Stuff
And Jacob boiled a boiling, and Esau came in from the field, and he was weary.
And Esau said to Jacob, "Let me gulp, please, some of the red — this red stuff — for I am weary." Therefore his name was called Edom.
And Jacob said, "Sell me, as of today, your birthright."
And Esau said, "Here I am, going to die. And what is this to me, a birthright?"
And Jacob said, "Swear to me as of today." And he swore to him, and he sold his birthright to Jacob.
And Jacob gave Esau bread and a boiling of lentils, and he ate and drank and rose and went. And Esau despised the birthright.

chapters.title: Isaac Digs His Father's Wells Again
chapters.html:
Genesis 26

1And there was a famine in the land, besides the first famine that was in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines, to Gerar.

2And the LORD appeared to him and said, "Do not go down to Egypt. Dwell in the land that I will say to you.

3Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and bless you. For to you and to your seed I will give all these lands, and I will raise up the oath that I swore to Abraham your father.

4And I will multiply your seed as the stars of the heavens, and I will give to your seed all these lands. And in your seed all the nations of the earth shall bless themselves —

5because Abraham listened to My voice, and kept My charge: My commands, My statutes, and My instructions."

6And Isaac settled in Gerar.

7And the men of the place asked about his wife, and he said, "She is my sister" — for he was afraid to say "my wife" — the men of the place might kill me over Rebekah, for she was good to look at.

8And it came to pass, when his days there had grown long, that Abimelech king of the Philistines looked down through the window, and saw — and here was Isaac laughing with Rebekah his wife.

9And Abimelech called Isaac and said, "So — here, she is your wife! And how did you say, 'She is my sister'?" And Isaac said to him, "Because I said to myself, I might die over her."

10And Abimelech said, "What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us."

11And Abimelech charged all the people, saying, "Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death."

The Wells

12And Isaac sowed in that land, and found in that year a hundredfold. And the LORD blessed him.

13And the man became great, and went on going and growing great, until he was very great.

14And he had livestock of flocks and livestock of cattle, and a great household of servants. And the Philistines envied him.

15And all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines stopped up, and filled them with dust.

16And Abimelech said to Isaac, "Go from us, for you have become much mightier than we."

17And Isaac went from there and camped in the wadi of Gerar, and settled there.

18And Isaac went back and dug out the wells of water that they had dug in the days of Abraham his father, and the Philistines had stopped them up after Abraham's death. And he called them by the names his father had called them.

19And Isaac's servants dug in the wadi, and found there a well of living water.

20And the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen, saying, "The water is ours." And he called the name of the well Esek, for they had contended with him.

21And they dug another well, and they quarreled over that one too, and he called its name Sitnah.

22And he moved on from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it, and he called its name Rehoboth, and said, "For now the LORD has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land."

23And he went up from there to Beersheba.

24And the LORD appeared to him that night and said, "I am the God of Abraham your father. Do not fear, for I am with you, and I will bless you and multiply your seed, for the sake of Abraham My servant."

25And he built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD, and pitched his tent there. And Isaac's servants dug a well there.

26And Abimelech went to him from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his companion and Phicol the commander of his army.

27And Isaac said to them, "Why have you come to me, and you hated me and sent me away from you?"

28And they said, "We have seen, seeing, that the LORD has been with you, and we said: let there be an oath between us — between us and you — and let us cut a covenant with you,

29that you will not do evil with us, just as we have not touched you, and just as we have done with you only good, and sent you away in peace. You now are blessed of the LORD."

30And he made them a feast, and they ate and drank.

31And they rose early in the morning and swore, each to his brother. And Isaac sent them off, and they went from him in peace.

32And it came to pass on that same day that Isaac's servants came and told him about the well they had dug, and said to him, "We have found water."

33And he called it Shibah. Therefore the name of the city is Beersheba to this day.

34And Esau was forty years old, and he took as wives Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite.

35And they were a bitterness of spirit to Isaac and to Rebekah.

Notes

  • v1 "besides the first famine" — the narrator says it outright: this has happened before. Genesis 12:10 sent Abraham down to Egypt in a famine, where he passed his wife off as his sister and was paid to leave. Isaac is about to do all of it again, and the text tells you so in the first verse.

  • v2 "Do not go down to Egypt" — the one thing his father did. Isaac is the only patriarch never to leave Canaan, and this is why.

  • v5 "My charge: My commands, My statutes, and My instructions" — mishmarti, mitsvotai, chuqqotai, ve-torotai. Four terms of legal vocabulary, and they belong to the law given at Sinai, centuries after Abraham. The verse says Abraham kept them. That is not an oversight; it is the narrator describing Abraham in the language of the covenant his descendants will receive. And torotai is the plural of torah, which here simply means instructions.

  • v8 "Isaac laughing with Rebekah his wife" — Yitschaq metsacheq. The man's name is the verb: he laughs, laughing. And this is the same participle as 21:9, where Sarah saw Ishmael metsacheq and demanded he be driven out — the word whose meaning the whole Hagar episode turns on, and which no translation admits is undecidable.

    Here the context decides it. Whatever Isaac is doing to Rebekah through that window, a king sees it and concludes instantly that they are married, not siblings. In this verse the word plainly means something between a husband and a wife. That is evidence about 21:9 which the text itself supplies, five chapters later, using the same form — and it is why "mocking" there is a choice and not a translation.

  • v10 "might easily have lain with your wife" — shakhav, the lying-down verb, in the mouth of a foreign king describing what nearly happened. Two verses after the knowing-word appeared as a pun on Isaac's name, the other verb arrives for the act stripped of any bond. The book keeps them apart even here.

  • v13 "went on going and growing great" — va-yelekh halokh ve-gadel, the doubled infinitive Hebrew uses for a process that will not stop, the same construction as the waters going and returning in 8:3. Three forms of gadol in one verse.

  • v15, 18 "stopped up… filled them with dust" — aphar, the dust the human was made from and returns to. Filling a well with it is the most complete insult available: you do not take the water, you make the place forget it was ever water.

  • v18 "he called them by the names his father had called them" — the whole chapter in one clause. Isaac does nothing new. He re-digs his father's wells, restores his father's names, receives his father's promise, repeats his father's lie to his father's Abimelech, and makes a treaty at his father's Beersheba. He is the only patriarch whose story is mostly someone else's story, told again.

  • vv20–22 "Esek… Sitnah… Rehoboth" — three wells, three names, and each is the argument it came from. Esek is contention, from the verb in the same verse, hit'assequ, they contended. Sitnah is hostility, from a root meaning to oppose or accuse — the root behind the word satan, which in Hebrew is a common noun for an adversary. Rehoboth is wide places, from rachav, broad — and Isaac explains it himself: the LORD has made room, hirchiv. Three names, three verbs, each planted in its own verse.

  • v28 "We have seen, seeing" — ra'o ra'inu, the doubled verb for emphasis. They are conceding something.

  • v29 "just as we have not touched you" — Abimelech's men had stopped his wells (v15) and driven him out (v16). The treaty is written as though none of that happened, and Isaac signs it and throws them a feast.

  • v33 "Shibah… Beersheba" — Shiv'ah is seven; shava is to swear. In 21:31 Abraham named this same place from the same pun, after a treaty with a man called Abimelech and a commander called Phicol. It is named twice, by father and son, for the same reason.

  • vv34–35 "a bitterness of spirit" — morat ruach, literally a bitterness of breath or spirit. The chapter of Isaac quietly repeating his father ends with his son marrying outside the family, which is the one thing Abraham sent a servant a thousand miles to prevent. The next chapter is the stolen blessing.

chapters.title: The Voice Is Jacob's, the Hands Are Esau's
chapters.html:
Genesis 27

1And it came to pass, when Isaac was old and his eyes were too dim to see, that he called Esau his elder son and said to him, "My son." And he said to him, "Here I am."

2And he said, "Look now — I am old. I do not know the day of my death.

3And now take up, please, your gear — your quiver and your bow — and go out to the field, and hunt me game.

4And make me savory food, such as I have loved, and bring it to me, and let me eat, so that my soul may bless you before I die."

5And Rebekah was listening as Isaac spoke to Esau his son. And Esau went to the field to hunt game, to bring it.

6And Rebekah said to Jacob her son, "Look — I have heard your father speaking to Esau your brother, saying,

7'Bring me game and make me savory food, and let me eat, and let me bless you before the LORD before my death.'

8And now, my son, listen to my voice, to what I am commanding you.

9Go, please, to the flock, and take me from there two good kids of the goats, and I will make them into savory food for your father, such as he has loved.

10And you shall bring it to your father, and he will eat, so that he may bless you before his death."

11And Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, "Look — Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man.

12Perhaps my father will feel me, and I shall be in his eyes like a mocker, and I will bring on myself a curse and not a blessing."

13And his mother said to him, "Upon me be your curse, my son. Only listen to my voice, and go, take them for me."

14And he went and took and brought them to his mother, and his mother made savory food, such as his father had loved.

15And Rebekah took the garments of Esau her elder son — the precious ones that were with her in the house — and clothed Jacob her younger son.

16And the skins of the kids of the goats she put on his hands, and on the smooth of his neck.

17And she gave the savory food and the bread that she had made into the hand of Jacob her son.

The Touching

18And he came to his father and said, "My father." And he said, "Here I am. Who are you, my son?"

19And Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau your firstborn. I have done as you spoke to me. Rise, please, sit, and eat from my game, so that your soul may bless me."

20And Isaac said to his son, "How is it you found it so quickly, my son?" And he said, "Because the LORD your God made it happen before me."

21And Isaac said to Jacob, "Come near, please, and let me feel you, my son — whether you are this, my son Esau, or not."

22And Jacob came near to Isaac his father, and he felt him, and he said, "The voice is the voice of Jacob, and the hands are the hands of Esau."

23And he did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like the hands of Esau his brother. And he blessed him.

24And he said, "Are you this, my son Esau?" And he said, "I am."

25And he said, "Bring it near to me, and let me eat from my son's game, so that my soul may bless you." And he brought it near to him, and he ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank.

26And Isaac his father said to him, "Come near, please, and kiss me, my son."

27And he came near and kissed him. And he smelled the smell of his garments, and he blessed him, and said,
"See — the smell of my son
is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed.

28And may God give you from the dew of the heavens,
and from the fat places of the earth,
and abundance of grain and new wine.

29Peoples shall serve you,
and nations shall bow down to you.
Be master to your brothers,
and let your mother's sons bow down to you.
Those who curse you, cursed;
and those who bless you, blessed."

Too Late

30And it came to pass, as Isaac finished blessing Jacob — and it came to pass, Jacob had only just gone out from the face of Isaac his father — that Esau his brother came in from his hunting.

31And he also made savory food and brought it to his father, and said to his father, "Let my father rise and eat from his son's game, so that your soul may bless me."

32And Isaac his father said to him, "Who are you?" And he said, "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau."

33And Isaac trembled a very great trembling, and said, "Who then was it that hunted game and brought it to me, and I ate of it all before you came, and I blessed him? He shall indeed be blessed."

34When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out a cry, great and bitter beyond measure, and said to his father, "Bless me — me also, my father!"

35And he said, "Your brother came with deceit and took your blessing."

36And he said, "Is it because his name is called Jacob that he has heeled me these two times? My birthright he took, and here, now, he has taken my blessing." And he said, "Have you not reserved a blessing for me?"

37And Isaac answered and said to Esau, "Look — I have set him as master over you, and all his brothers I have given to him as servants, and with grain and new wine I have sustained him. And for you, then — what can I do, my son?"

38And Esau said to his father, "Is there only one blessing to you, my father? Bless me — me also, my father!" And Esau lifted his voice and wept.

39And Isaac his father answered and said to him,
"Look — away from the fat places of the earth shall be your dwelling,
and away from the dew of the heavens above.

40And by your sword you shall live,
and your brother you shall serve.
And it shall be, when you break loose,
that you will tear his yoke from off your neck."

41And Esau harbored hatred against Jacob over the blessing with which his father had blessed him. And Esau said in his heart, "Let the days of mourning for my father draw near, and I will kill Jacob my brother."

42And the words of Esau her elder son were told to Rebekah. And she sent and called Jacob her younger son and said to him, "Look — Esau your brother is consoling himself concerning you, to kill you.

43And now, my son, listen to my voice. Rise, flee for yourself to Laban my brother, to Harran.

44And stay with him a few days, until your brother's heat turns away —

45until your brother's anger turns from you, and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send and take you from there. Why should I be bereaved of both of you in one day?"

46And Rebekah said to Isaac, "I am disgusted with my life because of the daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of Heth like these, from the daughters of the land — what is life to me?"

Notes

  • v1 "his eyes were too dim to see" — the chapter turns entirely on the senses. Isaac cannot see, so he tests by hearing (v22), by touch (v21–23), by taste (v25), and by smell (v27). Four senses, and three of them lie to him. Only hearing gets it right, and he overrules it.

  • v4, 19, 25, 31 "so that my soul may bless you" — nafshi, the throat-word again. The blessing is located in the nephesh, and nephesh begins as the throat — which is why the whole scene is about food going down it. Isaac must eat before he can bless; the blessing comes up out of the same passage the meal went into.

  • v12 "like a mocker" — ki-mta'tea, from a root meaning to mock or mislead. The same fear that shadows metsacheq in 21:9 and 26:8: a word for playing that can turn into a word for deceiving.

  • v13 "Upon me be your curse" — Rebekah takes the curse onto herself in one clause and moves straight on to the instruction. She is the only person in the chapter who is never uncertain.

  • vv8, 13, 43 "listen to my voice" — shema be-qoli, three times, all from Rebekah. It is the same phrase God used of Abraham in 26:5 (Abraham listened to My voice) and commanded Abraham in 21:12 (listen to her voice). The formula for obedience to God is what the mother uses to arrange a fraud.

  • v22 "The voice is the voice of Jacob, and the hands are the hands of Esau" — the most quoted line in the chapter, and in Hebrew it is four words against four: ha-qol qol Ya'aqov ve-ha-yadayim yedei Esav. Isaac states the contradiction out loud, in perfect balance, and then blesses anyway. He has the evidence and does not act on it.

  • v24 "Are you this, my son Esau?" And he said, "I am." — ani. One word. It is the plainest lie in the book and the shortest sentence in the chapter.

  • v27 "the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed" — he is smelling Esau's clothes, which smell of the outdoors because Esau is a man of the field (25:27). The one sense that tells him the truth about the garments tells him a lie about the man.

  • vv28–29 against vv39–40 — read them as a pair. Jacob gets from the dew of the heavens and from the fat places of the earth; Esau gets the same two phrases in the same order, but the preposition min can mean from in the sense of out of or in the sense of away from. Esau's blessing is either the same gift or its exact negation, and the Hebrew will not say which. English Bibles split on this verse, and they are not being careless — the ambiguity is real.

  • v33 "trembled a very great trembling" — va-yecherad… charadah gedolah ad me'od, the verb doubled by its own noun and then intensified twice. This is the strongest description of fear in Genesis, and it belongs to the man who has just been deceived by his own son, in the instant he realizes he cannot take it back.

  • v33 "He shall indeed be blessed" — Isaac does not revoke it. Whatever a blessing is in this book, it is not a wish that can be withdrawn; it has left him and gone somewhere, and he speaks about it as a thing already standing.

  • v34 "cried out a cry, great and bitter" — va-yits'aq tse'aqah gedolah u-marah. Tse'aqah is the outcry of someone wronged — the word for the cry of Sodom in 18:20 and for Abel's blood in 4:10. It is the word for a cry that reaches a judge, and here it is Esau's, and no judge answers it.

  • v36 "he has heeled me these two times" — va-ya'qeveni, the verb made from aqev, heel, which is what his name is made from (25:26). English cannot do it: Jacob would have to become a verb. He was named for grabbing a heel, and his brother uses the name as an accusation twice over.

  • v38 "Is there only one blessing to you, my father?" — and then he weeps. Hebrews narrative almost never reports weeping from men; this is the second time in four chapters, after Abraham for Sarah.

  • v40 "when you break loose" — ka'asher tarid, and the verb is uncertain. It may mean to grow restless, to roam, to become unruly. Something about not staying still. The prophecy of Edom's eventual freedom rests on a word nobody can pin down.

  • v42 "consoling himself concerning you" — mitnachem lekha, from nacham, the root of Noah's name and of God's relenting in 6:6. What consoles Esau is the plan to kill his brother. The comfort-word is put to that use without comment.

  • v45 "Why should I be bereaved of both of you in one day?" — she foresees that a killing costs two sons: the one dead and the one who must flee or be executed for it. She is right. Jacob leaves in the next chapter and she never sees him again — the text never records them meeting, and her death is never reported.

  • v46 "I am disgusted with my life" — qatsti be-chayyai. Having just arranged the fraud, she goes to her blind husband and gives an entirely different reason for sending Jacob away: Hittite wives. It is true (26:34–35) and it is not why.

The Touching
And he came to his father and said, "My father." And he said, "Here I am. Who are you, my son?"
And Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau your firstborn. I have done as you spoke to me. Rise, please, sit, and eat from my game, so that your soul may bless me."
And Isaac said to his son, "How is it you found it so quickly, my son?" And he said, "Because the LORD your God made it happen before me."
And Isaac said to Jacob, "Come near, please, and let me feel you, my son — whether you are this, my son Esau, or not."
And Jacob came near to Isaac his father, and he felt him, and he said, "The voice is the voice of Jacob, and the hands are the hands of Esau."
And he did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like the hands of Esau his brother. And he blessed him.
And he said, "Are you this, my son Esau?" And he said, "I am."
And he said, "Bring it near to me, and let me eat from my son's game, so that my soul may bless you." And he brought it near to him, and he ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank.
And Isaac his father said to him, "Come near, please, and kiss me, my son."
And he came near and kissed him. And he smelled the smell of his garments, and he blessed him, and said, "See — the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed.
And may God give you from the dew of the heavens, and from the fat places of the earth, and abundance of grain and new wine.
Peoples shall serve you, and nations shall bow down to you. Be master to your brothers, and let your mother's sons bow down to you. Those who curse you, cursed; and those who bless you, blessed."
Too Late
And it came to pass, as Isaac finished blessing Jacob — and it came to pass, Jacob had only just gone out from the face of Isaac his father — that Esau his brother came in from his hunting.
And he also made savory food and brought it to his father, and said to his father, "Let my father rise and eat from his son's game, so that your soul may bless me."
And Isaac his father said to him, "Who are you?" And he said, "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau."
And Isaac trembled a very great trembling, and said, "Who then was it that hunted game and brought it to me, and I ate of it all before you came, and I blessed him? He shall indeed be blessed."
When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out a cry, great and bitter beyond measure, and said to his father, "Bless me — me also, my father!"
And he said, "Your brother came with deceit and took your blessing."

And he said, "Is it because his name is called Jacob that he has heeled me these two times? My birthright he took, and here, now, he has taken my blessing." And he said, "Have you not reserved a blessing for me?"

And Isaac answered and said to Esau, "Look — I have set him as master over you, and all his brothers I have given to him as servants, and with grain and new wine I have sustained him. And for you, then — what can I do, my son?"
And Esau said to his father, "Is there only one blessing to you, my father? Bless me — me also, my father!" And Esau lifted his voice and wept.
And Isaac his father answered and said to him, "Look — away from the fat places of the earth shall be your dwelling, and away from the dew of the heavens above.
And by your sword you shall live, and your brother you shall serve. And it shall be, when you break loose, that you will tear his yoke from off your neck."

And Esau harbored hatred against Jacob over the blessing with which his father had blessed him. And Esau said in his heart, "Let the days of mourning for my father draw near, and I will kill Jacob my brother."
And the words of Esau her elder son were told to Rebekah. And she sent and called Jacob her younger son and said to him, "Look — Esau your brother is consoling himself concerning you, to kill you.
And now, my son, listen to my voice. Rise, flee for yourself to Laban my brother, to Harran.
And stay with him a few days, until your brother's heat turns away —
until your brother's anger turns from you, and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send and take you from there. Why should I be bereaved of both of you in one day?"

And Rebekah said to Isaac, "I am disgusted with my life because of the daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of Heth like these, from the daughters of the land — what is life to me?"

chapters.title: The Stairway at Luz
chapters.html:
Genesis 28

1And Isaac called Jacob and blessed him, and charged him and said to him, "You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.

2Rise, go to Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel your mother's father, and take yourself a wife from there, from the daughters of Laban your mother's brother.

3And may God Almighty bless you, and make you fruitful and multiply you, and you shall become an assembly of peoples.

4And may He give you the blessing of Abraham — to you and to your seed with you — that you may possess the land of your sojournings, which God gave to Abraham."

5And Isaac sent Jacob off, and he went to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, brother of Rebekah, mother of Jacob and Esau.

6And Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to take himself a wife from there — that in blessing him he charged him, saying, "You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan" —

7and that Jacob had listened to his father and his mother and had gone to Paddan-aram.

8And Esau saw that the daughters of Canaan were evil in the eyes of Isaac his father.

9And Esau went to Ishmael, and took Mahalath daughter of Ishmael son of Abraham, sister of Nebaioth, in addition to his wives, for himself as a wife.

The Place

10And Jacob went out from Beersheba and went toward Harran.

11And he struck upon the place, and spent the night there, for the sun had come in. And he took from the stones of the place and set them at his head, and lay down in that place.

12And he dreamed — and here, a stairway set on the earth, and its head reaching to the heavens. And here, messengers of God going up and coming down on it.

13And here, the LORD standing over him, and He said, "I am the LORD, God of Abraham your father and God of Isaac. The land on which you are lying — to you I will give it, and to your seed.

14And your seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and you shall burst out to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south. And in you all the families of the ground shall bless themselves, and in your seed.

15And here — I am with you, and I will keep you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this ground. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have spoken to you."

16And Jacob woke from his sleep and said, "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I — I did not know."

17And he was afraid and said, "How fearful is this place! This is nothing but the house of God, and this is the gate of the heavens."

18And Jacob rose early in the morning and took the stone that he had set at his head, and set it up as a standing-stone, and poured oil on its head.

19And he called the name of that place Bethel — but Luz was the name of the city at first.

20And Jacob vowed a vow, saying, "If God will be with me, and keep me on this way that I am going, and give me bread to eat and a garment to wear,

21and I return in peace to my father's house — then the LORD shall be my God.

22And this stone, which I have set as a standing-stone, shall be the house of God. And all that You give me, tithing I will tithe to You."

Notes

  • vv1–5 against 27:46 — Rebekah told Isaac that Jacob must leave because of Hittite wives. Isaac now sends him away for exactly that reason, and never mentions Esau, the blessing, or the deceit. Either he has not been told, or he is taking the reason offered. The text does not say which, and the silence is the whole shape of the scene.

  • v9 "in addition to his wives" — Esau, seeing that Canaanite women displease his father, marries a granddaughter of Abraham. He has correctly identified the rule and is trying to satisfy it after the fact, having already married two Hittites. It is the most sympathetic thing he does, and it changes nothing.

  • v11 "he struck upon the place" — va-yifga ba-maqom. Paga is to strike against, to encounter by collision — it is used of meeting someone by accident and of falling upon someone in violence. He does not choose the spot; he runs into it. And ha-maqom, the place, with the definite article, three times in the verse, before anything has happened there.

  • v11 "for the sun had come in" — ki va ha-shemesh, the ordinary idiom for sunset, kept literal because the chapter is about what is above and below: the sun goes in, a stairway goes up, and Jacob is on the ground.

  • v11 "set them at his head" — mera'ashotav. Not "for a pillow," which is an English softening; the word means the place at the head, and stones are what is there. He is a man sleeping on the ground with rocks by his head, which is the point of what happens next.

  • v12 "a stairway" — sullam, and the word occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, here. "Ladder" comes through the Greek and Latin. The root is probably salal, to heap up or build a raised way — which suits a ramp or a flight of steps, like the stairways built up the sides of Mesopotamian temple towers, better than it suits a ladder. Nobody can settle it, and the note is that the most famous object in the chapter is named by a word used nowhere else.

  • v12 "going up and coming down" — in that order. They start on the ground. Whatever the messengers are doing, they were already here.

  • v12 "its head reaching to the heavens" — ve-rosho maggia ha-shamaymah. In 11:4 the builders at Babel said let us build a tower with its head in the heavens — ve-rosho va-shamayim. The same phrase, and this time it is not built and not climbed; it is dreamed, and it is already there. Babel's tower was a project; this one is a given.

  • v13 "standing over him" — nitsav alav. The preposition can mean over him, beside him, or on it — that is, on the stairway. Hebrew leaves it open whether God is at the top of the stairs or standing next to a sleeping man.

  • v13 "The land on which you are lying" — shokhev, the lying-down verb. He owns nothing, he is running for his life, and the promise is measured by the patch of ground his body covers.

  • v15 "I am with you" — the promise to Jacob is different from the ones to Abraham and Isaac. They were promised land, seed, and blessing. He is promised company, protection, and return — the things a man running away at night needs, in that order.

  • v16 "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I — I did not know" — ve-anokhi lo yadati. The anokhi is emphatic and unnecessary; Hebrew has already marked the person in the verb. He puts it in anyway. And I — I did not know.

  • v17 "How fearful is this place" — mah nora ha-maqom ha-zeh. Nora is the passive of the verb to fear: fear-inducing, awe-bearing. Not "awesome," which English has spent.

  • v17 "the gate of the heavens" — sha'ar ha-shamayim. Worth knowing that Babylon's own name for itself, Bab-ilu, means gate of god, the etymology set against the Hebrew pun in 11:9. The exile from that city called itself the gate of heaven; here a man sleeping on stones in an empty field says the phrase about a place that has no city in it at all.

  • v18 "a standing-stone" — matsevah, an upright stone set as a marker or witness. The same root as nitsav in v13, standing, used of the LORD. What he saw standing over him, he answers with a stone stood up.

  • v19 "Bethel — but Luz was the name of the city at first" — Beit-El is house of God, which is what he called it in v17. The narrator immediately notes that it already had a name. Jacob renames a place that was not his, on the strength of one night.

  • vv20–22 "If God will be with me…" — the first vow in the Bible, and it is conditional. God has just promised, unprompted and without terms, to be with him, keep him, and bring him back. Jacob's reply repeats those three items back as conditions — if He will be with me, and keep me, and I return — and adds bread and clothing. He has been offered everything and responds by negotiating. It is entirely in character for the man who asked his starving brother for an oath before handing over soup.

  • v22 "tithing I will tithe" — asser a'asrennu, the doubled verb. The second time in the book someone gives a tenth; the first was Abraham to Melchizedek in 14:20, given freely after a victory. This one is offered in advance, in exchange.

chapters.title: And in the Morning, Here — It Was Leah
chapters.html:
Genesis 29

1And Jacob lifted his feet and went to the land of the sons of the east.

2And he looked, and here — a well in the field, and here, three flocks of sheep lying beside it, for from that well they watered the flocks. And the stone on the mouth of the well was large.

3And all the flocks would gather there, and they would roll the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep, and return the stone to its place on the mouth of the well.

4And Jacob said to them, "My brothers, where are you from?" And they said, "We are from Harran."

5And he said to them, "Do you know Laban son of Nahor?" And they said, "We know him."

6And he said to them, "Is it well with him?" And they said, "Well. And here — Rachel his daughter, coming with the sheep."

7And he said, "Look, the day is still long. It is not time for the livestock to be gathered. Water the sheep and go, graze them."

8And they said, "We cannot, until all the flocks are gathered and they roll the stone from the mouth of the well. Then we water the sheep."

9He was still speaking with them, and Rachel came with the sheep that were her father's, for she was a shepherd.

10And it came to pass, when Jacob saw Rachel daughter of Laban his mother's brother, and the sheep of Laban his mother's brother, that Jacob came near and rolled the stone from the mouth of the well, and watered the sheep of Laban his mother's brother.

11And Jacob kissed Rachel, and he lifted his voice and wept.

12And Jacob told Rachel that he was her father's brother, and that he was Rebekah's son. And she ran and told her father.

13And it came to pass, when Laban heard the report of Jacob his sister's son, that he ran to meet him and embraced him and kissed him, and brought him to his house. And he recounted to Laban all these things.

14And Laban said to him, "Surely you are my bone and my flesh." And he stayed with him a month of days.

Seven Years

15And Laban said to Jacob, "Because you are my brother, should you serve me for nothing? Tell me — what shall your wages be?"

16And Laban had two daughters. The name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.

17And Leah's eyes were soft, and Rachel was beautiful in form and beautiful to look at.

18And Jacob loved Rachel, and he said, "I will serve you seven years for Rachel your younger daughter."

19And Laban said, "Better that I give her to you than that I give her to another man. Stay with me."

20And Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they were in his eyes like a few days, in his loving her.

21And Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife, for my days are filled, and let me come to her."

22And Laban gathered all the men of the place and made a feast.

23And it came to pass in the evening that he took Leah his daughter and brought her to him, and he came to her.

24And Laban gave her Zilpah his servant girl — to Leah his daughter, a servant girl.

25And it came to pass in the morning — and here, it was Leah. And he said to Laban, "What is this you have done to me? Was it not for Rachel that I served with you? And why have you deceived me?"

26And Laban said, "It is not done so in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn.

27Fill out this week, and we will give you that one also, for the service you will serve with me yet another seven years."

28And Jacob did so, and filled out this week, and he gave him Rachel his daughter as a wife.

29And Laban gave to Rachel his daughter Bilhah his servant girl, to her as a servant girl.

30And he came also to Rachel, and he loved Rachel also, more than Leah. And he served with him yet another seven years.

The Sons of the Hated One

31And the LORD saw that Leah was hated, and He opened her womb. And Rachel was barren.

32And Leah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Reuben, for she said, "Because the LORD has seen my affliction — for now my husband will love me."

33And she conceived again and bore a son, and she said, "Because the LORD has heard that I am hated, He has given me this one also." And she called his name Simeon.

34And she conceived again and bore a son, and she said, "Now, this time, my husband will be joined to me, for I have borne him three sons." Therefore he called his name Levi.

35And she conceived again and bore a son, and she said, "This time I will give thanks to the LORD." Therefore she called his name Judah. And she stopped bearing.

Notes

  • v1 "lifted his feet" — va-yissa Ya'aqov raglav, an idiom found only here. Everywhere else in these chapters people lift their eyes — Lot in 13:10, Abraham in 22:4 and 22:13, Rebekah in 24:64. Jacob, leaving home with nothing after the night at Bethel, lifts his feet.

  • vv2–10 the well scene — this is the third betrothal at a well in the book: Abraham's servant meets Rebekah at one (24), and Moses will meet Zipporah at one later. The shape repeats — a traveler, a well, a woman with a flock, water drawn, a run home with news, a welcome. Here the roles are reversed from chapter 24: there, the woman drew the water for the man and his camels; here, the man rolls the stone away and waters her flock.

  • v2, 3, 8, 10 "the stone… the stone… the stone" — four times, and the shepherds explain that it takes all the flocks gathered to move it. Then Jacob moves it alone, on sight of Rachel, and the text does not comment. The man who has so far achieved everything by cunning does the one purely physical thing in his story the moment he sees her.

  • v11 "And Jacob kissed Rachel, and he lifted his voice and wept" — in that order. He weeps before he explains who he is.

  • v13 "he ran to meet him and embraced him and kissed him" — Laban runs, exactly as he ran in 24:29 — where the narrator noted that he ran after seeing the gold. Here Jacob arrives with nothing, and the greeting is the same. The reader who remembers the earlier verse is meant to notice that this time there is no jewelry.

  • v14 "my bone and my flesh" — atsmi u-vesari, the phrase Adam used of the woman in 2:23. Laban uses the language of the first marriage to open a labor negotiation, and the very next verse is about wages.

  • v17 "Leah's eyes were soft" — rakkot. The word means tender, soft, delicate, weak. It is used of soft ground, of a tender child, of a faint heart. Whether it is a compliment or a defect is not decidable from the word, and the sentence sets it against Rachel's beauty with a plain and, which may be a contrast or may not. Translations print "weak," "dull," "lovely," "delicate" — all of them choosing. This is one of the places where a single adjective decides how a reader sees a woman for the rest of the book, and the Hebrew declines to help.

  • v20 "like a few days, in his loving her" — ke-yamim achadim. And yamim achadim is exactly what his mother said in 27:44: stay with him a few days. She meant until Esau cooled. He serves fourteen years and stays twenty.

  • v21 "Give me my wife, for my days are filled" — blunt, and the second clause is a contract term. He is calling in a debt.

  • v23 "And it came to pass in the evening" — and the whole deception fits in one verse. The text does not explain the veil, the dark, the wine at the feast, or how it was possible. It simply reports the evening and then the morning.

  • v25 "And it came to pass in the morning — and here, it was Leah" — ve-hinneh hi Leah. Four words in Hebrew. It is the finest sentence in the chapter and one of the great sentences in the book: the hinneh, look, that Hebrew uses to put the reader inside someone's eyes at the moment of seeing.

    And it is the exact reversal of chapter 27. There, a younger son put on the elder brother's clothing and stood before a father who could not see, and was asked are you this, my son Esau? — and said I am. Here the elder daughter is put in the younger sister's place in a dark tent, and the deceiver wakes to find he has been given the elder instead of the younger, exactly as his father was given the younger instead of the elder. He asks Laban why have you deceived me — rimmitani, from the root ramah, and in 27:35 Isaac told Esau your brother came with deceit, be-mirmah, the same root. The word Jacob's fraud was named with is the word he now uses as an accusation.

  • v26 "to give the younger before the firstborn" — ha-tse'irah lifnei ha-bekhirah. Laban's excuse names the two categories the previous two chapters were fought over: the younger and the firstborn. He says it as though it were simply how things are done, and it is the one sentence in the chapter that answers Genesis 25:23.

  • v31 "hated" — senu'ah, the ordinary passive of sane, to hate. It is a hard word, and v30 has just said Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah — a comparative. Hebrew legal language uses loved/hated for the preferred and unpreferred wife, so the word may be technical rather than emotional. It may also be exactly what it says. The text uses it three times about her and never softens it.

  • vv32–35 the four names — each is a sentence Leah says, and each is built on a verb: Re'uven — ra'ah, see: the LORD has seen my affliction, and re'u ben, see, a son. Shim'on — shama, hear: the LORD has heard that I am hated. Levi — lavah, to join: now my husband will be joined to me. Yehudah — yadah, to give thanks: this time I will give thanks. The first three are about her husband. Only the fourth is not — she stops explaining herself by what he might do, and the naming stops with it. That fourth name is the one the kingdom of Judah, and the word Jew, come from.

  • v34 "Therefore he called his name Levi" — the verb shifts. She names the first two and the fourth; this one the text gives to him, in the only verse where she says he will be joined to her.

chapters.title: Give Me Sons, and If Not, I Am Dead
chapters.html:
Genesis 30

1And Rachel saw that she had borne Jacob no children, and Rachel was jealous of her sister. And she said to Jacob, "Give me sons — and if not, I am dead."

2And Jacob's anger burned against Rachel, and he said, "Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?"

3And she said, "Here is my maidservant Bilhah. Come to her, and let her bear upon my knees, and I too will be built up from her."

4And she gave him Bilhah her servant girl as a wife, and Jacob came to her.

5And Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.

6And Rachel said, "God has judged me, and He has also heard my voice and given me a son." Therefore she called his name Dan.

7And Bilhah, Rachel's servant girl, conceived again and bore a second son to Jacob.

8And Rachel said, "Wrestlings of God I have wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed." And she called his name Naphtali.

9And Leah saw that she had stopped bearing, and she took Zilpah her servant girl and gave her to Jacob as a wife.

10And Zilpah, Leah's servant girl, bore Jacob a son.

11And Leah said, "Fortune has come." And she called his name Gad.

12And Zilpah, Leah's servant girl, bore a second son to Jacob.

13And Leah said, "In my happiness — for the daughters will call me happy." And she called his name Asher.

The Mandrakes

14And Reuben went out in the days of the wheat harvest and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them to Leah his mother. And Rachel said to Leah, "Give me, please, some of your son's mandrakes."

15And she said to her, "Is it a small thing, your taking my husband — and you would take my son's mandrakes as well?" And Rachel said, "Then let him lie with you tonight, for your son's mandrakes."

16And Jacob came in from the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him and said, "You will come to me, for I have surely hired you with my son's mandrakes." And he lay with her that night.

17And God heard Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.

18And Leah said, "God has given my wages, because I gave my servant girl to my husband." And she called his name Issachar.

19And Leah conceived again and bore a sixth son to Jacob.

20And Leah said, "God has endowed me with a good endowment. This time my husband will dwell with me, for I have borne him six sons." And she called his name Zebulun.

21And afterward she bore a daughter, and she called her name Dinah.

22And God remembered Rachel, and God heard her, and He opened her womb.

23And she conceived and bore a son, and she said, "God has gathered up my disgrace."

24And she called his name Joseph, saying, "May the LORD add to me another son."

Name Your Wages

25And it came to pass, when Rachel had borne Joseph, that Jacob said to Laban, "Send me away, and let me go to my own place and to my land.

26Give me my wives and my children, for whom I served you, and let me go — for you yourself know my service, how I served you."

27And Laban said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes — I have read the omens: the LORD has blessed me because of you."

28And he said, "Name your wages upon me, and I will give them."

29And he said to him, "You yourself know how I served you, and what your livestock became with me.

30For the little that was yours before me has broken out into a multitude, and the LORD has blessed you at my foot. And now — when shall I do something for my own house, I also?"

31And he said, "What shall I give you?" And Jacob said, "You shall give me nothing. If you will do this thing for me, I will go back, I will graze your flock, I will keep it.

32Let me pass through all your flock today, removing from it every speckled and spotted sheep, and every dark one among the lambs, and the spotted and speckled among the goats. And that shall be my wages.

33And my righteousness will answer for me on a later day, when you come over my wages before you: every one among the goats that is not speckled and spotted, and among the lambs that is not dark, it is stolen, with me."

34And Laban said, "Here — let it be according to your word."

35And on that day he removed the striped and spotted he-goats, and all the speckled and spotted she-goats, every one that had white in it, and every dark one among the lambs, and he gave them into the hand of his sons.

36And he set a distance of three days' journey between himself and Jacob. And Jacob was grazing the rest of Laban's flock.

37And Jacob took for himself fresh rods of poplar and almond and plane, and peeled white peelings in them, exposing the white that was on the rods.

38And he set the rods that he had peeled in the troughs, in the watering channels where the flocks came to drink, right in front of the flocks — and they went into heat when they came to drink.

39And the flocks went into heat at the rods, and the flocks bore striped, speckled, and spotted.

40And the lambs Jacob separated out, and he set the faces of the flock toward the striped and toward every dark one in Laban's flock. And he made himself droves of his own, and did not put them with Laban's flock.

41And it came to pass, whenever the vigorous of the flock went into heat, that Jacob would set the rods before the eyes of the flock, in the troughs, to make them heat at the rods.

42And when the flock was feeble he would not set them. So the feeble went to Laban, and the vigorous to Jacob.

43And the man broke out exceedingly, exceedingly, and he had many flocks, and maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys.

Notes

  • v1 "Give me sons — and if not, I am dead" — seven words in Hebrew: havah li vanim, ve-im ayin, metah anokhi. The last two are not "I will die." Metah is a participle and anokhi is the emphatic "I" — dead, I am. She is not predicting; she is describing her present condition. And she says it to Jacob, having just been told by the narrator in 29:31 who it is that opens wombs.

  • v2 "Am I in the place of God" — ha-tachat Elohim anokhi. He answers her anokhi with his own. Two people in two verses each saying I, and the argument is about which of them is not God. This is also the first time in the book that Jacob is angry — va-yichar af, his nose burned, which is what Hebrew anger does.

  • v3 "let her bear upon my knees, and I too will be built up from her" — ve-ibbaneh, from banah, to build. Ben, son, comes from the same root: in Hebrew, to get a child is to be built. The sentence is not new. Sarai said it in 16:2 — bo na el shifchati, ulai ibbaneh mimmennah, come to my servant girl, perhaps I will be built from her — the identical verb, the identical arrangement, and that one produced Ishmael, Hagar's contempt, and a woman driven into the desert twice. Rachel repeats it word for word two generations later.

    She also changes the word for Bilhah between verses. In her own mouth Bilhah is amati, my maidservant; when the narrator reports the handover in v4 she is shifchatah, her servant girl. Both are slave words. The one Rachel uses is the slightly higher of the two.

  • v6 "God has judged me" — dananni Elohim, root din: to judge, and specifically to decide a case in someone's favor. Not "God punished me" — vindicated me. She has won something. And it is Rachel who names him, not Bilhah, who bore him; the woman who gave birth does not speak in this chapter at all.

  • v8 "Wrestlings of God I have wrestled" — naftulei Elohim niftalti. The root is patal, to twist — used of a twisted cord and of crooked, devious speech. The noun naftulim occurs nowhere else in the Bible, so what the phrase weighs is genuinely open: Elohim may be doing the work Hebrew often gives it of an intensifier, mighty wrestlings, or she may mean the struggle was with God and her sister was only where it happened.

    What is not open is the last word. Gam yakholti, and I have prevailed — and in 32:28 the man at the ford tells Jacob you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed, va-tukhal, the same verb. The wrestling words differ; the prevailing word is the same. Rachel says of her sister, twenty years early, what the angel will say of her husband — and Jacob gets a new name for it while she gets a son she did not carry.

  • v11 "Fortune has come" — this verse preserves a scribal split that is visible on the page. The consonants written are בגד, one word; what is read aloud is בָּא גָד, two words, ba gad, fortune has come. The scribes kept a written form they did not pronounce and marked the reading beside it rather than correcting the text — the same conservatism that left Mehujael spelled two ways in one verse at 4:18.

    And gad is not only a common noun. Isaiah 65:11 condemns those who set a table for Gad, where the word is the name of a god of luck. Leah, in the middle of a fertility contest, names a son Luck.

  • v13 "In my happiness — for the daughters will call me happy" — be-oshri... ishsheruni banot, root ashar, to be happy, to be called fortunate. Two sons in a row named for good luck, from a woman who was hated in the previous chapter. And she says daughters will call her happy. She has no daughter yet; one arrives eight verses later and is not named for happiness or for anything else.

  • v14 "mandrakes" — duda'im. The consonants are those of dod, beloved, the word that runs through the Song of Songs on every page: the mandrake is the love-plant, a forked root vaguely shaped like a body, held to bring on conception. Then the chapter does what it does with everything: Rachel buys them and stays barren for eight more verses; Leah, who sells them, conceives that night.

  • v15 "Is it a small thing, your taking my husband" — ha-me'at qachtekh et ishi. This is the only sentence Leah is ever recorded saying to Rachel, and the only line in Genesis spoken between the two sisters. From Leah's side of chapter 29, Jacob was hers first: she was married to him, and Rachel arrived a week later.

  • v16 "I have surely hired you" — sakhor sekhartikha, the infinitive doubled for emphasis, and it is the vocabulary of wage labour, the same root Jacob and Laban use for his contract in vv28–33. Leah goes out to the field to tell her husband she has paid for him. The verb for what follows is va-yishkav immah, he lay with her — not the yada, to know, of 4:1. Jacob's night is a transaction on both ends.

  • v18 "Issachar" — natan Elohim sekhari, God has given my wages, root sakhar, the word from the verse before. And the name has an oddity you can see: it is written יִשָּׂשכָר, with two sibilants where only one is pronounced. The written form carries a letter the reading drops, and the scribes preserved it rather than tidy the spelling.

  • v20 "God has endowed me with a good endowment. This time my husband will dwell with me" — one sentence, two different roots, and the name matches the second. Zevadani... zeved tov is zabad, to bestow a gift. Yizbeleni is zabal, a rare verb whose noun zevul means an exalted dwelling — it is used of the temple. So the sixth name is explained twice over, and neither explanation is quite the name: it is a sentence about a gift wrapped around a sentence about finally being lived with. Six sons in, that is still what she is asking for.

  • v21 "And afterward she bore a daughter, and she called her name Dinah" — fifteen words of explanation for every son in this chapter, and for her, nothing. She is the only child here whose name is given without a reason, and she is the only daughter. Dinah is the feminine of Dan, from din, to judge — the root that got Rachel a whole sentence at v6 and gets Leah none here. Chapter 34 is hers, and it is about what is done to her rather than anything she says.

  • v22 "And God remembered Rachel" — va-yizkor Elohim, the verb used of Noah in the ark at 8:1 and of Abraham at 19:29. In these verses it never means God had forgotten. Zakhar is remembering as an act: the moment God moves on something owed.

  • vv23–24 "Joseph" — named twice in two verses, off two different roots. Asaf Elohim et cherpati, God has gathered up my disgrace — asaf, to gather in, to take away. Then yosef YHWH li ben acher, may the LORD add me another son — yasaf, to add. The name as spelled is the second. But her first sentence is the one that says what happened, and her second is a request made in the same breath as the answer: at the exact moment of getting what she said she would die without, she asks for one more. She gets him in 35:18, and it kills her.

  • v27 "I have read the omens" — nichashti, root nachash, the word for divination by signs. Laban says it plainly, in the middle of a compliment, and he is the man who in 31:30 will accuse Jacob of stealing his gods. The house Jacob married into keeps omens and idols, and nobody in the chapter treats this as remarkable.

  • vv35, 37 "everything Laban has is white" — the trick is built on his name. Lavan means white. In v35 Laban removes kol asher lavan bo, which reads word for word as every one that has white in it and also as every one that Laban is in. In v37 Jacob cuts rods of livneh — poplar, a tree named for its whiteness, the same three consonants — and peels petsalot levanot, white peelings, machsof ha-lavan, the exposing of the white. Four white words in three verses, aimed at a man named White. The Hebrew is doing out loud what the story is doing quietly: Jacob is stripping Laban.

  • v43 "And the man broke out exceedingly" — va-yifrots ha-ish me'od me'od. In v30 Jacob complained to Laban that the little that was yours before me has broken out into a multitude — va-yifrots la-rov, the same verb, about Laban's wealth increasing on Jacob's labour. Thirteen verses later it happens to Jacob, off Laban's flock. The chapter closes by using the accusation as the verdict.
