chapters.title: As Her Soul Was Going Out
chapters.html:
Genesis 35

1And God said to Jacob, "Rise, go up to Bethel and settle there, and make there an altar to the God who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother."

2And Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, "Remove the foreign gods that are among you, and purify yourselves, and change your clothes.

3And let us rise and go up to Bethel, and let me make there an altar to the God who answered me in the day of my distress, and who was with me on the road I walked."

4And they gave Jacob all the foreign gods that were in their hand, and the rings that were in their ears, and Jacob hid them under the terebinth that is by Shechem.

5And they pulled up. And a terror of God was on the cities around them, and they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob.

6And Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan — that is Bethel — he and all the people who were with him.

7And he built there an altar and called the place El-Bethel, because there God had been revealed to him when he fled from the face of his brother.

8And Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and she was buried below Bethel, under the oak. And he called its name Allon-bacuth.

Your Name Is Jacob

9And God appeared to Jacob again, on his coming from Paddan-aram, and blessed him.

10And God said to him, "Your name is Jacob. Your name shall no longer be called Jacob — Israel shall be your name." And He called his name Israel.

11And God said to him, "I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation and an assembly of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come out of your loins.

12And the land that I gave to Abraham and to Isaac, to you I will give it, and to your seed after you I will give the land."

13And God went up from upon him, in the place where He had spoken with him.

14And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where He had spoken with him, a pillar of stone, and he poured out a drink offering on it and poured oil on it.

15And Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.

On the Road to Ephrath

16And they pulled up from Bethel. And there was still a stretch of ground to come to Ephrath, and Rachel gave birth, and her labour was hard.

17And it came to pass, when her labour was at its hardest, that the midwife said to her, "Do not be afraid, for this one also is a son for you."

18And it came to pass, as her soul was going out — for she was dying — that she called his name Ben-oni. And his father called him Benjamin.

19And Rachel died, and she was buried on the road to Ephrath — that is Bethlehem.

20And Jacob set up a pillar over her grave. That is the pillar of Rachel's grave, to this day.

21And Israel pulled up and pitched his tent beyond Migdal-eder.

22And it came to pass, while Israel was dwelling in that land, that Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine. And Israel heard. And the sons of Jacob were twelve.

23The sons of Leah: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and Simeon and Levi and Judah and Issachar and Zebulun.

24The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.

25And the sons of Bilhah, Rachel's servant girl: Dan and Naphtali.

26And the sons of Zilpah, Leah's servant girl: Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram.

27And Jacob came to Isaac his father at Mamre, Kiriath-arba — that is Hebron — where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned.

28And the days of Isaac were a hundred years and eighty years.

29And Isaac breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. And Esau and Jacob his sons buried him.

Notes

  • v1 "the God who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau" — God identifies himself to Jacob by the worst night of Jacob's life. Not the God of Abraham, not the God who made you rich in Paddan-aram: the God of the night you ran with nothing. And v7 says it a second time, when he fled from the face of his brother. The chapter will not let the twenty prosperous years stand in for that stone pillow.

  • v2 "the foreign gods that are among you" — elohei ha-nekhar, and Jacob's household has them. Rachel took her father's household gods in 31:19 and lied to his face about them; here they are being handed over, or some of them are, along with ha-nezamim asher be-ozneihem, the rings in their ears, which suggests amulets rather than jewelry. The text does not say whether Rachel's are in the pile.

  • v4 "Jacob hid them" — va-yitmon, to bury out of sight, to conceal. He does not smash them or burn them, which is what Israel is told to do with such things everywhere else. He hides them under the terebinth that is by Shechem — under a named tree, at the city his sons had just emptied, in ground they do not own. The verb and the location are both exact, and neither one is destruction.

  • v3 "in the day of my distress" — be-yom tsarati, from tsarar, to press in, to be tight. It is the noun of the verb in 32:7, va-yetser lo, and it was narrow for him, on the night before he met Esau. Jacob names God by the same pressure twice in three verses.

  • v5 "a terror of God" — chittat Elohim, from chatat, to be shattered or broken with fear. The noun is rare. After chapter 34 the surrounding cities have every reason to come after Jacob's sons, and the one sentence the narrator gives for why they did not is this. Nobody does anything; something falls on the cities.

  • v7 "God had been revealed to him" — niglu elav ha-Elohim, and the verb niglu is plural. Elohim is a plural-shaped word that takes singular verbs almost without exception in the Hebrew Bible — bara Elohim, God created, singular, in 1:1. In a small handful of places, and this is one, the verb agrees with the plural form instead. What it means is not decidable from the grammar: it may be an old idiom, it may be attraction to the plural ending. What can be said is that it is unusual and that the scribes left it standing.

  • v8 "Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died" — this woman has not been mentioned since 24:59, where Rebekah's unnamed nurse went with her to Canaan; she is named here for the first and only time, in the verse where she dies. And Rebekah herself never gets such a verse. The Bible records the deaths of Sarah, of Abraham, of Rachel, of Isaac, of Jacob — and never narrates Rebekah's. The only funeral in her family the text stops for is her nurse's, under a tree called Allon-bacuth, the oak of weeping.

  • v10 "Your name is Jacob. Your name shall no longer be called Jacob" — the sentence starts by confirming the old name and then cancels it, and the renaming of 32:28 is done over again, this time by God in daylight rather than by a man who would not give his name in the dark.

    And it does not take. Compare Abram, who after 17:5 is never called Abram again in the entire Bible. Jacob is called Jacob in v20 of this chapter, ten verses after this, and the narrator swaps between the two names freely for the rest of the book — Israel pulled up in v21, the sons of Jacob in v22. He is the only person in the Bible who keeps both names, and he keeps the one that means heel-grabber.

  • v11 "God Almighty" — El Shaddai, the name that came with the covenant of circumcision in 17:1 (see the note there for what the word does and does not support). What is new here is what follows: goy u-qehal goyim, a nation and an assembly of nations. Qahal is the word for the gathered community of Israel, and it is the word the Greek Old Testament renders ekklēsia, which is where English gets church. Its first appearance in the Bible is this promise, said to a man on a road with eleven sons and a dying wife.

  • v14 "a pillar of stone" — he does exactly what he did at this spot in 28:18, on the way out: set up a stone, pour oil on it. The addition is va-yassekh aleha nesekh, he poured a drink offering on it — the first libation in the Bible. Twenty years and two chapters of God-encounters later, the ritual has grown by one element, at the same rock.

  • v16 "a stretch of ground" — kivrat ha-arets, a measure of distance that occurs three times in the Hebrew Bible and is never defined. Nothing in the language fixes it. It means some distance short of arriving, and every English translation that prints a figure is supplying one.

  • v17 "this one also is a son for you" — the midwife's line answers a sentence from five chapters back. In 30:24 Rachel named Joseph may the LORD add me another son. The midwife tells her, while she is dying, that the prayer was granted, and the word she uses, gam, also, is the hinge: this one too. Rachel got what she asked for in 30:1 — give me sons, and if not, I am dead — and the text has now given her both halves of that sentence.

  • v18 "as her soul was going out" — be-tset nafshah. Nefesh is not a soul in the later sense; it is breath, throat, appetite, life itself — what leaves when a body stops. The Hebrew is describing the last exhalation, and it is one of very few places in the Torah where a death is watched from inside.

  • v18 "Ben-oni... Benjamin" — Ben-Oni is genuinely two words. On can be sorrow, and it can be strength, vigour, generative power — in 49:3 Jacob calls Reuben my strength and the first of my on, plainly the second sense. So the dying woman's name for her son is either son of my suffering or son of my strength, and Hebrew does not choose. Then Jacob overrides her: Binyamin, son of the right hand — the favoured side, the strong side, and also the south, since Hebrew orients by facing east.

    This is the only child in the Bible whose mother names him and whose father immediately renames him. And the man doing the renaming is the one who wrestled all night for a name of his own and was told your name shall no longer be called Jacob.

  • v20 "to this day" — ad ha-yom, and it is the narrator speaking to his own readers, pointing at a marker they could go and look at. Jacob has now set up three pillars: at Bethel going out (28:18), on the heap with Laban (31:45), and at Bethel again in v14 of this chapter. The fourth is a gravestone.

  • v22 "And Israel heard." — and then the sentence stops. There is no reaction, no rebuke, no scene; what comes next in the same verse is a headcount, and the sons of Jacob were twelve, and after that a list of their names. Jacob hears that his firstborn has slept with his wife's servant — the woman who bore Dan and Naphtali — and the narrator gives him three words and moves on. It is the second time in two chapters that Jacob is told something terrible and says nothing: in 34:5 Jacob kept silent until they came.

    He answers both eventually, in the same speech, on his deathbed. Reuben in 49:4: unstable as water, you shall not excel, for you went up to your father's bed. Simeon and Levi in 49:5–7. Everything Jacob does not say in chapters 34 and 35 comes out fourteen chapters later, all at once, as curses.

  • v22 "And the sons of Jacob were twelve" — placed immediately after the sentence that ruins the firstborn, and immediately before a list that still names Reuben first. The count is announced at the exact moment the order inside it has stopped meaning what it says.

  • v26 "born to him in Paddan-aram" — Benjamin was born eight verses earlier, on the road to Ephrath, in Canaan. The summary says all twelve were born in Paddan-aram and it is not true of the one the chapter just finished narrating. The text leaves the two statements standing next to each other without adjusting either, and this rendering does the same.

  • v29 "And Esau and Jacob his sons buried him" — Esau is named first. When Abraham was buried in 25:9 it was Isaac and Ishmael his sons — the son of the promise first, the elder second. Here the order flips: the elder goes first, and the brother who bought the birthright and stole the blessing is named second at his father's grave. Isaac lives to a hundred and eighty, longer than Abraham, which means he was alive through every chapter of this story — through the twenty years in Paddan-aram, through Shechem, through Rachel's death — and the text has not mentioned him since chapter 28. He was blind and thought he was dying then. He outlasts the entire quarrel.

speech.text: Genesis 35
And God said to Jacob, "Rise, go up to Bethel and settle there, and make there an altar to the God who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother."
And Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, "Remove the foreign gods that are among you, and purify yourselves, and change your clothes.
And let us rise and go up to Bethel, and let me make there an altar to the God who answered me in the day of my distress, and who was with me on the road I walked."
And they gave Jacob all the foreign gods that were in their hand, and the rings that were in their ears, and Jacob hid them under the terebinth that is by Shechem.
And they pulled up. And a terror of God was on the cities around them, and they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob.
And Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan — that is Bethel — he and all the people who were with him.
And he built there an altar and called the place El-Bethel, because there God had been revealed to him when he fled from the face of his brother.
And Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and she was buried below Bethel, under the oak. And he called its name Allon-bacuth.
Your Name Is Jacob
And God appeared to Jacob again, on his coming from Paddan-aram, and blessed him.
And God said to him, "Your name is Jacob. Your name shall no longer be called Jacob — Israel shall be your name." And He called his name Israel.
And God said to him, "I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation and an assembly of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come out of your loins.
And the land that I gave to Abraham and to Isaac, to you I will give it, and to your seed after you I will give the land."
And God went up from upon him, in the place where He had spoken with him.
And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where He had spoken with him, a pillar of stone, and he poured out a drink offering on it and poured oil on it.
And Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
On the Road to Ephrath
And they pulled up from Bethel. And there was still a stretch of ground to come to Ephrath, and Rachel gave birth, and her labour was hard.
And it came to pass, when her labour was at its hardest, that the midwife said to her, "Do not be afraid, for this one also is a son for you."
And it came to pass, as her soul was going out — for she was dying — that she called his name Ben-oni. And his father called him Benjamin.
And Rachel died, and she was buried on the road to Ephrath — that is Bethlehem.
And Jacob set up a pillar over her grave. That is the pillar of Rachel's grave, to this day.
And Israel pulled up and pitched his tent beyond Migdal-eder.
And it came to pass, while Israel was dwelling in that land, that Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine. And Israel heard. And the sons of Jacob were twelve.
The sons of Leah: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and Simeon and Levi and Judah and Issachar and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
And the sons of Bilhah, Rachel's servant girl: Dan and Naphtali.
And the sons of Zilpah, Leah's servant girl: Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram.
And Jacob came to Isaac his father at Mamre, Kiriath-arba — that is Hebron — where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned.
And the days of Isaac were a hundred years and eighty years.
And Isaac breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. And Esau and Jacob his sons buried him.

chapters.title: These Are the Generations of Esau — He Is Edom
chapters.html:
Genesis 36

1And these are the generations of Esau — he is Edom.

2Esau took his wives from the daughters of Canaan: Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Oholibamah daughter of Anah daughter of Zibeon the Hivite,

3and Basemath daughter of Ishmael, sister of Nebaioth.

4And Adah bore Eliphaz to Esau, and Basemath bore Reuel,

5and Oholibamah bore Jeush and Jalam and Korah. These are the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of Canaan.

6And Esau took his wives and his sons and his daughters and all the souls of his house, and his livestock and all his beasts and all his property that he had gotten in the land of Canaan, and went to a land away from the face of Jacob his brother.

7For their goods were too many for them to settle together, and the land of their sojourning could not carry them, because of their livestock.

8And Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau — he is Edom.

The Chiefs

9And these are the generations of Esau, father of Edom, in the hill country of Seir.

10These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz son of Adah, Esau's wife; Reuel son of Basemath, Esau's wife.

11And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz.

12And Timna was a concubine to Eliphaz son of Esau, and she bore Amalek to Eliphaz. These are the sons of Adah, Esau's wife.

13And these are the sons of Reuel: Nahath and Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. These were the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife.

14And these were the sons of Oholibamah daughter of Anah daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: she bore to Esau Jeush and Jalam and Korah.

15These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn: chief Teman, chief Omar, chief Zepho, chief Kenaz,

16chief Korah, chief Gatam, chief Amalek. These are the chiefs of Eliphaz in the land of Edom. These are the sons of Adah.

17And these are the sons of Reuel son of Esau: chief Nahath, chief Zerah, chief Shammah, chief Mizzah. These are the chiefs of Reuel in the land of Edom. These are the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife.

18And these are the sons of Oholibamah, Esau's wife: chief Jeush, chief Jalam, chief Korah. These are the chiefs of Oholibamah daughter of Anah, Esau's wife.

19These are the sons of Esau, and these are their chiefs. He is Edom.

The Sons of Seir

20These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land: Lotan and Shobal and Zibeon and Anah,

21and Dishon and Ezer and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horite, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom.

22And the sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam, and Lotan's sister was Timna.

23And these are the sons of Shobal: Alvan and Manahath and Ebal, Shepho and Onam.

24And these are the sons of Zibeon: both Aiah and Anah. That is the Anah who found the yemim in the wilderness while he was pasturing the donkeys of Zibeon his father.

25And these are the children of Anah: Dishon, and Oholibamah daughter of Anah.

26And these are the sons of Dishan: Hemdan and Eshban and Ithran and Cheran.

27These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan and Zaavan and Akan.

28These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.

29These are the chiefs of the Horite: chief Lotan, chief Shobal, chief Zibeon, chief Anah,

30chief Dishon, chief Ezer, chief Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horite, by their chieftainships, in the land of Seir.

The Kings

31And these are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the sons of Israel.

32And Bela son of Beor reigned in Edom, and the name of his city was Dinhabah.

33And Bela died, and Jobab son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.

34And Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanite reigned in his place.

35And Husham died, and Hadad son of Bedad, who struck Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his place, and the name of his city was Avith.

36And Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.

37And Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth-on-the-River reigned in his place.

38And Shaul died, and Baal-hanan son of Achbor reigned in his place.

39And Baal-hanan son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his place, and the name of his city was Pau, and his wife's name was Mehetabel daughter of Matred daughter of Me-zahab.

40And these are the names of the chiefs of Esau, by their clans, by their places, by their names: chief Timna, chief Alvah, chief Jetheth,

41chief Oholibamah, chief Elah, chief Pinon,

42chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mibzar,

43chief Magdiel, chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, by their settlements in the land of their holding. He is Esau, father of Edom.

Notes

  • vv1, 8, 19, 43 "he is Edom" — the chapter says it four times, at the top, at the end of the first section, at the end of the second, and in the last words of the last verse. Hu Edom. Esav hu Edom. Hu Edom. Hu Esav avi Edom. The book has been building to this since 25:30, where Esau asked for ha-adom ha-adom ha-zeh, that red red stuff, and the narrator added therefore his name was called Edom. A whole nation is named after a bowl of lentils and one man's hunger, and this chapter is the receipt.

  • v2–3 the wives do not match — Esau's wives were named twice before this, and the names are different. In 26:34 he married Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite; in 28:9 he added Mahalath daughter of Ishmael, sister of Nebaioth. Here in v2–3 they are Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah daughter of Anah, and Basemath daughter of Ishmael, sister of Nebaioth.

    The pieces are the same pieces, reattached differently: Elon's daughter is Basemath in one list and Adah in the other; Ishmael's daughter, identified both times as Nebaioth's sister, is Mahalath in one and Basemath in the other. It is not a vague discrepancy — it is specific and checkable, and the text preserves both lists without adjusting either. This rendering does the same. What caused it is not recorded, and guessing would be inventing.

  • vv6–7 the second peaceful separation — for their goods were too many for them to settle together, and the land of their sojourning could not carry them. This is chapter 13 word for word. When Abram and Lot separated, 13:6 read the land could not carry them to settle together, for their goods were many — the same verb nasa, the same lashevet yachdav, the same rekhusham rav. The book has one formula for brothers who part without bloodshed, and it uses it exactly twice: for Abram and Lot, and here.

    And note who moves. Esau — cheated of the birthright, cheated of the blessing — is the one who packs up his household and goes, away from the face of Jacob his brother. He does it in one sentence, and the narrator supplies an economic reason and no grievance at all.

  • v12 "Timna was a concubine" — she is named again in v22 as Lotan's sister, and Lotan is the firstborn of Seir the Horite, a chief. So a chief's sister is a concubine in Esau's grandson's house. The chapter states both facts, ten verses apart, and does not connect them.

    And what she bore was Amalek — the nation that attacks Israel in the wilderness in Exodus 17 and that Israel is commanded in Deuteronomy 25 never to forget. The Bible's most implacable enemy is introduced here, in a subordinate clause, in a list, as the son of a concubine. He is Esau's great-grandson, which makes the feud between Jacob's line and Amalek the same feud, four generations on.

  • v15 "chiefs" — alluf, and the word is almost this chapter's private property. It occurs 42 times in Genesis, and all 42 are in chapter 36; the only comparable block anywhere else is in 1 Chronicles, where the Chronicler copies this same list. It is built on the consonants of eleph, a thousand, and behind that a clan-unit — a chief is the head of a thousand. The English "duke" of the older Bibles came in by way of the Latin dux, and it is not wrong so much as too aristocratic: this is a tribal head, not a nobleman.

  • v20 "the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land" — the chapter stops listing Esau's descendants and lists the people who were there first. Yoshvei ha-arets, the ones sitting in the land. Their chiefs get the same word, alluf, as Esau's.

    And the two lists are joined: Oholibamah, Esau's wife (v2), is daughter of Anah daughter of Zibeon — and Anah and Zibeon are Horites, sons of Seir (v20, v24–25). Esau's line married into the people it displaced. The genealogy makes Edom a mixture and shows the seam rather than hiding it, which is the opposite of what a national origin list usually does.

  • v24 "found the yemim in the wilderness" — ha-yemim occurs in the Bible only here, and what it names cannot be recovered. Nothing in the surrounding language constrains it. The old translations went in different directions — hot springs, mules, water — and every one of them is a guess dressed as a reading. What the verse establishes is that Anah was out pasturing his father's donkeys, that he found something, and that whoever preserved this list thought it was the one thing about him worth recording.

  • vv31–39 eight kings and not one son — before any king reigned over the sons of Israel. Read the list: Bela, then Jobab, then Husham, then Hadad, then Samlah, then Shaul, then Baal-hanan, then Hadar — and not once does the formula say his son. Each is ben somebody else, and most are tagged with a different home town: Bozrah, the land of the Temanite, Avith, Masrekah, Rehoboth-on-the-River, Pau. This is not a dynasty. It is eight kingships in a row that did not pass from father to son, recorded by people who counted that as the succession.

    And the verse that introduces them is looking backward from somewhere: before any king reigned over the sons of Israel is a sentence written by someone for whom Israel having kings is the known fact against which Edom's kings are dated.

  • v39 "Mehetabel daughter of Matred daughter of Me-zahab" — the last king in the list is also the only one whose death is not recorded, and he is the only one whose wife is named — named, and then traced back two generations through women, which the chapter does for no one else. Mehetav'el is one of those sentence-names, God does good. And the grandmother's name, Me-zahav, is two ordinary words: waters of gold.

  • vv5, 14 "Jeush" — the name is written יעיש, Ye'ish, and read Ye'ush, both times it appears. Another of the places, like Gad at 30:11, where the consonants on the page and the word said aloud were preserved side by side rather than reconciled.

  • On reading this chapter at all — it is a list, and it is meant to be. It has no story, no speech, and no comment; the only narrative sentence in forty-three verses is the one about Anah and the donkeys. What it is doing is giving Esau a full and honourable accounting — wives, sons, chiefs, the people he married into, eight kings with their cities — immediately before the book turns to Joseph and never comes back to him. Ishmael got the same treatment in 25:12–18 and was then dropped. Genesis closes out the brother it is not going to follow, at length, and with respect, and then lets him go.

chapters.title: Here Comes This Master of Dreams
chapters.html:
Genesis 37

1And Jacob settled in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan.

2These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, a son of seventeen years, was shepherding with his brothers among the flock — and he was a lad — with the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father's wives. And Joseph brought a bad report of them to their father.

3And Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, for he was a son of his old age to him, and he made him a long coat.

4And his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, and they hated him, and they could not speak to him in peace.

Two Dreams

5And Joseph dreamed a dream and told it to his brothers, and they added still more to hating him.

6And he said to them, "Listen, please, to this dream that I dreamed.

7And here — we were binding sheaves in the middle of the field, and here, my sheaf rose and also stood upright, and here, your sheaves came round and bowed down to my sheaf."

8And his brothers said to him, "Will you really reign over us? Will you really rule us?" And they added still more to hating him, over his dreams and over his words.

9And he dreamed yet another dream and recounted it to his brothers, and said, "Here, I have dreamed a dream again, and here — the sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me."

10And he recounted it to his father and to his brothers, and his father rebuked him and said to him, "What is this dream that you dreamed? Shall we really come — I and your mother and your brothers — to bow down to you, to the ground?"

11And his brothers were jealous of him. And his father kept the matter.

To Dothan

12And his brothers went to pasture their father's flock in Shechem.

13And Israel said to Joseph, "Are your brothers not pasturing in Shechem? Come, and let me send you to them." And he said to him, "Here I am."

14And he said to him, "Go, please, see the peace of your brothers and the peace of the flock, and bring me back word." And he sent him from the valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.

15And a man found him, and here — he was wandering in the field. And the man asked him, saying, "What are you looking for?"

16And he said, "I am looking for my brothers. Tell me, please, where they are pasturing."

17And the man said, "They have pulled up from here, for I heard them saying, 'Let us go to Dothan.'" And Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.

18And they saw him from far off, and before he came near to them they schemed against him, to put him to death.

19And they said, each man to his brother, "Here comes this master of dreams.

20And now, come, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits, and we will say a wild animal ate him. And we shall see what becomes of his dreams."

21And Reuben heard, and he delivered him from their hand, and said, "Let us not strike him — a life."

22And Reuben said to them, "Do not shed blood. Throw him into this pit that is in the wilderness, and do not send a hand against him" — so that he might deliver him from their hand, to bring him back to his father.

23And it came to pass, when Joseph came to his brothers, that they stripped Joseph of his coat, the long coat that was on him.

24And they took him and threw him into the pit. And the pit was empty; there was no water in it.

25And they sat down to eat bread. And they lifted their eyes and looked, and here — a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, and their camels carrying gum, balm, and ladanum, going to bring them down to Egypt.

26And Judah said to his brothers, "What profit is it that we kill our brother and cover his blood?

27Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let our hand not be against him, for he is our brother, our flesh." And his brothers listened.

28And Midianite men, traders, passed by, and they drew Joseph up out of the pit and sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. And they brought Joseph to Egypt.

Identify, Please

29And Reuben returned to the pit, and here — Joseph was not in the pit. And he tore his clothes.

30And he returned to his brothers and said, "The boy is gone. And I — where can I go?"

31And they took Joseph's coat and slaughtered a male goat and dipped the coat in the blood.

32And they sent the long coat and brought it to their father, and said, "This we found. Identify, please — is it your son's coat or not?"

33And he identified it and said, "My son's coat. A wild animal ate him. Torn, Joseph is torn."

34And Jacob tore his clothes and put sackcloth on his loins, and mourned for his son many days.

35And all his sons and all his daughters rose to comfort him, and he refused to be comforted, and said, "For I will go down to my son, mourning, to Sheol." And his father wept for him.

36And the Medanites sold him into Egypt, to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, chief of the slaughterers.

Notes

  • v2 "These are the generations of Jacob" — elleh toldot Ya'aqov, and the next word is not a list. It is Joseph. This formula has organized the whole book — 2:4, 5:1, 6:9, 10:1, 11:10, 11:27, 25:12, 25:19, and twice in the chapter just finished, 36:1 and 36:9 — and every previous time it introduced a genealogy. This is the last one in Genesis, and what follows it is thirteen chapters of story. Jacob's toldot turn out to be a life, not a list.

  • v2 "a bad report of them" — dibbatam ra'ah. Dibbah is not neutral information; it is the word for a whispering campaign, a defaming report. And the Hebrew is their dibbah — which can mean the report about them or the report belonging to them, so whether Joseph carried a true story or manufactured one is not settled by the grammar. What the verse does settle is that the first thing we learn about Joseph is that he informed on his brothers to their father.

  • v3 "a son of his old age" — ben zequnim, and Benjamin is younger. The text gives this as Jacob's reason and lets it be wrong on its face: the actual son of his old age is the one whose birth killed Rachel. What is true is that Joseph is her first, and the verse before called Bilhah and Zilpah his father's wives, not servant girls, which is the only place in Genesis they are called that.

  • v3 "a long coat" — ketonet passim, and the famous "coat of many colours" comes from the Greek and Latin translations, not from the Hebrew. Pas is the flat of the hand or the sole of the foot, so the likeliest sense is a tunic reaching to the palms and ankles — long-sleeved and full-length, a garment for someone who is not going to be doing work in it.

    There is one other ketonet passim in the entire Hebrew Bible, and it settles the register. 2 Samuel 13:18: and on her was a ketonet passim, for so the virgin daughters of the king were clothed. It is Tamar's garment, in the chapter where her brother rapes her — and she tears it. Both of the Bible's two passim coats are worn by a favoured child, and both are destroyed by siblings.

  • vv4, 14 "peace" — shalom, twice, and it is the cruellest pairing in the chapter. In v4 the brothers could not speak to him le-shalom, could not say a peaceable word to him. In v14 Jacob sends him out with go, please, see the shalom of your brothers. The father sends the boy to enquire after the welfare of men who cannot say hello to him.

  • vv5, 8 "they added still more to hating him" — va-yosifu od sno oto, and the verb is yasaf, to add — which is the verb Joseph's own name is made from. Rachel named him in 30:24 saying may the LORD add me another son. Twice in four verses, the text says his brothers added to their hatred, using his name as the verb. Hebrew does this without a wink; in English it cannot be heard at all.

  • v8 "Will you really reign... really rule" — ha-malokh timlokh... im mashol timshol, both verbs doubled in the infinitive-absolute construction Hebrew uses for emphasis or incredulity. Two kingship words in one breath. The brothers have understood the dream exactly, and their objection is not that it is nonsense but that it is intolerable.

  • v10 "I and your mother" — Rachel died in 35:19, two chapters ago. Jacob names her anyway in his rebuke, and the text does not comment, does not correct him, and never mentions her again in this chapter. The second dream has eleven stars, one for each brother; the moon has nobody left to be.

  • v11 "his father kept the matter" — shamar et ha-davar, to guard, to keep, to hold on to. This is Jacob's third silence in four chapters: he kept silent when Dinah was raped (34:5), he heard about Reuben and Bilhah and said nothing (35:22), and now he rebukes his son out loud and then quietly files the dream away. The narrator tells us what he did with it and not what he thought.

  • v12 "to pasture their father's flock" — the two letters of the word et, the object marker, carry a dot over each of them in the Hebrew manuscripts. It is the same kind of scribal mark that sits over and he kissed him in 33:4 — a signal made very early, copied ever since, and never explained in the text. This is the second one in five chapters.

  • vv15–17 the man in the field — va-yimtsa'ehu ish, a man found him, wandering. He has no name, no reason to be there, no connection to anyone in the book, and he never appears again. He gets three verses — more than several of Jacob's sons get in their lifetimes — and all he does is overhear where the brothers went and pass it on. Joseph was at Shechem, where his brothers were supposed to be and were not, and he would have turned around. Instead a stranger sends him to Dothan. The text neither comments on this nor calls him an angel.

  • v19 "this master of dreams" — ba'al ha-chalomot ha-lazeh. Ba'al is owner, husband, master of a thing; ha-lazeh is a contemptuous demonstrative, roughly that one over there. It is a sneer built out of two ordinary words, and it is one of the Bible's better insults: not the dreamer but the dream-proprietor.

  • v20 "we shall see what becomes of his dreams" — the brothers say it as the last word of their plan, and the remaining thirteen chapters of Genesis are the answer. The sentence is not marked as irony by the narrator in any way. It is simply left there.

  • vv21–22 Reuben" — va-yatsilehu mi-yadam, he delivered him from their hand, the verb natsal that has run through Jacob's story since 31:9. Reuben's plan is to have it both ways: no blood, a pit, and a quiet rescue later. It is the firstborn's instinct — he is the one with the most to answer for, and 35:22 already took his standing away. His concern surfaces plainly in v30: the boy is gone. And I — where can I go?

  • v24 "And the pit was empty; there was no water in it" — the narrator says it twice in six words. Hebrew doubles for emphasis, and what is being emphasized here is absence. The practical reading is that a dry cistern holds a boy alive; the sentence's own weight is on the nothing in it.

    And bor, pit, is the word Joseph himself uses in 40:15 from an Egyptian prison: they put me in the bor. The story puts him in the same hole twice, and both times his brothers' doing is what put him there.

  • v25 "And they sat down to eat bread" — the next sentence after throwing him in. No comment is made. It is the single coldest line in the chapter, and it works because the narrator declines to do anything with it.

  • vv25, 28, 36 Ishmaelites, Midianites, Medanites — three different names for the traders in twelve verses, and the grammar of v28 will not resolve them: and Midianite men, traders, passed by, and they drew Joseph up out of the pit and sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites — with no way to tell from the Hebrew whether they is the brothers or the Midianites. Then v36 says the Medanites sold him in Egypt, one letter different from Midianites. It is a genuine tangle in the text, and it is not this rendering's job to smooth it out.

    What can be said, and it is checkable, is who all three are. Ishmael is Abraham's son by Hagar. And 25:2 lists Keturah's sons to Abraham: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan and Midian, Ishbak and Shuah. Every name attached to the caravan that carries Joseph to Egypt belongs to Abraham's own line. The family sells its son to its cousins.

  • v28 "twenty pieces of silver" — Leviticus 27:5 sets the valuation of a male between five and twenty years old at twenty shekels. Joseph is seventeen (v2). The brothers get exactly the going rate, which is the detail that makes the transaction worse rather than better: it was not a panic sale.

  • vv31–33 the goat and the recognizing — this is chapter 27 turned back on the man who did it. There, Rebekah dressed Jacob in the skins of the kids of the goats (27:16) and sent him to a father who could not see, and the text says and he did not recognize him — ve-lo hikkiro (27:23) — and gave him the blessing. Here his sons kill a male goat, dip the coat in its blood, and send it to him with two words: hakker na, identify, please (v32). And va-yakkirah, and he identified it (v33). Same verb, nakhar, both times; goat both times; a garment used to fake an identity both times. Jacob deceived his father with a goat and was not recognized. His sons deceive him with a goat and make him do the recognizing himself.

    And the two words hakker na are said to a man one more time in this book, in the very next chapter: Tamar sends them to Judah in 38:25, with his own staff and seal in her hand. Judah is the brother who proposed the sale in v27.

  • v33 "Torn, Joseph is torn" — tarof toraf Yosef, the doubled verb again, and the root is taraf, the word for an animal killed by a predator. Its noun, terefah, is what Jacob threw at Laban in 31:39: torn flesh I did not bring to you — I made it good myself. For twenty years he absorbed every terefah in the herd rather than claim it. Now he believes his son is one, and there is nobody to make it good.

  • v35 "to Sheol" — she'olah, and this is the first appearance of the word in Genesis, and so the first in the Bible. She'ol is where the dead are, and the Hebrew Bible says remarkably little about it: not a place of punishment, not yet a judgement, simply down, and everyone goes. Jacob's sentence is that he will go down to his son still mourning — he expects to arrive there grieving rather than to be relieved of it.

    And all his sons and all his daughters rose to comfort him. Daughters, plural. Only one is ever named.

  • v36 "chief of the slaughterers" — sar ha-tabbachim, from tabach, to butcher. English Bibles print "captain of the guard," which is what the office is, but the Hebrew title is literally the head butcher, and it is the last phrase of the chapter. Saris, here rendered officer, is the ordinary word for a court official and in later Hebrew means eunuch; in this verse it is a rank, and the story will have something to say about Potiphar's household soon enough.

chapters.title: She Is More in the Right Than I
chapters.html:
Genesis 38

1And it came to pass at that time that Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to an Adullamite man whose name was Hirah.

2And Judah saw there the daughter of a Canaanite man whose name was Shua, and he took her and came to her.

3And she conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Er.

4And she conceived again and bore a son, and she called his name Onan.

5And she bore yet again, a son, and she called his name Shelah. And he was at Chezib when she bore him.

6And Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn, and her name was Tamar.

7And Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death.

8And Judah said to Onan, "Come to your brother's wife and do the brother's duty by her, and raise up seed for your brother."

9And Onan knew that the seed would not be his, and it came about that when he came to his brother's wife he ruined it to the ground, so as not to give seed to his brother.

10And what he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD, and He put him to death also.

11And Judah said to Tamar his daughter-in-law, "Sit as a widow in your father's house until Shelah my son grows up" — for he said, "He might die too, like his brothers." And Tamar went and sat in her father's house.

At the Opening of Enaim

12And the days multiplied, and the daughter of Shua, Judah's wife, died. And Judah was comforted, and he went up to his sheepshearers, he and Hirah his friend the Adullamite, to Timnah.

13And it was told to Tamar, saying, "Here — your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his flock."

14And she took off her widow's clothes from upon her and covered herself with a veil and wrapped herself, and sat at the opening of Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah — for she saw that Shelah had grown up, and she had not been given to him as a wife.

15And Judah saw her and reckoned her a prostitute, because she had covered her face.

16And he turned aside to her by the road and said, "Come now, let me come to you" — for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. And she said, "What will you give me, that you may come to me?"

17And he said, "I will send a kid of the goats from the flock." And she said, "If you give a pledge until you send it."

18And he said, "What is the pledge that I shall give you?" And she said, "Your seal and your cord, and your staff that is in your hand." And he gave them to her, and came to her, and she conceived by him.

19And she rose and went, and took off her veil from upon her, and put on her widow's clothes.

20And Judah sent the kid of the goats by the hand of his friend the Adullamite, to take the pledge from the woman's hand, and he did not find her.

21And he asked the men of her place, saying, "Where is the consecrated woman, the one at Enaim by the road?" And they said, "There has been no consecrated woman here."

22And he returned to Judah and said, "I did not find her. And the men of the place also said, 'There has been no consecrated woman here.'"

23And Judah said, "Let her take them for herself, or we will become a laughingstock. Here, I sent this kid, and you did not find her."

Identify, Please

24And it came to pass, about three months later, that it was told to Judah, saying, "Tamar your daughter-in-law has played the whore, and here, she is also pregnant by whoring." And Judah said, "Bring her out, and let her be burned."

25She was being brought out, and she sent to her father-in-law, saying, "By the man to whom these belong I am pregnant." And she said, "Identify, please — whose are this seal and these cords and this staff?"

26And Judah identified them and said, "She is more in the right than I, because I did not give her to Shelah my son." And he did not know her again.

27And it came to pass at the time of her giving birth, and here — twins in her womb.

28And it came to pass, as she gave birth, that one put out a hand, and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, "This one came out first."

29And it came to pass, as he drew back his hand, that here — his brother came out. And she said, "How you have breached — a breach upon you!" And he called his name Perez.

30And afterward his brother came out, the one with the scarlet thread on his hand. And he called his name Zerah.

Notes

  • v1 "went down from his brothers" — va-yered, he went down. The previous chapter ended with Joseph brought down to Egypt; this one opens with Judah going down from his family, and the two departures are set side by side. The chapter interrupts the Joseph story completely and does not return to it, and the man it follows is the brother who said in 37:27 let us sell him. Whatever else it is doing, the book chooses this moment to leave Joseph in Potiphar's house and spend thirty verses on what became of Judah.

  • v8 "do the brother's duty" — yabbem, a verb made directly from yavam, brother-in-law: to act the brother-in-law. English has no such word and has to spell the custom out. The obligation is codified much later in Deuteronomy 25:5 — her brother-in-law shall come to her... and do the brother's duty by her, the same verb — but here it is already simply assumed, with no law cited and no one surprised by it.

  • v9 "he ruined it to the ground" — ve-shichet artsah, from shachat, to spoil or destroy. The English word onanism comes from this verse, and it names the wrong thing. The text states the offence in the same sentence: so as not to give seed to his brother. Onan takes the marriage and withholds what it was for — the son who would carry his dead brother's name and inherit in his place.

  • v11 "Lest he die also, like his brothers" — the narrator hands us Judah's private reason for sending Tamar home, and it is not care for her. He has buried two sons married to this woman and he thinks she is the cause. He tells her to wait for Shelah; verse 14 says Shelah grew up and she was never sent for.

  • v14 "the opening of Enaim" — petach Einayim. It is a place, and the name is the ordinary Hebrew word for eyes, so the sentence reads as the opening of the eyes as much as it reads as a location. She sits at the eye-opening on the Timnah road, and the whole chapter is about who sees what: Judah sees her and reckons wrongly (v15), and is made to identify his own belongings (v25).

  • v15 "because she had covered her face" — the covering is given as the reason he took her for a prostitute, which runs opposite to a modern reader's instinct. The veil is not what hides an ordinary woman here; it is what marks this one as available. Tamar has read the customs of the road better than her father-in-law reads them.

  • vv15, 21 two different words for what she is — the narrator says Judah reckoned her a zonah, the plain word for a prostitute. But when Hirah asks after her in public he says qedeshah (twice, vv21–22), a word built on q-d-sh, holy, set apart, the root behind qadosh and Qodesh ha-Qodashim, the Holy of Holies. Asking for a zonah by name in a strange town would say one thing; asking for a qedeshah says another. The messenger changes the word.

  • v18 "your seal and your cord, and your staff" — chotam, petil, matteh. A seal is what a man presses into clay to make a document his; the cord hangs it at the neck; the staff is carried and recognized. Tamar does not ask for silver. She asks for the three objects that prove who he is, and keeps them for three months.

  • v24 "let her be burned" — Judah passes a death sentence on his daughter-in-law for an act he paid a goat for on the Timnah road twelve verses earlier. The narrator makes no comment and needs none: both scenes are in the same chapter, and the reader has just read the first one.

  • v25 "Identify, please" — hakker na, and these are the two words Judah's own brothers used in 37:32, sending their father the bloodied coat: identify, please — is it your son's coat or not? Judah was part of that. One chapter later the same two words come back at him with his own seal and staff in the woman's hand, and the answering verb is the same one his father used: va-yakker, and he identified. The man who helped fake a son's death with a goat is exposed by a goat he never managed to deliver.

  • v26 "She is more in the right than I" — tsadeqah mimmenni, from tsadaq, to be in the right, the root behind tsaddiq, a righteous person. It can be read as a comparison — she is more righteous than I — or as a verdict: she is right, and I am not. Either way it is the first time anyone in Genesis says such a sentence about himself, and Judah says it in public, about a woman he has just condemned to death.

  • v29 "Perez" — parats, to break out, breach a wall, burst through. The midwife's line is mah paratsta alekha parets, the verb and the noun together. It is the same root Jacob used of his own wealth in 30:30 and 30:43, and here it names a baby who shoves past his brother in the birth canal. Once more in this book the younger comes out ahead of the elder — and this time it happens physically, in front of a witness, with a scarlet thread already tied on the other one's wrist.

  • v30 "Zerah" — zarach, to rise or shine, the verb used of the sun coming up on Jacob at Penuel in 32:31. The hand with the scarlet thread on it comes out first and the name means dawning, and he is the one who loses.

  • the chapter's point arrives outside the chapter — Ruth 4:18–22 runs the line: Perez fathered Hezron, then Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse — and Jesse fathered David. Ten generations from this birth to the king. And the Greek of Matthew 1:3 keeps the mother in: Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar, one of four women named in that genealogy. The son who mattered came from the daughter-in-law Judah refused to provide for and then sentenced to death.

And the days multiplied, and the daughter of Shua, Judah's wife, died. And Judah was comforted, and he went up to his sheepshearers, he and Hirah his friend the Adullamite, to Timnah.
And it was told to Tamar, saying, "Here — your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his flock."

And she took off her widow's clothes from upon her and covered herself with a veil and wrapped herself, and sat at the opening of Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah — for she saw that Shelah had grown up, and she had not been given to him as a wife.
And Judah saw her and reckoned her a prostitute, because she had covered her face.
And he turned aside to her by the road and said, "Come now, let me come to you" — for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. And she said, "What will you give me, that you may come to me?"
And he said, "I will send a kid of the goats from the flock." And she said, "If you give a pledge until you send it."

And he said, "What is the pledge that I shall give you?" And she said, "Your seal and your cord, and your staff that is in your hand." And he gave them to her, and came to her, and she conceived by him.
And she rose and went, and took off her veil from upon her, and put on her widow's clothes.
And Judah sent the kid of the goats by the hand of his friend the Adullamite, to take the pledge from the woman's hand, and he did not find her.
And he asked the men of her place, saying, "Where is the consecrated woman, the one at Enaim by the road?" And they said, "There has been no consecrated woman here."
And he returned to Judah and said, "I did not find her. And the men of the place also said, 'There has been no consecrated woman here.'"
And Judah said, "Let her take them for herself, or we will become a laughingstock. Here, I sent this kid, and you did not find her."
Identify, Please

And it came to pass, about three months later, that it was told to Judah, saying, "Tamar your daughter-in-law has played the whore, and here, she is also pregnant by whoring." And Judah said, "Bring her out, and let her be burned."

She was being brought out, and she sent to her father-in-law, saying, "By the man to whom these belong I am pregnant." And she said, "Identify, please — whose are this seal and these cords and this staff?"
And Judah identified them and said, "She is more in the right than I, because I did not give her to Shelah my son." And he did not know her again.
And it came to pass at the time of her giving birth, and here — twins in her womb.
And it came to pass, as she gave birth, that one put out a hand, and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, "This one came out first."
And it came to pass, as he drew back his hand, that here — his brother came out. And she said, "How you have breached — a breach upon you!" And he called his name Perez.
And afterward his brother came out, the one with the scarlet thread on his hand. And he called his name Zerah.

chapters.title: And the LORD Was With Joseph
chapters.html:
Genesis 39

1And Joseph was brought down to Egypt, and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, chief of the slaughterers, an Egyptian man, bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there.

2And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a man who prospered, and he was in the house of his Egyptian master.

3And his master saw that the LORD was with him, and that all he did the LORD made prosper in his hand.

4And Joseph found favor in his eyes and served him, and he appointed him over his house, and all he had he gave into his hand.

5And it came to pass, from the time he appointed him over his house and over all he had, that the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house on account of Joseph. And the blessing of the LORD was on all he had, in the house and in the field.

6And he left all he had in Joseph's hand, and he knew nothing of what was with him except the bread he ate. And Joseph was beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance.

Lie With Me

7And it came to pass after these things that his master's wife lifted her eyes to Joseph, and she said, "Lie with me."

8And he refused, and said to his master's wife, "Look — my master does not know what is with me in the house, and all he has he has given into my hand.

9He is no greater in this house than I, and he has withheld nothing from me except you, since you are his wife. And how could I do this great evil, and sin against God?"

10And it came to pass, as she spoke to Joseph day by day, that he did not listen to her, to lie beside her, to be with her.

11And it came to pass on a day like this that he came into the house to do his work, and none of the men of the house was there in the house.

12And she caught him by his garment, saying, "Lie with me." And he left his garment in her hand and fled, and went outside.

13And it came to pass, when she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and fled outside,

14that she called to the men of her house and said to them, saying, "See — he has brought us a Hebrew man to make sport of us. He came to me, to lie with me, and I called out in a loud voice.

15And it came to pass, when he heard that I raised my voice and called, that he left his garment beside me and fled, and went outside."

16And she laid his garment beside her until his master came to his house.

17And she spoke to him according to these words, saying, "The Hebrew slave whom you brought to us came to me, to make sport of me.

18And it came to pass, as I raised my voice and called, that he left his garment beside me and fled outside."

19And it came to pass, when his master heard the words of his wife which she spoke to him, saying, "According to these words your slave did to me," that his anger burned.

20And Joseph's master took him and put him into the round house, the place where the king's prisoners were bound. And he was there in the round house.

21And the LORD was with Joseph, and extended kindness to him, and gave him favor in the eyes of the keeper of the round house.

22And the keeper of the round house gave into Joseph's hand all the prisoners who were in the round house, and everything that was done there, he was the one doing it.

23The keeper of the round house did not look at anything in his hand, because the LORD was with him, and what he did the LORD made prosper.

Notes

  • v1 "was brought down" — hurad, a passive: Joseph does not go, he is taken down. It is the third descent in three chapters. Joseph is brought down to Egypt (37:36), Judah goes down from his brothers (38:1), and now the word comes back twice in one verse, hurad and horiduhu. Everything in this part of the book moves downward before it moves anywhere else.

  • vv2, 3, 5, 21, 23 "the LORD" — the divine name YHWH appears eight times in this chapter, and outside it, in the whole fourteen-chapter Joseph story, it appears four more times in total. Everywhere else God is Elohim — in Joseph's own mouth, in Pharaoh's, in the dream interpretations. This chapter is the exception, and it says the same sentence at both ends: the LORD was with Joseph in the house he runs (v2) and in the prison he is thrown into (v21). The frame is the point.

  • v6 "beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance" — yefeh to'ar vi-yfeh mar'eh, and the phrase is his mother's. 29:17 describes Rachel with the identical words in the feminine: yefat to'ar vi-yfat mar'eh. It is used of no one else in Genesis. Joseph is the only man in the book whose looks are reported, and the sentence used to report them was written for the woman Jacob worked fourteen years to marry.

  • v6 "except the bread he ate" — lo yada itto me'umah ki im ha-lechem asher hu okhel. It may be plain: Potiphar handed over everything but his own meals. It may be a discreet way of saying what a master keeps to himself. Nothing in the sentence settles it, and 43:32 will say that Egyptians could not eat bread with Hebrews, which makes the literal reading do real work.

  • v7 "Lie with me" — shikhvah immi. Two words in Hebrew, and the verb is shakhav, to lie down — the one the book keeps for acts that sit outside the bond they belong in, against yada, to know, which it keeps for the ones inside it (see 4:1). She says the same two words again in v12 while holding his clothes.

  • v8 "And he refused" — va-yema'en, a rare verb, and the whole chapter turns on it. It is the same word used of Jacob in 37:35, who refused to be comforted over this boy's supposed death.

  • v9 "and sin against God" — Joseph's argument runs through Potiphar's trust for two verses and then lands somewhere else entirely. He does not say against my master; he says ve-chatati le-Elohim, and sin against God. It is the first time anyone in Genesis names an act as a sin against God before committing it rather than after.

  • v12 "he left his garment in her hand" — the second time a garment of Joseph's is taken off him and used to tell a lie about him. In 37:23 his brothers stripped his long coat and dipped it in goat's blood so their father would draw the wrong conclusion; here his master's wife keeps a garment in her hand and does the same thing to her husband. Both times the cloth is produced as evidence, and both times what it proves did not happen.

  • vv14, 17 "to make sport of" — le-tsacheq, from tsachaq, to laugh — the root of Isaac's name. The verb turns up in exactly this suggestive register in 26:8, where Abimelech looks out a window and sees Isaac playing with Rebekah his wife and knows at once she is not his sister. It is the same form Sarah saw Ishmael doing in 21:9. She chooses a word that can mean anything from mocking to what the window showed Abimelech.

  • vv14, 17 who she blames, and to whom — to the household she says he has brought us a Hebrew man to make sport of us, which makes the servants fellow-victims and leaves the he unnamed. To her husband the same story becomes the Hebrew slave whom you brought to us... to make sport of me. Between the two tellings the man is demoted from ish to eved, the household drops out, and the blame lands on Potiphar.

  • v19 "his anger burned" — va-yichar appo, and the Hebrew does not say at whom. It says his anger burned, and the next thing he does is put Joseph in the prison that holds the king's own prisoners rather than execute a slave who has been accused of assaulting his wife. The text reports both facts and draws no conclusion from them.

  • v20 "the round house" — beit ha-sohar, and sohar occurs nowhere in the Bible outside this story. Its meaning is not recoverable from Hebrew; the word may not be Hebrew at all. Round is one old guess and a fortress or tower is another, and nothing in the language decides it. This same verse also carries a written-and-read pair the scribes preserved rather than tidy: the consonants אסורי stand on the page while the reading is asirei, prisoners.

  • vv22–23 it happens twice — read verses 4–6 and verses 21–23 side by side and they are the same paragraph. Master sees the LORD is with him; Joseph finds favor; everything is given into his hand; the man over him stops looking at the accounts. Potiphar's house, then the king's prison. The story of Joseph rising is told once, then told again after he has lost everything, in the same words — and the second time he is a convict.

chapters.title: Pharaoh Will Lift Your Head
chapters.html:
Genesis 40

1And it came to pass after these things that the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and the baker offended their lord, the king of Egypt.

2And Pharaoh was furious at his two officers, at the chief of the cupbearers and at the chief of the bakers.

3And he put them in custody in the house of the chief of the slaughterers, into the round house, the place where Joseph was bound.

4And the chief of the slaughterers appointed Joseph to be with them, and he served them. And they were days in custody.

5And the two of them dreamed a dream, each man his dream in one night, each man according to the interpretation of his dream — the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were bound in the round house.

6And Joseph came to them in the morning and saw them, and here — they were downcast.

7And he asked Pharaoh's officers who were with him in custody in his master's house, saying, "Why are your faces bad today?"

8And they said to him, "We have dreamed a dream, and there is no one to interpret it." And Joseph said to them, "Do not interpretations belong to God? Recount them to me, please."

The Vine

9And the chief of the cupbearers recounted his dream to Joseph, and said to him, "In my dream — and here, a vine before me.

10And on the vine three tendrils, and it was as though budding; its blossom went up, its clusters ripened into grapes.

11And Pharaoh's cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup, and I put the cup on Pharaoh's palm."

12And Joseph said to him, "This is its interpretation. The three tendrils are three days.

13In three more days Pharaoh will lift your head and restore you to your place, and you will put Pharaoh's cup in his hand, according to the former custom, when you were his cupbearer.

14Only remember me when it goes well with you, and do kindness with me, please, and mention me to Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house.

15For I was stolen, stolen, from the land of the Hebrews, and here too I have done nothing that they should put me in the pit."

The Baskets

16And the chief of the bakers saw that he had interpreted well, and he said to Joseph, "I also — in my dream, and here, three baskets of white bread on my head.

17And in the topmost basket, from all Pharaoh's food, the work of a baker. And the birds were eating them out of the basket from off my head."

18And Joseph answered and said, "This is its interpretation. The three baskets are three days.

19In three more days Pharaoh will lift your head from off you and hang you on a tree, and the birds will eat your flesh from off you."

20And it came to pass on the third day, the day of Pharaoh's birth, that he made a feast for all his servants. And he lifted the head of the chief of the cupbearers and the head of the chief of the bakers, among his servants.

21And he restored the chief of the cupbearers to his cupbearing, and he put the cup on Pharaoh's palm.

22And the chief of the bakers he hanged, just as Joseph had interpreted to them.

23And the chief of the cupbearers did not remember Joseph, and he forgot him.

Notes

  • v3 "the house of the chief of the slaughterers" — that is Potiphar's title, given in 37:36 and 39:1. The prison Joseph was thrown into in 39:20 sits inside the household he was thrown out of, and in v7 Joseph calls it my master's house. He has been demoted from running the estate to serving prisoners in its lockup, without changing address.

  • v5 "each man according to the interpretation of his dream" — ish ke-fitron chalomo, said before anyone has interpreted anything. The sentence assumes the meaning is already in the dream, waiting, and the only question is who can read it. That assumption is what the next two chapters are built on.

  • v8 "Do not interpretations belong to God?" — ha-lo le-Elohim pitronim, and the first half of their complaint is the setup: u-foter ein oto, there is no interpreter for it. Egypt was full of professional dream-readers; what these two lack is not expertise but access, because they are locked up. Joseph's answer moves the whole business out of the profession and hands it to God — and then he says recount them to me, please.

  • v11 "pressed them into Pharaoh's cup" — va-eschat, from sachat, a verb that appears nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. Whatever its precise force, the action in the dream is immediate: the grapes go from the vine to the cup to the king's hand with nothing in between, which is not how wine is made and is exactly how a dream works.

  • vv13, 19, 20 "Pharaoh will lift your head" — yissa Par'oh et roshekha, and Joseph says the same four words to both men. To the cupbearer it is an idiom for being summoned and restored — the raised head of a man brought back into favour. To the baker it is the same phrase with two words added, me-alekha, from off you.

    Then v20 uses it once for both at the same party: Pharaoh lifted the head of the chief of the cupbearers and the head of the chief of the bakers. One idiom, one sentence, two men, and opposite outcomes. English cannot carry it without the seam showing, and the Hebrew does it without a word of comment.

  • v14 "remember me... mention me" — zekhartani and ve-hizkartani, the same root zakhar twice, the verb used of God remembering Noah in 8:1 and Rachel in 30:22. And asita immadi chased, do kindness with me — chesed, the loyalty word Jacob used in 32:10. Joseph asks a fellow prisoner for what the book has so far only ever said about God.

  • v15 "I was stolen, stolen" — gunnov gunnavti, the verb doubled for emphasis, and it is ganav, the word that ran six times through chapter 31 when Rachel took the household gods and Jacob stole Laban's heart. Joseph says he was stolen. He was sold, by his brothers, and he does not say so — not here, and not to Potiphar, and not to Pharaoh.

  • v15 "the pit" — ba-bor, the same word as the dry cistern his brothers threw him into in 37:24. He uses it of an Egyptian prison. Whatever the building was, the word he reaches for is the one from the field at Dothan.

  • v16 "three baskets of white bread" — sallei chori, and chori is not recoverable. It has been read as white, and as wicker or holed, and nothing in the language settles it. What is clear is the position: the baskets are stacked on his head, the topmost holds the king's own food, and the birds are already eating out of it while he stands there.

  • v19 "hang you on a tree" — ve-talah otekha al ets. The Hebrew says hung on wood and does not specify how; impaling and hanging are both within the word. The detail the dream supplies is the one Joseph repeats back: the birds eat the flesh, which means the body stays up.

  • v16 "he saw that he had interpreted well" — the baker asks only after hearing a good answer. He would not have asked otherwise, and he gets three days' notice of his own execution from a man who owes him nothing and does not soften it. Joseph gives the reading as it is, to a frightened man, with no preamble.

  • v23 "did not remember... and he forgot him" — ve-lo zakhar... va-yishkachehu. Two verbs for one failure, the second one making sure of the first, and they answer Joseph's remember me in v14 exactly. It is the last sentence of the chapter, and the next one begins at the end of two full years.
