chapters.title: A Man in Whom Is the Spirit of God
chapters.html:
Genesis 41

1And it came to pass at the end of two years of days that Pharaoh was dreaming, and here — he was standing by the Nile.

2And here, coming up out of the Nile, seven cows, beautiful of appearance and fat of flesh, and they grazed in the reeds.

3And here, seven other cows coming up after them out of the Nile, bad of appearance and thin of flesh, and they stood beside the cows on the bank of the Nile.

4And the cows bad of appearance and thin of flesh ate the seven cows beautiful of appearance and fat. And Pharaoh awoke.

5And he slept and dreamed a second time, and here — seven ears of grain coming up on one stalk, fat and good.

6And here, seven ears thin and scorched by the east wind, sprouting after them.

7And the thin ears swallowed the seven fat and full ears. And Pharaoh awoke, and here — it was a dream.

8And it came to pass in the morning that his spirit was beaten, and he sent and called all the magicians of Egypt and all her wise men. And Pharaoh recounted his dream to them, and there was no one to interpret them for Pharaoh.

My Offenses I Mention Today

9And the chief of the cupbearers spoke to Pharaoh, saying, "My offenses I mention today.

10Pharaoh was furious at his servants, and he put me in custody in the house of the chief of the slaughterers, me and the chief of the bakers.

11And we dreamed a dream in one night, I and he — each man according to the interpretation of his dream we dreamed.

12And there with us was a Hebrew lad, a slave of the chief of the slaughterers, and we recounted to him, and he interpreted our dreams for us — each man according to his dream he interpreted.

13And it came to pass, just as he interpreted for us, so it was: me he restored to my place, and him he hanged."

14And Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they rushed him out of the pit. And he shaved and changed his clothes, and came to Pharaoh.

15And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I have dreamed a dream, and there is no one to interpret it. And I have heard it said of you that you hear a dream, to interpret it."

16And Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, "Not I. God will answer Pharaoh's welfare."

17And Pharaoh spoke to Joseph: "In my dream — here I was, standing on the bank of the Nile.

18And here, coming up out of the Nile, seven cows fat of flesh and beautiful of form, and they grazed in the reeds.

19And here, seven other cows coming up after them, poor and very bad of form and lean of flesh — I have never seen their like in all the land of Egypt for badness.

20And the lean and bad cows ate the first seven fat cows.

21And they came into their innards, and it was not known that they had come into their innards, and their appearance was as bad as at the beginning. And I awoke.

22And I saw in my dream, and here — seven ears coming up on one stalk, full and good.

23And here, seven ears shriveled, thin, scorched by the east wind, sprouting after them.

24And the thin ears swallowed the seven good ears. And I said it to the magicians, and there was no one telling me."

Pharaoh's Dream Is One

25And Joseph said to Pharaoh, "Pharaoh's dream is one. What God is doing, He has told Pharaoh.

26The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years. It is one dream.

27And the seven lean and bad cows coming up after them are seven years, and the seven empty ears scorched by the east wind — they will be seven years of famine.

28That is the thing I spoke to Pharaoh: what God is doing, He has shown Pharaoh.

29Here — seven years are coming, great plenty in all the land of Egypt.

30And seven years of famine will rise after them, and all the plenty in the land of Egypt will be forgotten, and the famine will finish off the land.

31And the plenty will not be known in the land, because of that famine afterward, for it will be very heavy.

32And as for the dream being repeated to Pharaoh twice — it is because the thing is fixed from God, and God is hurrying to do it.

33And now, let Pharaoh look out a man discerning and wise, and set him over the land of Egypt.

34Let Pharaoh act, and appoint overseers over the land, and take a fifth of the land of Egypt in the seven years of plenty.

35And let them gather all the food of these good years that are coming, and pile up grain under Pharaoh's hand — food in the cities — and keep it.

36And the food shall be a deposit for the land, for the seven years of famine that will be in the land of Egypt, and the land will not be cut off by the famine."

Only the Throne

37And the thing was good in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of all his servants.

38And Pharaoh said to his servants, "Shall we find one like this, a man in whom is the spirit of God?"

39And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has made all this known to you, there is none discerning and wise like you.

40You shall be over my house, and by your mouth all my people shall order themselves. Only by the throne will I be greater than you."

41And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt."

42And Pharaoh took off his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph's hand, and clothed him in garments of fine linen, and put the gold collar on his neck.

43And he had him ride in the second chariot that was his, and they called out before him, "Abrek!" And he set him over all the land of Egypt.

44And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh. And without you no man shall lift his hand or his foot in all the land of Egypt."

45And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphenath-paneah, and gave him Asenath daughter of Poti-phera, priest of On, as a wife. And Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.

46And Joseph was a son of thirty years when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph went out from before Pharaoh and passed through all the land of Egypt.

47And in the seven years of plenty the land produced by handfuls.

48And he gathered all the food of the seven years that were in the land of Egypt, and put food in the cities — the food of the field around each city he put inside it.

49And Joseph piled up grain like the sand of the sea, very much, until he stopped counting, for there was no number.

50And to Joseph were born two sons before the year of famine came, whom Asenath daughter of Poti-phera, priest of On, bore to him.

51And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh — "for God has made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house."

52And the name of the second he called Ephraim — "for God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction."

53And the seven years of plenty that were in the land of Egypt came to an end.

54And the seven years of famine began to come, just as Joseph had said. And there was famine in all the lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.

55And all the land of Egypt was hungry, and the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread. And Pharaoh said to all Egypt, "Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do."

56And the famine was over all the face of the earth, and Joseph opened all that was in them and sold grain to Egypt. And the famine grew strong in the land of Egypt.

57And all the earth came to Egypt to buy grain, to Joseph, because the famine was strong in all the earth.

Notes

  • v1 "at the end of two years of days" — mi-qets shnatayim yamim, and the last sentence of the previous chapter was he forgot him. The text counts the forgetting in years. Nothing happens in them; they are named only to be measured.

  • v1 "the Nile" — ha-ye'or, not the ordinary Hebrew word for a river. It is an Egyptian word taken into Hebrew, and it is used almost exclusively of the Nile. The narrator has moved into Egyptian vocabulary along with the story, and the same happens with chartummim, the magicians of v8.

  • v8 "his spirit was beaten" — va-tippa'em rucho, from pa'am, to strike or beat, the root behind the word for a footstep and for a pulse. Something in him was knocking. Then comes ve-ein poter otam, and there was no one to interpret them — the identical complaint the two prisoners made in 40:8. Pharaoh has every magician in Egypt and is in exactly the position of two convicts in a cell.

  • v9 "My offenses I mention today" — et chata'ai ani mazkir, and mazkir is from zakhar, the very verb 40:23 used twice to say he did not remember and forgot. Joseph had asked him to mention me to Pharaoh (40:14), same root. Two years later he finally mentions — and the first thing he mentions is his own guilt, to save himself in front of a king who has just executed a man over bread.

  • v12 "a Hebrew lad, a slave" — three words, three demotions: na'ar, young; Ivri, foreign; eved, owned. He does not give Joseph's name. He remembers the interpretation exactly and the interpreter not at all.

  • v14 "they rushed him out of the pit" — min ha-bor, the same word Joseph used in 40:15 and the same word for the cistern at Dothan in 37:24. And then va-yegallach, he shaved, and changed his clothes. Egyptians were clean-shaven and Semites were not. Before he may stand in front of the king, the Hebrew is made to look Egyptian — which is why nobody recognizes him in chapter 42.

  • v16 "Not I" — bil'adai, one word, and it is the first thing Joseph says to the most powerful man on earth. He has been in a hole for years and he opens by disclaiming the only skill that can get him out. Pharaoh had said you hear a dream, to interpret it; Joseph gives the credit away before he has been offered anything.

  • vv17–24 Pharaoh changes the dream in the retelling — set his account beside the narrator's in vv2–7 and he has added things nobody told him. Verse 19: I have never seen their like in all the land of Egypt for badness. Verse 21: they came into their innards, and it was not known that they had come into their innards, and their appearance was as bad as at the beginning. Neither sentence is in the dream as reported. The horror of the thing is the king's own, and it is the part he cannot stop saying.

  • v25 "Pharaoh's dream is one" — chalom Par'oh echad hu, and it is Joseph's first move: two dreams, one meaning. Every magician in Egypt had two problems. He tells the king he has one.

  • v32 "the dream being repeated twice" — Joseph interprets not only what the dream shows but the fact that there were two of them. The doubling is itself information: the thing is fixed from God, and God is hurrying to do it. It is the most technically impressive sentence he says, and it is what turns a reading into advice.

  • vv33–36 nobody asked him for a plan — Pharaoh asked for an interpretation. Joseph gives it in eight verses and then keeps going: appoint overseers, take a fifth, store it in the cities under central control, hold it as a piqqadon, a deposit or trust, against the seven years. He is a foreign convict, mid-audience, telling the king how to run the country.

  • v38 "a man in whom is the spirit of God" — ish asher ruach Elohim bo, said by Pharaoh, about a Hebrew slave he met minutes ago. The phrase is God-language in the mouth of a man who is himself worshipped, and the narrator lets it stand without any comment about whose God is meant.

  • v40 "by your mouth all my people shall order themselves" — ve-al pikha yishaq kol ammi. The verb is the problem: yishaq is the ordinary word for kiss, which gives all my people shall kiss upon your mouth, and something in the sense of being ordered or arrayed is the other possibility. Neither reading is secure. What is secure is the next clause — only by the throne will I be greater than you — which fixes how much authority is being handed over even if the idiom is lost.

  • vv42, 45 made Egyptian — a signet ring, linen, a gold collar, a chariot, an Egyptian name (Zaphenath-paneah, whose meaning Hebrew cannot recover), and an Egyptian wife who is a priest's daughter. In v43 the crowd shouts avrekh, a word that appears nowhere else in the Bible and has never been explained. Joseph disappears into Egypt so completely that the chapter can no longer say what his own title means.

  • v46 "a son of thirty years" — he was seventeen in 37:2. Thirteen years between the pit and the chariot, and the text gives them in two numbers and no description.

  • v49 "like the sand of the sea... there was no number" — the phrase God used for the promise to Abraham in 22:17 and Jacob quoted back in 32:12, your seed like the sand of the sea which cannot be counted. Here it is grain. The covenant's own words turn up in a warehouse inventory, and the family it was made to is about to be kept alive by what is in there.

  • vv51–52 the names of his sons — Menasheh from nashah, to forget: God has made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house. He puts his father's house in the same clause as his suffering and names his firstborn after being rid of both. Efrayim from parah, to be fruitful: God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction. He is vizier of Egypt with a wife and two sons, and he still calls it that.

speech.text: Genesis 41
And it came to pass at the end of two years of days that Pharaoh was dreaming, and here — he was standing by the Nile.
And here, coming up out of the Nile, seven cows, beautiful of appearance and fat of flesh, and they grazed in the reeds.
And here, seven other cows coming up after them out of the Nile, bad of appearance and thin of flesh, and they stood beside the cows on the bank of the Nile.
And the cows bad of appearance and thin of flesh ate the seven cows beautiful of appearance and fat. And Pharaoh awoke.
And he slept and dreamed a second time, and here — seven ears of grain coming up on one stalk, fat and good.
And here, seven ears thin and scorched by the east wind, sprouting after them.
And the thin ears swallowed the seven fat and full ears. And Pharaoh awoke, and here — it was a dream.

And it came to pass in the morning that his spirit was beaten, and he sent and called all the magicians of Egypt and all her wise men. And Pharaoh recounted his dream to them, and there was no one to interpret them for Pharaoh.
My Offenses I Mention Today
And the chief of the cupbearers spoke to Pharaoh, saying, "My offenses I mention today.
Pharaoh was furious at his servants, and he put me in custody in the house of the chief of the slaughterers, me and the chief of the bakers.
And we dreamed a dream in one night, I and he — each man according to the interpretation of his dream we dreamed.
And there with us was a Hebrew lad, a slave of the chief of the slaughterers, and we recounted to him, and he interpreted our dreams for us — each man according to his dream he interpreted.
And it came to pass, just as he interpreted for us, so it was: me he restored to my place, and him he hanged."
And Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they rushed him out of the pit. And he shaved and changed his clothes, and came to Pharaoh.
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I have dreamed a dream, and there is no one to interpret it. And I have heard it said of you that you hear a dream, to interpret it."
And Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, "Not I. God will answer Pharaoh's welfare."
And Pharaoh spoke to Joseph: "In my dream — here I was, standing on the bank of the Nile.
And here, coming up out of the Nile, seven cows fat of flesh and beautiful of form, and they grazed in the reeds.
And here, seven other cows coming up after them, poor and very bad of form and lean of flesh — I have never seen their like in all the land of Egypt for badness.
And the lean and bad cows ate the first seven fat cows.
And they came into their innards, and it was not known that they had come into their innards, and their appearance was as bad as at the beginning. And I awoke.
And I saw in my dream, and here — seven ears coming up on one stalk, full and good.
And here, seven ears shriveled, thin, scorched by the east wind, sprouting after them.
And the thin ears swallowed the seven good ears. And I said it to the magicians, and there was no one telling me."
Pharaoh's Dream Is One
And Joseph said to Pharaoh, "Pharaoh's dream is one. What God is doing, He has told Pharaoh.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years. It is one dream.
And the seven lean and bad cows coming up after them are seven years, and the seven empty ears scorched by the east wind — they will be seven years of famine.
That is the thing I spoke to Pharaoh: what God is doing, He has shown Pharaoh.
Here — seven years are coming, great plenty in all the land of Egypt.
And seven years of famine will rise after them, and all the plenty in the land of Egypt will be forgotten, and the famine will finish off the land.
And the plenty will not be known in the land, because of that famine afterward, for it will be very heavy.
And as for the dream being repeated to Pharaoh twice — it is because the thing is fixed from God, and God is hurrying to do it.
And now, let Pharaoh look out a man discerning and wise, and set him over the land of Egypt.
Let Pharaoh act, and appoint overseers over the land, and take a fifth of the land of Egypt in the seven years of plenty.
And let them gather all the food of these good years that are coming, and pile up grain under Pharaoh's hand — food in the cities — and keep it.
And the food shall be a deposit for the land, for the seven years of famine that will be in the land of Egypt, and the land will not be cut off by the famine."
Only the Throne
And the thing was good in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of all his servants.
And Pharaoh said to his servants, "Shall we find one like this, a man in whom is the spirit of God?"
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has made all this known to you, there is none discerning and wise like you.
You shall be over my house, and by your mouth all my people shall order themselves. Only by the throne will I be greater than you."
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt."
And Pharaoh took off his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph's hand, and clothed him in garments of fine linen, and put the gold collar on his neck.
And he had him ride in the second chariot that was his, and they called out before him, "Abrek!" And he set him over all the land of Egypt.
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh. And without you no man shall lift his hand or his foot in all the land of Egypt."
And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphenath-paneah, and gave him Asenath daughter of Poti-phera, priest of On, as a wife. And Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.
And Joseph was a son of thirty years when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph went out from before Pharaoh and passed through all the land of Egypt.
And in the seven years of plenty the land produced by handfuls.
And he gathered all the food of the seven years that were in the land of Egypt, and put food in the cities — the food of the field around each city he put inside it.
And Joseph piled up grain like the sand of the sea, very much, until he stopped counting, for there was no number.
And to Joseph were born two sons before the year of famine came, whom Asenath daughter of Poti-phera, priest of On, bore to him.
And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh — "for God has made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house."
And the name of the second he called Ephraim — "for God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction."
And the seven years of plenty that were in the land of Egypt came to an end.
And the seven years of famine began to come, just as Joseph had said. And there was famine in all the lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.
And all the land of Egypt was hungry, and the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread. And Pharaoh said to all Egypt, "Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do."
And the famine was over all the face of the earth, and Joseph opened all that was in them and sold grain to Egypt. And the famine grew strong in the land of Egypt.
And all the earth came to Egypt to buy grain, to Joseph, because the famine was strong in all the earth.

chapters.title: And They Did Not Know That Joseph Was Listening
chapters.html:
Genesis 42

1And Jacob saw that there was grain in Egypt, and Jacob said to his sons, "Why do you look at one another?"

2And he said, "Here, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy grain for us from there, and let us live and not die."

3And ten of Joseph's brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.

4But Benjamin, Joseph's brother, Jacob did not send with his brothers, for he said, "Harm might come to him."

5And the sons of Israel came to buy among those who were coming, for the famine was in the land of Canaan.

6And Joseph — he was the ruler over the land, he was the one who sold grain to all the people of the land. And Joseph's brothers came and bowed down to him, faces to the ground.

7And Joseph saw his brothers and recognized them, and he made himself a stranger to them and spoke harshly with them. And he said to them, "Where have you come from?" And they said, "From the land of Canaan, to buy food."

8And Joseph recognized his brothers, and they did not recognize him.

9And Joseph remembered the dreams he had dreamed about them, and he said to them, "You are spies. You have come to see the nakedness of the land."

10And they said to him, "No, my lord. Your servants have come to buy food.

11All of us are sons of one man. We are honest men. Your servants have never been spies."

12And he said to them, "No — you have come to see the nakedness of the land."

13And they said, "Your servants are twelve brothers, sons of one man in the land of Canaan. And here, the youngest is with our father today, and the one is not."

14And Joseph said to them, "That is what I said to you: you are spies.

15By this you shall be tested: by the life of Pharaoh, you shall not go out from here unless your youngest brother comes here.

16Send one of you, and let him take your brother, and you be bound, and let your words be tested, whether there is truth with you. And if not — by the life of Pharaoh, you are spies."

17And he gathered them into custody for three days.

We Are Guilty Concerning Our Brother

18And Joseph said to them on the third day, "Do this and live — I fear God.

19If you are honest men, let one of your brothers be bound in your house of custody, and you go, bring grain for the hunger of your houses.

20And bring your youngest brother to me, so your words will be confirmed and you will not die." And they did so.

21And they said, each man to his brother, "Truly we are guilty concerning our brother, whose soul's distress we saw when he pleaded with us, and we did not listen. That is why this distress has come to us."

22And Reuben answered them, saying, "Did I not say to you, 'Do not sin against the boy,' and you did not listen? And now, look, his blood is being required."

23And they did not know that Joseph was listening, because the interpreter was between them.

24And he turned away from them and wept, and returned to them and spoke to them. And he took Simeon from among them and bound him before their eyes.

25And Joseph commanded, and they filled their vessels with grain, and returned each man's silver to his sack, and gave them provisions for the road. And it was done for them so.

26And they loaded their grain on their donkeys and went from there.

27And one of them opened his sack to give fodder to his donkey at the lodging place, and he saw his silver — and here, it was in the mouth of his bag.

28And he said to his brothers, "My silver has been returned, and here — it is in my bag." And their heart went out, and they trembled, each man to his brother, saying, "What is this God has done to us?"

All of Them Are Against Me

29And they came to Jacob their father, to the land of Canaan, and told him all that had befallen them, saying,

30"The man, the lord of the land, spoke harshly with us, and made us out to be spies of the land.

31And we said to him, 'We are honest men. We have never been spies.

32We are twelve brothers, sons of our father. The one is not, and the youngest is with our father today in the land of Canaan.'

33And the man, the lord of the land, said to us, 'By this I will know that you are honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, and take grain for the hunger of your houses and go.

34And bring your youngest brother to me, and I will know that you are not spies, that you are honest men. I will give you your brother, and you may trade in the land.'"

35And it came to pass, as they were emptying their sacks, that here — each man's bundle of silver was in his sack. And they saw their bundles of silver, they and their father, and they were afraid.

36And Jacob their father said to them, "You have bereaved me. Joseph is not, and Simeon is not, and you would take Benjamin. All of them are against me."

37And Reuben said to his father, saying, "You may put my two sons to death if I do not bring him back to you. Give him into my hand, and I will return him to you."

38And he said, "My son shall not go down with you, for his brother is dead and he alone is left. And if harm befalls him on the road you go, you will bring my grey head down in sorrow to Sheol."

Notes

  • vv1, 2 "grain" — shever, and the verb for buying it is lishbor, from shavar, to break. The same noun in the same form means a fracture or a smashing. Hebrew's word for the rations that keep a family alive is its word for something broken, and the chapter uses it eight times without ever needing to explain why.

  • v1 "Why do you look at one another?" — lammah titra'u, an odd form of ra'ah, to see: why are you eyeing each other. It is the first thing Jacob says in the famine, and it is aimed at ten grown men standing in a circle doing nothing.

  • vv4, 38 "lest harm befall him" — ason, a rare word for disaster. It occurs three times in Genesis and all three are Jacob, about Benjamin — here, in v38, and again in 44:29. He has one word for what he is afraid of, and he uses it only about this one son.

  • vv6, 9 the dream, and then the remembering — va-yishtachavu lo appayim artsah, they bowed down to him, faces to the ground, which is 37:7 happening. Three verses later: and Joseph remembered the dreams he had dreamed about them. The text puts the bowing first and the remembering second. He does not recognize the moment as it arrives; he recognizes it afterward, and what he does next he does knowing.

  • vv7, 8 recognized, and made himself a stranger — va-yakkirem va-yitnakker aleihem: two verbs from the same root, nakar, back to back, meaning to recognize and to act the stranger. Then v8 says it again from both sides — Joseph recognized his brothers, and they did not recognize him. This is the fourth chapter running to turn on this root: the bloodied coat in 37:32, Judah's seal in 38:25, and now a man using one half of the word to hide behind the other.

  • v9 "the nakedness of the land" — ervat ha-arets. Ervah is the word for exposed genitals; it is the term Leviticus uses for forbidden sexual uncovering. Applied to a country it means the undefended places, where the walls are weak — but the word he picks is a shame word, and he is saying it to his own brothers.

  • vv11, 19, 31, 33, 34 "honest men" — kenim, from ken, true, upright, so. They say it about themselves five times in one chapter, and Joseph feeds it back to them twice. Everything they say about their family is accurate except one clause, and they have been saying that clause for twenty years.

  • vv13, 32 "and the one is not" — ve-ha-echad einennu, twice, and it is the family's settled formula. Not died, not was killed: he is not. Reuben used the same word at the empty pit in 37:30, ha-yeled einennu, the boy is not. Jacob uses it of two sons at once in v36. The man they are standing in front of has been einennu since they made him so.

  • vv15, 18 two oaths in four verses — Joseph swears chei Far'oh, by the life of Pharaoh, twice, in the voice of an Egyptian official. Then on the third day he tells them et ha-Elohim ani yare, I fear God. The reader knows which one is his. The brothers hear an Egyptian who has mentioned a god.

  • v21 something chapter 37 never told us — whose soul's distress we saw when he pleaded with us, and we did not listen. Go back to 37:23–24 and there is none of this: the coat is stripped, he is thrown in the pit, they sit down to eat. Not one word about Joseph begging, and not one word about them hearing him. Twenty years later his brothers supply it themselves, in front of him, and the narrator lets the earlier silence stand uncorrected. The pleading was always in the story; it was just never written down.

    And the word they use for his suffering is tsarah — tsarat nafsho — and then they use it again for their own: that is why this tsarah has come to us. Same word, his and theirs.

  • v23 "because the interpreter was between them" — ha-melits beinotam, a word that appears in only one other place in the Hebrew Bible. It explains the entire scene: they have been talking freely in Hebrew in front of an Egyptian official, and confessing to his face because they are certain he cannot understand. He can. And the sentence that tells us is placed immediately after their confession, not before it — so the reader hears it the way Joseph did.

  • v24 "he turned away from them and wept" — the first of the times he cries in this story, and he goes out of the room to do it. Then he comes back and continues the interrogation.

  • v24 he takes Simeon — not Reuben, the firstborn, who has just been heard reminding them he tried to stop it (v22). Simeon is the next in line, and he is one of the two who emptied Shechem in chapter 34. The text gives the choice and no reason for it.

  • vv28, 35 the silver — planted by Joseph (v25), found at the lodging place, and found again in every sack when they get home. Their response is what is this God has done to us? Silver has been in this family's story before: twenty pieces of it, in chapter 37, for a brother. It is the one thing they cannot get rid of.

  • v36 "All of them are against me" — alai hayu khullanah, and the sentence before it names his losses in order: Joseph is not, and Simeon is not. He does not know that Simeon is with Joseph and that neither is lost. He is the only person in the chapter who is wrong about everything, and he is the only one who has not done anything.

  • v38 "down in sorrow to Sheol" — ve-horadtem et seivati be-yagon she'olah, and he said almost this in 37:35 when they brought him the coat: I will go down to my son, mourning, to Sheol. The two are the only times Sheol appears in Genesis, and both are Jacob, and both are about Rachel's sons. He also says his brother is dead, plainly, for the first time.

chapters.title: I Will Stand Surety for Him
chapters.html:
Genesis 43

1And the famine was heavy in the land.

2And it came to pass, when they had finished eating the grain they had brought from Egypt, that their father said to them, "Go back, buy us a little food."

3And Judah said to him, saying, "The man solemnly warned us, saying, 'You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you.'

4If you will send our brother with us, we will go down and buy you food.

5And if you will not send him, we will not go down — for the man said to us, 'You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you.'"

6And Israel said, "Why did you do me this harm, telling the man you had another brother?"

7And they said, "The man asked closely about us and about our kindred, saying, 'Is your father still alive? Do you have a brother?' And we told him according to these words. Could we possibly know that he would say, 'Bring your brother down'?"

8And Judah said to Israel his father, "Send the boy with me, and let us rise and go, and let us live and not die — we, and you, and our little ones.

9I will stand surety for him. From my hand you shall require him. If I do not bring him to you and set him before you, then I will have sinned against you all my days.

10For if we had not delayed, we would have been back twice by now."

11And Israel their father said to them, "If it must be so, then do this. Take some of the land's choice produce in your vessels and bring the man down a gift: a little balm and a little honey, gum and ladanum, pistachios and almonds.

12And take double silver in your hand, and the silver that was returned in the mouth of your bags — take it back in your hand. Perhaps it was an oversight.

13And take your brother, and rise, go back to the man.

14And may God Almighty give you compassion before the man, so he sends away with you your other brother, and Benjamin. And I — as I have been bereaved, I am bereaved."

Bring the Men to the House

15And the men took this gift, and they took double silver in their hand, and Benjamin. And they rose and went down to Egypt and stood before Joseph.

16And Joseph saw Benjamin with them, and said to the one over his house, "Bring the men to the house, and slaughter a slaughter and prepare it, for the men will eat with me at noon."

17And the man did as Joseph said, and the man brought the men to Joseph's house.

18And the men were afraid because they had been brought to Joseph's house, and they said, "It is over the matter of the silver returned in our bags the first time that we are being brought in — to roll himself upon us and fall upon us, and take us as slaves, and our donkeys."

19And they came up to the man who was over Joseph's house and spoke to him at the door of the house,

20and said, "Please, my lord — we came down, came down the first time to buy food.

21And it came to pass, when we came to the lodging place and opened our bags, that here — each man's silver was in the mouth of his bag, our silver by its weight. And we have brought it back in our hand.

22And we have brought down other silver in our hand to buy food. We do not know who put our silver in our bags."

23And he said, "Peace to you. Do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your father gave you treasure in your bags. Your silver came to me." And he brought Simeon out to them.

24And the man brought the men into Joseph's house and gave water, and they washed their feet, and he gave fodder to their donkeys.

25And they prepared the gift for Joseph's coming at noon, for they had heard that they would eat bread there.

Is It Well With Your Father?

26And Joseph came to the house, and they brought him the gift that was in their hand, into the house, and bowed down to him to the ground.

27And he asked them about their peace, and said, "Is it well with your father, the old man you spoke of? Is he still alive?"

28And they said, "It is well with your servant our father. He is still alive." And they knelt and bowed down.

29And he lifted his eyes and saw Benjamin his brother, his mother's son, and said, "Is this your youngest brother, whom you spoke of to me?" And he said, "God be gracious to you, my son."

30And Joseph hurried, for his compassion grew hot toward his brother, and he sought to weep. And he came into the chamber and wept there.

31And he washed his face and came out, and he held himself in, and said, "Set out bread."

32And they set it out for him by himself, and for them by themselves, and for the Egyptians eating with him by themselves — because Egyptians could not eat bread with Hebrews, for that is an abomination to Egypt.

33And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his youth, and the men looked at one another in astonishment.

34And he had portions carried to them from before his face, and Benjamin's portion was five times more than the portions of all of them. And they drank and became drunk with him.

Notes

  • vv3, 5 "You shall not see my face" — lo tir'u fanai, and Judah quotes it twice in three verses. Joseph did not say this in chapter 42; what he said there was you shall not go out from here (42:15). The brothers have been carrying the demand around in terms of a face they may not look at, and the word panim is the one this whole reunion turns on: they bow before his face (v26), he sends portions from before his face (v34), and in 45:3 he will finally say I am Joseph.

  • v7 "The man asked closely about us" — sha'ol sha'al, the verb doubled: he questioned and questioned. Except that he did not. Read 42:13 again and the brothers volunteer the whole family — twelve of us, one gone, the youngest at home — with no question asked. Under their father's anger they remember an interrogation instead. It is the second time in two chapters that the brothers narrate an earlier scene differently from how it was written, and the narrator corrects neither.

  • v9 "I will stand surety for him" — anokhi e'ervennu, from arav, to pledge, to go bail. Its noun is eravon, and the last time this root appeared was 38:17–18, when Judah handed a woman on the road his seal and staff as a pledge and lost them. He now offers himself as the pledge, for the brother of the boy he sold. And mi-yadi tevaqshennu, from my hand you shall require him, is what Reuben's his blood is being required (42:22) was pointing at.

  • v9 against 37:26 — the last plan Judah proposed about a brother of Joseph's was what profit is it that we kill our brother... let us sell him. This is the same man, to the same father, about the same mother's other son, offering to answer for him with everything he has. The book puts the two sentences six chapters apart and says nothing.

  • v11 "the land's choice produce" — mi-zimrat ha-arets, and zimrah elsewhere means music, a song. What it is doing here is not settled; the sense required is something like the land's best or its yield, and no other passage pins it down. The old translations reach for the best fruits, which is a guess with a long pedigree.

  • v11 the gift is the cargo that carried Joseph away — Jacob's list includes tsori, nekhot and lot — balm, gum, ladanum. In 37:25 the Ishmaelite caravan his sons sold Joseph to was carrying nekhot u-tsori va-lot, the same three commodities, down to Egypt. Jacob, who does not know, sends after his lost son the exact goods that were on the camels that took him.

  • v14 "give you compassion" — rachamim, a plural noun built on rechem, womb. Hebrew's word for mercy is the organ a mother carries a child in. Jacob asks El Shaddai for womb-feeling from an Egyptian official, on behalf of Rachel's last son.

  • v14 "as I have been bereaved, I am bereaved" — ka'asher shakholti shakhalti. The same verb twice, perfect tense both times, with nothing between them. He is not saying if I lose him I lose him; he is speaking as a man already robbed, agreeing to be robbed again.

  • v16 "slaughter a slaughter" — u-tvoach tevach, verb and its own noun. The root is tabach, and it is the root of Potiphar's title, sar ha-tabbachim, chief of the slaughterers (37:36). The word that named the man who owned Joseph is now an order Joseph gives about lunch.

  • v18 "take us as slaves" — la-avadim, and this is what the ten of them are afraid of, standing in Egypt. They are the men who took twenty pieces of silver for a brother and let him be taken there as one. The narrator reports the fear without a flicker.

  • v23 "Your God and the God of your father gave you treasure" — the steward, an Egyptian, answers a question about missing silver by naming their God, tells them their money reached him, and produces Simeon. Every word of it is a cover story, and it is the kindest speech anyone makes to them in three chapters.

  • vv27–28 "peace" — shalom, four times in two verses. He asks after their shalom, then after their father's; they answer shalom. In 37:4 these men could not speak to him le-shalom, could not say a peaceable word. In 37:14 their father sent him to see the shalom of your brothers, which is the errand that ended in the pit. He is now standing in front of them asking the question he was sent to ask, and they answer it.

  • v30 "his compassion grew hot" — nikhmeru rachamav, from kamar, to be heated or stirred up; rachamim is the womb-word again, the one his father used in v14. Jacob asked God to give the Egyptian rachamim toward his sons. Sixteen verses later the Egyptian's rachamim boil over and he has to leave the room.

  • v31 "he held himself in" — va-yit'appaq, a rare verb for forcing back what is rising. He washes his face first, then does it, then gives an order about food. The same verb comes back in 45:1, where he could not do it any more.

  • v32 three tables — Egyptians will not eat bread with Hebrews, ki to'evah hi le-Mitsrayim, because it is an abomination. And Joseph eats alone, at neither table. It is also the sentence that makes 39:6 literal: Potiphar left Joseph everything except the bread he ate.

  • v33 seated in birth order — ha-bekhor ki-vkhorato ve-ha-tsa'ir ki-ts'irato, the firstborn by his birthright, the youngest by his youth, and va-yitmehu ha-anashim, the men were astonished at one another. An Egyptian official has just seated eleven strangers in the exact order they were born. They have no explanation and the text offers them none.

  • v34 "five times more" — chamesh yadot, five hands. He has the youngest son of his own mother served five portions in front of ten older brothers, and then they drink together. It is the arrangement that started all of this — one favoured boy, ten watching — rebuilt deliberately by the boy, who sits where the father used to sit.

chapters.title: Let Your Servant Stay Instead of the Boy
chapters.html:
Genesis 44

1And he commanded the one over his house, saying, "Fill the men's bags with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man's silver in the mouth of his bag.

2And my goblet, the silver goblet, put in the mouth of the youngest one's bag, with his grain silver." And he did according to Joseph's word that he spoke.

3The morning was light, and the men were sent off, they and their donkeys.

4They had gone out of the city, not far, and Joseph said to the one over his house, "Rise, pursue after the men, and overtake them, and say to them, 'Why have you repaid evil for good?

5Is this not the one my lord drinks from, and by which he certainly divines? You have done evil in what you have done.'"

6And he overtook them and spoke these words to them.

7And they said to him, "Why does my lord speak such words? Far be it from your servants to do such a thing.

8Look — the silver we found in the mouth of our bags, we brought back to you from the land of Canaan. How then could we steal silver or gold from your lord's house?

9The one of your servants it is found with shall die, and we also will be slaves to my lord."

10And he said, "Now also, let it be according to your words: the one it is found with shall be my slave, and you shall be clear."

11And they hurried and each man lowered his bag to the ground, and each man opened his bag.

12And he searched — he began with the eldest and finished with the youngest — and the goblet was found in Benjamin's bag.

13And they tore their clothes, and each man loaded his donkey, and they returned to the city.

14And Judah came, and his brothers, to Joseph's house — and he was still there — and they fell before him to the ground.

15And Joseph said to them, "What is this deed you have done? Did you not know that a man like me certainly divines?"

16And Judah said, "What shall we say to my lord? What shall we speak, and how shall we justify ourselves? God has found out the guilt of your servants. Here we are, slaves to my lord — we, and also the one in whose hand the goblet was found."

17And he said, "Far be it from me to do this. The man in whose hand the goblet was found, he shall be my slave, and you — go up in peace to your father."

Judah Comes Near

18And Judah came near to him and said, "Please, my lord — let your servant speak a word in my lord's ears, and let your anger not burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh.

19My lord asked his servants, saying, 'Do you have a father, or a brother?'

20And we said to my lord, 'We have an old father, and a child of his old age, a little one. And his brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother, and his father loves him.'

21And you said to your servants, 'Bring him down to me, and let me set my eye on him.'

22And we said to my lord, 'The boy cannot leave his father. If he leaves his father, he will die.'

23And you said to your servants, 'If your youngest brother does not come down with you, you shall not see my face again.'

24And it came to pass, when we went up to your servant my father, that we told him my lord's words.

25And our father said, 'Go back, buy us a little food.'

26And we said, 'We cannot go down. If our youngest brother is with us, then we will go down — for we cannot see the man's face unless our youngest brother is with us.'

27And your servant my father said to us, 'You know that my wife bore me two.

28And the one went out from me, and I said, Surely he is torn, torn — and I have not seen him since.

29And if you take this one also from my face, and harm befalls him, you will bring my grey head down in evil to Sheol.'

30And now, when I come to your servant my father and the boy is not with us — and his soul is bound up with his soul —

31it will come to pass, when he sees that the boy is not, that he will die. And your servants will bring the grey head of your servant our father down in sorrow to Sheol.

32For your servant became surety for the boy with my father, saying, 'If I do not bring him to you, then I will have sinned against my father all my days.'

33And now, let your servant stay instead of the boy as a slave to my lord, and let the boy go up with his brothers.

34For how can I go up to my father and the boy not with me — and see the evil that would find my father."

Notes

  • v2 "the silver goblet" — gevia ha-kesef, and silver is what this family does. Twenty pieces of it bought Joseph in 37:28; it turned up in every sack in 42:35 and they were terrified of it; they carried it back double in 43:12. Now a silver cup is planted on the one brother who was not there when the first silver changed hands.

  • vv5, 15 "he certainly divines by it" — nachesh yenachesh, from nachash, reading omens. The only other person in Genesis who says this word is Laban, in 30:27: nichashti, I have read the omens. Joseph, dressed as an Egyptian, now has the practice of Jacob's father-in-law attributed to him — and in v15 he says it of himself, a man like me certainly divines. Whether he does or is bluffing, the text does not say. It is part of the costume either way.

  • v8 "How then could we steal" — ve-eikh nignov, the verb ganav that ran six times through chapter 31 and that Joseph used of himself in 40:15: I was stolen, stolen. These ten men are protesting, with complete sincerity, that theft is not the sort of thing they do.

  • v9 "shall die" — they pronounce sentence on themselves unprompted, and it has happened in this family before. In 31:32 Jacob told Laban with whomever you find your gods, he shall not live, not knowing Rachel had taken them. Here Rachel's other son has the cup. Both times a man swears blind about something hidden in the baggage, and both times the person he has condemned is the one he would least choose.

  • v12 "he began with the eldest and finished with the youngest" — the steward could have gone straight to the bag he packed. Instead he works down the line in birth order while ten men watch their brother's turn come. It is the same knowledge of their ages that astonished them at the table in 43:33, used this time to draw the thing out.

  • v13 "And they tore their clothes" — va-yiqre'u simlotam. Their father did this in 37:34, over a coat they had dipped in goat's blood and sent him. They are now doing it themselves, over a brother they have not harmed, in a trouble they did not arrange.

  • v14 "And Judah came, and his brothers" — not Reuben, who is the firstborn and who offered his own two sons as security in 42:37. From here to the end of the chapter, Judah speaks for all of them.

  • v16 "How shall we justify ourselves?" — ma nitstaddaq, from tsadaq, to be in the right. Judah is the one man in Genesis who uses this root about himself, and both times it is a surrender: in 38:26 she is more in the right than I, and here what shall we say... God has found out the guilt of your servants. They are not guilty of the cup. He confesses anyway, to something he does not name, in front of the brother it was done to.

  • vv18–34 seventeen verses, uninterrupted — Judah speaks and nobody answers him until the next chapter. And he argues nothing. He cites no law, denies no charge, offers no evidence about the cup; he simply retells the story from his father's side and then asks to take the punishment. It works, and chapter 45 begins with Joseph unable to keep it up any longer.

  • v20 "a child of his old age" — yeled zequnim, and that is the narrator's phrase for Joseph in 37:3: Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, for he was a son of his old age. Judah is describing Benjamin to a stranger in the exact words the book used for the brother he sold.

  • v20 "and his father loves him" — Judah says this out loud, as an argument, to the man whose being loved is the reason he was thrown in a pit. The sentence that made Joseph hated in 37:4 is now the one being used to plead for Benjamin's life, by the brother who proposed the sale.

  • v27 "my wife bore me two" — Jacob's words, relayed by Judah, who is Leah's son. Four of the men standing there are Leah's, and their father speaks of Rachel as my wife and counts his children as two. Judah repeats it to a foreign official without a flicker, as though it were simply how things are.

  • v28 "Surely he is torn, torn" — tarof toraf, precisely what Jacob said in 37:33 when he identified the coat. Judah is quoting his father quoting a lie that Judah helped stage, to the man the lie was about, who is listening.

  • v29 "harm befalls him" — ason, the third and last time the word appears in Genesis. All three are Jacob, all three about Benjamin (42:4, 42:38, and here). Judah has heard it often enough to quote it.

  • v30 "his soul is bound up with his soul" — ve-nafsho qeshurah be-nafsho, from qashar, to tie or knot. Nefesh is the breath and the life, not a spirit in the later sense. Judah's case is not that Benjamin will be hurt; it is that the two lives are knotted together and cutting one cuts both.

  • v33 "let your servant stay instead of the boy" — tachat ha-na'ar, in his place, eved, a slave. This is Judah, who said in 37:27 let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, offering to be sold himself so that Rachel's remaining son can go home to the father who loves him more. Nothing in the chapter marks it as the turning point. It simply is one.

  • v34 the last word — he does not finish on Benjamin. Lest I see the evil that would find my father. Twenty-two years earlier this man watched his father shown a bloodied coat and said nothing.

chapters.title: I Am Joseph. Is My Father Still Alive?
chapters.html:
Genesis 45

1And Joseph could not hold himself in before all those standing by him, and he called out, "Take every man out from me!" And no man stood with him when Joseph made himself known to his brothers.

2And he gave his voice in weeping, and Egypt heard, and the house of Pharaoh heard.

3And Joseph said to his brothers, "I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?" And his brothers could not answer him, for they were terrified before his face.

4And Joseph said to his brothers, "Come near to me, please." And they came near. And he said, "I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold into Egypt.

5And now, do not be grieved, and do not let it burn in your eyes that you sold me here — for it was to preserve life that God sent me ahead of you.

6For these two years the famine has been within the land, and there are five more years in which there is no plowing and no harvest.

7And God sent me ahead of you to set for you a remnant in the land, and to keep you alive for a great deliverance.

8And now — it was not you who sent me here, but God. And He has made me a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house, and ruler in all the land of Egypt.

9Hurry and go up to my father and say to him, 'So says your son Joseph: God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me, do not stand still.

10And you shall dwell in the land of Goshen, and you shall be near me — you and your sons and your sons' sons, and your flocks and your herds and all that is yours.

11And I will sustain you there, for there are five more years of famine — otherwise you will be dispossessed, you and your house and all that is yours.'

12And here, your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin, that it is my mouth speaking to you.

13And you shall tell my father of all my weight in Egypt, and all that you have seen. And hurry, and bring my father down here."

14And he fell on the neck of Benjamin his brother and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck.

15And he kissed all his brothers and wept over them, and after that his brothers spoke with him.

Pharaoh Hears

16And the sound was heard in Pharaoh's house, saying, "Joseph's brothers have come." And it was good in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of his servants.

17And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Say to your brothers, 'Do this: load your beasts and go, come to the land of Canaan.

18And take your father and your households and come to me, and I will give you the good of the land of Egypt, and you will eat the fat of the land.'

19And you are commanded: 'Do this — take wagons for yourselves from the land of Egypt, for your little ones and for your wives, and carry your father, and come.

20And let your eye not pity your belongings, for the good of all the land of Egypt is yours.'"

21And the sons of Israel did so. And Joseph gave them wagons, by Pharaoh's mouth, and gave them provisions for the road.

22To all of them he gave, to each man, changes of clothing — and to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of clothing.

23And to his father he sent the like of this: ten donkeys carrying the good of Egypt, and ten she-donkeys carrying grain and bread and food for his father for the road.

24And he sent his brothers off, and they went, and he said to them, "Do not be stirred up on the road."

25And they went up from Egypt and came to the land of Canaan, to Jacob their father.

26And they told him, saying, "Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler in all the land of Egypt." And his heart went numb, for he did not believe them.

27And they spoke to him all Joseph's words that he had spoken to them, and he saw the wagons Joseph had sent to carry him. And the spirit of Jacob their father revived.

28And Israel said, "Enough. Joseph my son is still alive. Let me go and see him before I die."

Notes

  • v1 "could not hold himself in" — ve-lo yakhol Yosef le-hit'appeq, and the verb is the rare one from 43:31, where he washed his face and did hold himself in. Same word, two chapters apart, this time with a could not in front of it. Judah's speech is what stands between them.

  • v1 "made himself known" — be-hitvadda Yosef el echav, and the root is yada, to know — the verb of 4:1 and of the tree of knowing. Three chapters have run on nakar, recognizing and refusing to recognize; the recognition itself, when it finally comes, is not nakar at all. He makes himself known.

  • vv1–2 he clears the room and then everyone hears — take every man out from me, and no man stood with him. Then he gave his voice in weeping, and Egypt heard, and the house of Pharaoh heard. He arranges privacy and immediately makes it useless. It is the third time he has wept in three chapters (42:24, 43:30), and the first time he does not hide it.

  • v3 "I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?" — he asked this in 43:27 and was told yes. He asks it again in the same breath as his own name, which means the first answer was given to an Egyptian official and does not count. And they could not answer him, for they were terrified before his face — nivhalu mi-panav. They have spent three chapters trying to see this face.

  • v4 "whom you sold into Egypt" — he says it plainly, to their faces, and it is the first time anyone in the book has stated it out loud. In 42:21 they said we are guilty concerning our brother without naming what they did. In 40:15 Joseph told the cupbearer he had been stolen, not sold. Here the sentence is complete for the first time, and the man saying it is the one it was done to.

  • vv5, 7, 8 "God sent me" — shelachani Elohim, three times in four verses, and the third goes furthest: it was not you who sent me here, but God. It does not cancel v4. He has just said you sold me, and he does not withdraw it. Both sentences are allowed to stand, and the text never reconciles them.

  • v7 "a great deliverance" — lifleitah gedolah, and peleitah is an escape, a remnant that gets out. Jacob used it in 32:9, splitting his camps before meeting Esau: the camp that is left will be an escape. The word his father reached for in terror is the word Joseph uses for what the whole family has become.

  • v8 "a father to Pharaoh" — le-av le-Far'oh, a court title for a senior counsellor. The boy who was taken from his father, and who named his firstborn for forgetting all my father's house (41:51), is styled father to a king — three verses before he starts begging for his own father to be brought down.

  • v12 "that it is my mouth speaking to you" — ki fi ha-medabber aleikhem. In 42:23 there was an interpreter between them, and they said things in front of him they would never have said to him. He is telling them that the translator is gone, and has been for some time.

  • v15 "and after that his brothers spoke with him" — they have not said one word since verse 3. Joseph talks for twelve verses, weeps on Benjamin's neck, kisses all of them, and only then do they speak. What they said is not recorded.

  • v22 he does it again, on purpose — everyone gets a change of clothing; Benjamin gets three hundred pieces of silver and five. In 43:34 Benjamin's portion at the table was five times the others'. And the thing that started all of this in 37:3 was a garment given to one son and not the rest. Joseph hands ten older brothers the exact arrangement that got him sold, and then in v24 tells them not to get worked up on the way home.

  • v24 "Do not be stirred up on the road" — al tirgezu ba-darekh, from ragaz, to tremble, quake, be agitated — and in some uses, to quarrel. So it reads either as do not be afraid or as do not fight among yourselves, and the Hebrew does not choose. Given what is in Benjamin's saddlebags, both readings have something to work with.

  • v26 "his heart went numb" — va-yafag libbo, from pug, to grow faint or go slack; it is a rare verb and this is its picture of shock. The narrator adds the reason without softening it: ki lo he'emin lahem, for he did not believe them. His sons tell him the truth and he does not believe them, which is the exact consequence of what they did in 37:32.

  • v27 the wagons are what convince him — and he saw the wagons Joseph had sent to carry him, and only then the spirit of Jacob their father revived. Words from these ten men were not enough. Physical evidence sent from Egypt was. The last time they brought him evidence from a distance it was a coat.

  • v28 "Enough" — rav, one word, and the narrator switches his name in the same sentence: and Israel said. He has been Jacob for two verses of numb disbelief. He becomes Israel when he decides to go.

chapters.title: I Will Go Down With You, and I Will Surely Bring You Up
chapters.html:
Genesis 46

1And Israel pulled up, and all that was his, and came to Beersheba, and sacrificed sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.

2And God said to Israel in the visions of the night, and He said, "Jacob, Jacob." And he said, "Here I am."

3And He said, "I am the God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make you a great nation there.

4I Myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I Myself will surely bring you up again. And Joseph will set his hand on your eyes."

5And Jacob rose from Beersheba, and the sons of Israel carried Jacob their father, and their little ones and their wives, in the wagons Pharaoh had sent to carry him.

6And they took their livestock and their goods that they had gotten in the land of Canaan, and came to Egypt — Jacob and all his seed with him,

7his sons and his sons' sons with him, his daughters and his sons' daughters, and all his seed he brought with him to Egypt.

The Names

8And these are the names of the sons of Israel coming to Egypt — Jacob and his sons. Jacob's firstborn, Reuben.

9And the sons of Reuben: Hanoch and Pallu and Hezron and Carmi.

10And the sons of Simeon: Jemuel and Jamin and Ohad and Jachin and Zohar, and Shaul son of the Canaanite woman.

11And the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

12And the sons of Judah: Er and Onan and Shelah and Perez and Zerah — and Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. And the sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.

13And the sons of Issachar: Tola and Puvah and Job and Shimron.

14And the sons of Zebulun: Sered and Elon and Jahleel.

15These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan-aram, and Dinah his daughter. All the souls of his sons and his daughters: thirty-three.

16And the sons of Gad: Ziphion and Haggi, Shuni and Ezbon, Eri and Arodi and Areli.

17And the sons of Asher: Imnah and Ishvah and Ishvi and Beriah, and Serah their sister. And the sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel.

18These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to Leah his daughter, and she bore these to Jacob — sixteen souls.

19The sons of Rachel, Jacob's wife: Joseph and Benjamin.

20And there were born to Joseph in the land of Egypt, whom Asenath daughter of Poti-phera, priest of On, bore to him: Manasseh and Ephraim.

21And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher and Ashbel, Gera and Naaman, Ehi and Rosh, Muppim and Huppim and Ard.

22These are the sons of Rachel, who were born to Jacob — all the souls, fourteen.

23And the sons of Dan: Hushim.

24And the sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel and Guni and Jezer and Shillem.

25These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel his daughter, and she bore these to Jacob — all the souls, seven.

26All the souls coming with Jacob to Egypt, who came out of his loins, apart from the wives of Jacob's sons — all the souls were sixty-six.

27And the sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were two souls. All the souls of the house of Jacob coming to Egypt: seventy.

Goshen

28And he sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph, to point the way before him to Goshen. And they came to the land of Goshen.

29And Joseph harnessed his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father at Goshen. And he appeared to him, and fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a long while.

30And Israel said to Joseph, "Let me die this time, after seeing your face, since you are still alive."

31And Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's house, "I will go up and tell Pharaoh, and say to him, 'My brothers and my father's house, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.

32And the men are shepherds of flocks, for they have been men of livestock, and they have brought their flocks and their herds and all that is theirs.'

33And it will come to pass, when Pharaoh calls you and says, 'What is your work?' —

34then you shall say, 'Your servants have been men of livestock from our youth until now, both we and our fathers' — so that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, for every shepherd of flocks is an abomination to Egypt."

Notes

  • v1 "to Beersheba" — he stops where his family's story has stopped before. Abraham planted a tamarisk at Beersheba and called on the name of El Olam there (21:33); Isaac lived there. Jacob is on his way out of the land for good and he pulls up at the last place in it that belongs to his father and grandfather, and offers sacrifices there.

  • v2 "Jacob, Jacob" — the doubled name, answered with hinneni, here I am. It happened once before in this book: Abraham, Abraham at the knife, in 22:11, answered the same way. It is the form of address for the moment before something irreversible.

  • v3 "Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt" — and one generation earlier God told Isaac the exact opposite. In 26:2, in a famine, the LORD appeared to him and said, do not go down to Egypt, same verb yarad. And Abram in 12:10 went down in a famine with no divine word at all, and it went badly. Three generations, three descents, three different answers — forbidden, unmentioned, and now commanded.

  • v4 "I will go down with you... and I will surely bring you up" — anokhi ered immekha... ve-anokhi a'alkha gam aloh, with the emphatic I Myself twice. Down and up: yarad and alah are the two verbs the Bible will use for Egypt for the next four hundred years. The whole Exodus is promised here, in one sentence, to one frightened old man who will not live to see it.

  • v4 "Joseph will set his hand on your eyes" — closing the eyes of the dead. It is the last clause of the promise and the smallest: after the nation and the going up, God tells him who will be standing there when he dies.

  • v7 "his daughters and his sons' daughters" — plural, twice. The book names exactly two women in this generation: Dinah in v15 and Serah daughter of Asher in v17, and Serah is named for no stated reason at all. The rest are counted and not named.

  • v12 "Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan" — they are listed among Judah's sons and then immediately reported dead, in the same verse. The list does not drop them. It carries them and then tells you.

  • v15 "thirty-three" — count the names in verses 9–15 and there are thirty-four: six sons of Leah, twenty-five grandsons, two great-grandsons through Perez, and Dinah. The total says thirty-three. There are several ways to reach the smaller figure — subtract the two who are stated dead and add Jacob himself, or leave Dinah out of the count of sons and daughters she is standing in the middle of — and the text specifies none of them. The arithmetic is left showing.

  • vv26–27 "sixty-six... seventy" — the chapter gives two totals four words apart. Sixty-six is those who came out of his loins, not counting the sons' wives. Then Joseph's two Egyptian-born sons are added, and Joseph, and Jacob, and the figure is seventy. Both numbers are correct under their own definitions, and the text supplies both rather than choosing.

  • v19 "the sons of Rachel, Jacob's wife" — Rachel is the only one of the four called Jacob's wife in this list. Leah is Leah (v15); Zilpah and Bilhah are identified by which daughter Laban gave them to. Forty years after her death and two chapters after Judah quoted him saying my wife bore me two (44:27), the register still has only one wife in it.

  • v28 "to point the way before him" — le-horot lefanav, from yarah, to throw, to aim, to point — and it is the root of Torah, which is the pointing, the direction given. Jacob sends Judah ahead to aim the family at Goshen. Reuben is the firstborn; Judah has been leading since chapter 44 and the text simply keeps handing him the job.

  • v29 "wept on his neck a long while" — va-yevk al tsavva'rav od, and od means still, yet, more. Joseph weeps; Jacob does not. The old man's line is the next verse, and it is about dying.

  • v30 "after seeing your face" — panim, the word this reunion has run on since 42:6 — the face they could not see, the face he hid, the face he sent gifts ahead of. Jacob gets the one thing the phrase has been withholding for five chapters and immediately says he is ready to die.

  • vv32, 34 "an abomination to Egypt" — to'evat Mitsrayim, the same word used in 43:32 for Egyptians eating bread with Hebrews. Joseph coaches his family to describe themselves in the terms most offensive to the country he governs, precisely so they will be housed apart in Goshen. He is using Egyptian contempt as a wall around them, and he is the one Egyptian-named, Egyptian-married, Egyptian-dressed man in the room.
