chapters.title: Few and Evil Have Been the Days of the Years of My Life
chapters.html:
Genesis 47

1And Joseph came and told Pharaoh, and said, "My father and my brothers, and their flocks and their herds and all that is theirs, have come from the land of Canaan. And here they are in the land of Goshen."

2And from the whole of his brothers he took five men and set them before Pharaoh.

3And Pharaoh said to his brothers, "What is your work?" And they said to Pharaoh, "Your servants are shepherds of flocks — both we and our fathers."

4And they said to Pharaoh, "We have come to sojourn in the land, for there is no pasture for the flocks that belong to your servants, since the famine is heavy in the land of Canaan. And now, let your servants please dwell in the land of Goshen."

5And Pharaoh said to Joseph, saying, "Your father and your brothers have come to you.

6The land of Egypt is before you. In the best of the land settle your father and your brothers — let them dwell in the land of Goshen. And if you know there are capable men among them, then set them as chiefs of livestock over what is mine."

7And Joseph brought Jacob his father and stood him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.

8And Pharaoh said to Jacob, "How many are the days of the years of your life?"

9And Jacob said to Pharaoh, "The days of the years of my sojournings are a hundred and thirty years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not reached the days of the years of the lives of my fathers in the days of their sojournings."

10And Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and went out from before Pharaoh.

11And Joseph settled his father and his brothers, and gave them a holding in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.

12And Joseph sustained his father and his brothers and all his father's house with bread, according to the little ones.

The Buying of Egypt

13And there was no bread in all the land, for the famine was very heavy, and the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan languished before the famine.

14And Joseph gathered up all the silver found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, for the grain they were buying, and Joseph brought the silver to Pharaoh's house.

15And the silver ran out from the land of Egypt and from the land of Canaan, and all Egypt came to Joseph, saying, "Give us bread — why should we die in front of you? For the silver is gone."

16And Joseph said, "Give your livestock, and I will give you for your livestock, if the silver is gone."

17And they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them bread for the horses, and for the livestock of the flocks, and for the livestock of the herds, and for the donkeys. And he led them along with bread that year, for all their livestock.

18And that year ran out, and they came to him in the second year and said to him, "We will not hide from my lord that the silver is spent and the herds of beasts belong to my lord. Nothing is left before my lord but our bodies and our ground.

19Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our ground? Buy us and our ground for bread, and we and our ground will be slaves to Pharaoh. And give seed, that we may live and not die, and the ground not be laid waste."

20And Joseph bought all the ground of Egypt for Pharaoh, for every Egyptian sold his field, because the famine was strong upon them. And the land became Pharaoh's.

21And the people — he moved them into the cities, from one end of the border of Egypt to the other.

22Only the ground of the priests he did not buy, for the priests had an allotment from Pharaoh, and they ate their allotment that Pharaoh gave them. Therefore they did not sell their ground.

23And Joseph said to the people, "Look — I have bought you today, and your ground, for Pharaoh. Here is seed for you, and you shall sow the ground.

24And it will come to pass at the harvests that you shall give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four of the hands shall be yours, for seed of the field and for your food, and for those in your houses, and for your little ones to eat."

25And they said, "You have kept us alive. Let us find favor in the eyes of my lord, and we will be slaves to Pharaoh."

26And Joseph made it a statute to this day over the ground of Egypt — a fifth for Pharaoh. Only the ground of the priests alone did not become Pharaoh's.

Do Not Bury Me in Egypt

27And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen, and they took holding in it, and were fruitful and multiplied greatly.

28And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. And the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were a hundred and forty-seven years.

29And the days of Israel drew near to die, and he called his son Joseph and said to him, "If I have found favor in your eyes, put your hand, please, under my thigh, and do kindness and truth with me: do not bury me, please, in Egypt.

30And I will lie with my fathers, and you shall carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burial place." And he said, "I myself will do according to your word."

31And he said, "Swear to me." And he swore to him. And Israel bowed himself at the head of the bed.

Notes

  • vv7, 10 "Jacob blessed Pharaoh" — twice, once entering and once leaving, and the two sentences frame the audience. A hundred-and-thirty-year-old shepherd from a famine country, whose trade the Egyptians find abominable, blesses the man Egypt worshipped, and the narrator reports it without a syllable of comment on either side.

  • v9 "Few and evil" — me'at ve-ra'im. He is a hundred and thirty and calls it few, and he is right by the family's own arithmetic: Abraham reached 175, Isaac 180. He is also the only one of the three to say a word about how his life went. And he calls them yemei shnei megurai, the years of my sojournings — magur, from gur, to reside as an outsider. Asked how old he is, he answers with how long he has been a stranger.

  • v11 "in the land of Rameses" — the best land in Egypt, given as a holding. And Exodus 1:11 names the two store-cities the Israelites are later forced to build under the whip: Pithom and Rameses. The gift and the slave-labour site carry one name. Nothing in Genesis points this out; the word simply sits there and Exodus picks it up.

  • v13 "languished" — va-telah, from a root so rare its force is hard to fix. The sense required is exhaustion, the land wrung out. What the verb does carry is that Egypt and Canaan are named together, suffering the same thing — which is the sentence that brings Jacob's family and Pharaoh's kingdom into one economy.

  • vv14–21 how Egypt was bought — read it as a sequence and it is a foreclosure in three steps. First the silver goes to Pharaoh's house (v14). When the silver runs out, the livestock (vv16–17). When that year ends, the people themselves offer their bodies and their ground (vv18–19). Joseph accepts, buys the whole country, and moves the population into the cities. He is not accused of anything and he does not defend himself. The text lays out the ledger and moves on.

  • v22 "Only the ground of the priests" — one class keeps its land, because Pharaoh already feeds them from a state allotment. Joseph's own wife is the daughter of a priest of On (41:45). The exemption is reported as a fact of administration, with no remark attached.

  • v25 "we will be slaves to Pharaoh" — avadim, and they say it as thanks: you have kept us alive. It is the word the whole Joseph story has been circling. He was sold as an eved (39:17); his brothers were terrified of being made avadim (43:18); Judah offered to become one in Benjamin's place (44:33). Here a whole nation asks for the status, and the man who grants it is the one who was sold into it.

  • v26 "a fifth... to this day" — the twenty percent is the same figure Joseph proposed to Pharaoh in 41:34 for the years of plenty. What was an emergency levy becomes permanent law, and the narrator says it is still in force at the time of writing.

  • v27 "were fruitful and multiplied greatly" — va-yifru va-yirbu, which is the blessing of 1:28 and 9:1, the words spoken over humanity at creation and again after the flood. Israel receives it here, in the same chapter where Egypt is reduced to tenancy, and va-ye'achazu bah, they took holding in it — achuzzah, the word for the cave Abraham bought in chapter 23 and for the land Canaan was promised as. They put down roots, and they put them down in the wrong country. Exodus 1:7 opens by repeating this sentence and expanding it, and Exodus 1:11 is four verses later.

  • v29 "put your hand under my thigh" — the oath gesture from 24:2, where Abraham made his servant swear this way about not taking a wife for Isaac from Canaan. It is used twice in the Bible, both times by a dying patriarch, both times about where the family belongs. And chesed ve-emet, kindness and truth, is the pair Jacob used of God in 32:11 when he was too small for all of it.

  • v30 "I will lie with my fathers" — ve-shakhavti im avotai, and shakhav is the ordinary verb to lie down. Hebrew's phrase for dying is lying down with the people you came from, which is why the burial place matters so much in the same breath. He is not asking for a grave. He is asking not to be left.

  • v31 "bowed himself at the head of the bed" — al rosh ha-mittah. The consonants are ה-מ-ט-ה, and vowelled the other way they read ha-matteh, the staff — bowing over the top of his staff. The Masoretic reading tradition points it mittah, a bed, and the Greek Old Testament read it as the staff. Both are in the letters; nothing else in the verse decides between them. A dying man propped in bed and an old man leaning on a stick are the same four consonants.

speech.text: Genesis 47

And Joseph came and told Pharaoh, and said, "My father and my brothers, and their flocks and their herds and all that is theirs, have come from the land of Canaan. And here they are in the land of Goshen."
And from the whole of his brothers he took five men and set them before Pharaoh.
And Pharaoh said to his brothers, "What is your work?" And they said to Pharaoh, "Your servants are shepherds of flocks — both we and our fathers."

And they said to Pharaoh, "We have come to sojourn in the land, for there is no pasture for the flocks that belong to your servants, since the famine is heavy in the land of Canaan. And now, let your servants please dwell in the land of Goshen."
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, saying, "Your father and your brothers have come to you.

The land of Egypt is before you. In the best of the land settle your father and your brothers — let them dwell in the land of Goshen. And if you know there are capable men among them, then set them as chiefs of livestock over what is mine."
And Joseph brought Jacob his father and stood him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.
And Pharaoh said to Jacob, "How many are the days of the years of your life?"

And Jacob said to Pharaoh, "The days of the years of my sojournings are a hundred and thirty years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not reached the days of the years of the lives of my fathers in the days of their sojournings."
And Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and went out from before Pharaoh.
And Joseph settled his father and his brothers, and gave them a holding in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.
And Joseph sustained his father and his brothers and all his father's house with bread, according to the little ones.
The Buying of Egypt
And there was no bread in all the land, for the famine was very heavy, and the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan languished before the famine.
And Joseph gathered up all the silver found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, for the grain they were buying, and Joseph brought the silver to Pharaoh's house.
And the silver ran out from the land of Egypt and from the land of Canaan, and all Egypt came to Joseph, saying, "Give us bread — why should we die in front of you? For the silver is gone."
And Joseph said, "Give your livestock, and I will give you for your livestock, if the silver is gone."

And they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them bread for the horses, and for the livestock of the flocks, and for the livestock of the herds, and for the donkeys. And he led them along with bread that year, for all their livestock.

And that year ran out, and they came to him in the second year and said to him, "We will not hide from my lord that the silver is spent and the herds of beasts belong to my lord. Nothing is left before my lord but our bodies and our ground.

Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our ground? Buy us and our ground for bread, and we and our ground will be slaves to Pharaoh. And give seed, that we may live and not die, and the ground not be laid waste."
And Joseph bought all the ground of Egypt for Pharaoh, for every Egyptian sold his field, because the famine was strong upon them. And the land became Pharaoh's.
And the people — he moved them into the cities, from one end of the border of Egypt to the other.
Only the ground of the priests he did not buy, for the priests had an allotment from Pharaoh, and they ate their allotment that Pharaoh gave them. Therefore they did not sell their ground.
And Joseph said to the people, "Look — I have bought you today, and your ground, for Pharaoh. Here is seed for you, and you shall sow the ground.

And it will come to pass at the harvests that you shall give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four of the hands shall be yours, for seed of the field and for your food, and for those in your houses, and for your little ones to eat."
And they said, "You have kept us alive. Let us find favor in the eyes of my lord, and we will be slaves to Pharaoh."
And Joseph made it a statute to this day over the ground of Egypt — a fifth for Pharaoh. Only the ground of the priests alone did not become Pharaoh's.
Do Not Bury Me in Egypt
And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen, and they took holding in it, and were fruitful and multiplied greatly.
And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. And the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were a hundred and forty-seven years.

And the days of Israel drew near to die, and he called his son Joseph and said to him, "If I have found favor in your eyes, put your hand, please, under my thigh, and do kindness and truth with me: do not bury me, please, in Egypt.
And I will lie with my fathers, and you shall carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burial place." And he said, "I myself will do according to your word."
And he said, "Swear to me." And he swore to him. And Israel bowed himself at the head of the bed.

chapters.title: I Know, My Son, I Know
chapters.html:
Genesis 48

1And it came to pass after these things that it was said to Joseph, "Here, your father is ill." And he took his two sons with him, Manasseh and Ephraim.

2And it was told to Jacob, and he said, "Here, your son Joseph has come to you." And Israel gathered his strength and sat up on the bed.

3And Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and blessed me,

4and said to me, 'Here I am making you fruitful and multiplying you, and I will make you an assembly of peoples, and I will give this land to your seed after you as an everlasting holding.'

5And now, your two sons born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt — they are mine. Ephraim and Manasseh, like Reuben and Simeon, shall be mine.

6And your offspring whom you father after them shall be yours. By the name of their brothers they shall be called in their inheritance.

7And I — when I came from Paddan, Rachel died on me in the land of Canaan, on the road, with still a stretch of ground to come to Ephrath. And I buried her there, on the road to Ephrath — that is Bethlehem."

The Crossing of the Hands

8And Israel saw Joseph's sons and said, "Who are these?"

9And Joseph said to his father, "They are my sons, whom God has given me here." And he said, "Take them, please, to me, and let me bless them."

10And Israel's eyes were heavy from age; he could not see. And he brought them near to him, and he kissed them and embraced them.

11And Israel said to Joseph, "I did not expect to see your face — and here, God has shown me your seed also."

12And Joseph brought them out from between his knees, and bowed with his face to the ground.

13And Joseph took the two of them — Ephraim at his right, from Israel's left, and Manasseh at his left, from Israel's right — and brought them near to him.

14And Israel put out his right hand and set it on Ephraim's head, and he was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh's head. He crossed his hands, for Manasseh was the firstborn.

15And he blessed Joseph and said, "The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has shepherded me from my beginning to this day,

16the angel who redeems me from all evil — may He bless the boys. And let my name be called in them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac. And let them teem into a multitude in the middle of the earth."

17And Joseph saw that his father was setting his right hand on Ephraim's head, and it was bad in his eyes, and he took hold of his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's head.

18And Joseph said to his father, "Not so, my father — for this one is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head."

19And his father refused and said, "I know, my son, I know. He too will become a people, and he too will be great. But his younger brother will be greater than he, and his seed will be a fullness of nations."

20And he blessed them that day, saying, "By you Israel will bless, saying, 'May God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh.'" And he set Ephraim before Manasseh.

21And Israel said to Joseph, "Here, I am dying. And God will be with you, and will bring you back to the land of your fathers.

22And I have given you one shoulder above your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow."

Notes

  • v3 "at Luz" — the place he is thinking of on his deathbed is the one he slept at with a stone under his head on the night he ran from Esau, which he renamed Bethel (28:19). Not the ford, not Shechem, not the twenty years. The stone, the ladder, and the promise.

  • v5 "like Reuben and Simeon, shall be mine" — he adopts Joseph's two Egyptian-born sons and names his own first and second sons as the measure. Reuben slept with his father's concubine (35:22) and Simeon emptied Shechem with a sword (34:25), and chapter 49 will take both of them apart for it. The two he names as the standard are the two he is about to disinherit.

  • v5 he says Ephraim first — before the boys are brought in, before anyone's hands are anywhere, the sentence reads Ephraim and Manasseh, younger before elder. What happens at verse 14 was decided nine verses earlier.

  • v7 "Rachel died on me" — metah alai Rachel, and it arrives with no connection to anything around it. He is in the middle of a legal adoption and he breaks off to say his wife died on the road, and he buried her there, and he gives the distance. The text offers no reason. It sits beside a sentence giving her grandsons a double share, and says nothing about why.

  • v8 "Who are these?" — the same two words Esau said to him at the reunion in 33:5, mi elleh lakh. And an old man who cannot see, asking who is standing in front of him, is chapter 27 again.

  • v10 "Israel's eyes were heavy from age; he could not see" — Isaac in 27:1: his eyes were too dim to see. Different verb, identical situation, and the same scene follows in both — the younger son ends up with the blessing meant for the elder. The difference is in verse 19.

  • v14 "He crossed his hands" — sikkel et yadav, a rare verb for laying them crosswise. He does not ask the boys to swap places, which would have been simpler. He leaves them where their father put them and crosses his own arms over them, so that everyone in the room can see what he is doing.

  • vv15–16 two names for God that begin here — ha-Elohim ha-ro'eh oti, the God who has shepherded me, and ha-mal'akh ha-go'el oti, the angel who redeems me. Both are first in the Bible in these two verses. The redeem-root, ga'al, occurs exactly once in all of Genesis, right here; it is the word for the kinsman who buys back a relative's land or freedom, and it becomes one of the largest words in the Bible for what God does. The Shepherd and the Redeemer both enter Scripture out of the mouth of a dying man describing his own life.

  • v16 "let them teem into a multitude" — ve-yidgu la-rov, and the verb is built on dag, fish. It occurs nowhere else. He asks that his grandsons multiply the way fish do — the one creature the first chapter of the book says God blessed and told to fill the waters.

  • v19 "I know, my son, I know" — yada'ti veni yada'ti, and this is the hinge of the chapter and the answer to chapter 27. Isaac was blind and deceived, and gave the blessing to the younger son because he could not tell them apart. Jacob is blind and not deceived. He is told plainly which boy is which, by the boys' own father, and he says he knows, and does it anyway. The same outcome, arrived at with open eyes.

  • v19 "a fullness of nations" — melo ha-goyim, and 48:4 has just quoted God's promise of an assembly of peoples. The blessing keeps widening past the family while the family is sitting in Egypt with seventy people in it.

  • v20 "May God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh" — Jacob says this is the form the blessing will take in Israel's mouth, and it is still the blessing spoken over Jewish sons. Two boys born in Egypt to an Egyptian mother, named by a man who spoke of forgetting his father's house, become the words a father says over his children.

  • v22 "one shoulder above your brothers" — shekhem achad, and shekhem is the ordinary word for a shoulder or a portion, and also the name of the town Shechem. The pun is unavoidable in Hebrew and invisible in English.

    And the claim raises a question the book does not answer. Jacob says he took it from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow. In 33:19 he bought that ground for a hundred qesitah. In chapter 34 Simeon and Levi took the city by sword while he was elsewhere, and he condemned them for it and condemns them again in 49:5–7. Three accounts of how the family came to hold Shechem, and this is the only one in which Jacob fought for it.

chapters.title: Gather, and I Will Tell You What Will Befall You
chapters.html:
Genesis 49

1And Jacob called to his sons and said, "Gather, and I will tell you what will befall you in the end of days.

2Assemble and hear, sons of Jacob,
and hear Israel your father.

3Reuben, you are my firstborn,
my strength and the first of my vigor,
surpassing in rank and surpassing in power.

4Reckless as water — you shall not surpass,
for you went up on your father's bed.
Then you defiled it — he went up on my couch.

5Simeon and Levi are brothers;
instruments of violence are their trade.

6Into their council let my soul not come,
in their assembly let my honor not be joined —
for in their anger they killed a man,
and in their pleasure they hamstrung an ox.

7Cursed be their anger, for it is strong,
and their fury, for it is hard.
I will divide them in Jacob
and scatter them in Israel.

8Judah — you, your brothers shall praise.
Your hand on the neck of your enemies.
Your father's sons shall bow down to you.

9A lion's cub is Judah.
From the prey, my son, you have gone up.
He crouched, he lay down like a lion,
and like a lioness — who will rouse him?

10The staff shall not turn aside from Judah,
nor the ruler's rod from between his feet,
until Shiloh comes,
and to him the obedience of peoples.

11Binding his foal to the vine,
and to the choice vine his donkey's colt,
he has washed his clothing in wine,
and his garment in the blood of grapes.

12Eyes darker than wine,
and teeth whiter than milk.

13Zebulun shall dwell at the shore of the seas,
and he shall be a shore for ships,
and his flank upon Sidon.

14Issachar is a bony donkey,
lying down between the saddlebags.

15And he saw that rest was good,
and that the land was pleasant,
and he bent his shoulder to bear,
and became a gang of forced labor.

16Dan shall judge his people,
as one of the tribes of Israel.

17Let Dan be a serpent on the road,
a horned viper on the path,
biting the horse's heels,
so his rider falls backward.

18For your salvation I have waited, LORD.

19Gad — a raiding band shall raid him,
and he shall raid at their heel.

20From Asher, his bread is rich,
and he shall give a king's delicacies.

21Naphtali is a doe let loose,
giving words of beauty.

22A fruitful son is Joseph,
a fruitful son over a spring,
branches striding over a wall.

23And the archers embittered him and shot,
and the masters of arrows hated him.

24But his bow stayed firm,
and the arms of his hands were made supple,
from the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob,
from there, the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel.

25From the God of your father — and may He help you —
and with the Almighty — and may He bless you:
blessings of the heavens above,
blessings of the deep crouching beneath,
blessings of breasts and womb.

26The blessings of your father have prevailed
over the blessings of my forebears,
to the boundary of the everlasting hills.
Let them be on the head of Joseph,
on the crown of the one set apart from his brothers.

27Benjamin is a wolf that tears.
In the morning he eats the prey,
and at evening he divides the spoil."

The Cave

28All these are the tribes of Israel, twelve, and this is what their father spoke to them. And he blessed them — each man according to his blessing he blessed them.

29And he commanded them and said to them, "I am being gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers, in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite,

30in the cave that is in the field of Machpelah, which faces Mamre in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought, the field, from Ephron the Hittite, as a holding for burial.

31There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife. And there I buried Leah.

32The purchase of the field and the cave that is in it was from the sons of Heth."

33And Jacob finished commanding his sons, and he gathered his feet into the bed, and expired, and was gathered to his people.

Notes

  • v1 "in the end of days" — be-acharit ha-yamim, and this is its first appearance in the Bible. It becomes the standing phrase of the prophets for the far horizon. Here it is a dying man in Egypt telling twelve sons what is coming, and what he tells them turns out to be mostly about land, war and character.

  • vv3–4 Reuben, and a sentence the father cannot finish to his face — kochi ve-reshit oni, my strength and the first of my on, the same ambiguous word Rachel used naming Ben-oni in 35:18. Then pachaz ka-mayim, reckless as water, a rare word for froth or instability. And watch the grammar break: for you went up on your father's bed. Then you defiled it — he went up on my couch. He is speaking to Reuben, and on the last three words he switches to the third person, as if turning away.

  • vv5–7 Simeon and Levi — not a blessing. Instruments of violence are their mekheroteihem — a word that occurs nowhere else and is not recoverable; weapons, plans, and dwellings have all been proposed from the consonants. What is clear is the sentence passed: I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel. Levi receives no territory and is dispersed through the other tribes; Simeon's portion is absorbed inside Judah's. A curse spoken over two sons becomes the map.

  • v6 "they hamstrung an ox" — singular, and chapter 34 mentions no ox. It says they killed every male in Shechem and drove off the flocks and herds. The poem remembers the day in two images, they killed a man and they hamstrung an ox, and neither matches the prose exactly.

  • v8 "your brothers shall praise you" — yodukha, from yadah, to give thanks or praise — the root Leah named him from in 29:35. And the next line is yadkha, your hand, on your enemies' neck: Yehudah, yodukha, yadkha, three sounds off one line. Then your father's sons shall bow down to you — which is Joseph's dream from 37:7, reassigned.

  • v9 "from the prey, my son, you have gone up" — mi-teref beni alita, and teref is the noun of tarof toraf, torn, torn, which is what Jacob cried over the bloodied coat in 37:33 and what Judah quoted back to him in 44:28. The word for the lie Judah helped stage is the word his blessing is built on.

  • v10 "until Shiloh comes" — the most disputed line in Genesis, and the Hebrew will not settle it. The consonants on the page are שילה and the reading tradition marks שילו, one of the places where written and read were preserved side by side. The candidates all come out of those letters: a place name, Shiloh; shai lo, tribute to him; she-lo, that which is his. Nothing in the verse decides. What is not in doubt is the frame — a staff that does not depart from Judah, until something or someone arrives.

  • v15 "became a gang of forced labor" — va-yehi le-mas oved. Mas is the corvée, conscripted state labour, and the word turns up again in Exodus 1:11: they set over them chiefs of forced labour... and he built store-cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Rameses. Issachar's blessing is that he saw the land was pleasant and lay down under the load.

  • v17 "a horned viper on the path" — shefifon, a snake-word that occurs once in the Bible and cannot be pinned down further than some kind of viper. The image is exact regardless: a small thing on the road that brings down a horse by the heel, so the rider goes over backwards. Dan is the tribe that judges, and his picture is an ambush.

  • v18 "For your salvation I have waited, LORD" — the poem stops. For one line Jacob is not talking to his sons at all; he turns and addresses God, by name, and then goes straight back to Gad in the next verse. It is the only sentence in the chapter aimed at anyone but the twelve, and nothing prepares it or follows from it.

  • v19 Gad, in sound — Gad gedud yegudennu ve-hu yagud aqev. Four words in the line are built from the same two consonants as his name. English can put raid next to raid and lose the rest; in Hebrew the whole line rattles.

  • vv24–25 three names for God, all new — avir Ya'aqov, the Mighty One of Jacob; ro'eh even Yisra'el, the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel. The shepherd title appeared for the first time in the previous chapter (48:15), out of the same mouth. And the blessings are stacked in a vertical line — the heavens above, the deep crouching beneath, breasts and womb. The deep is tehom, the dark water of 1:2. Creation's top, bottom and middle, invoked over one son.

  • v28 "he blessed them" — the narrator's summary calls all twelve speeches blessings, including cursed be their anger and you shall not surpass. And ish asher ke-virkhato, each according to his blessing — meaning the one that fits him. What each son gets is what he is.

  • v31 "And there I buried Leah" — the last thing he says about his own life. He lists the cave's occupants in pairs, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and then puts himself in beside Leah, the wife he did not choose and whose eyes the book would not describe. Rachel is not there. She is on the Ephrath road where he buried her (35:19), and he mentioned it two chapters ago for no reason anyone can see (48:7). He asks to be laid next to the other one.

  • v33 "he gathered his feet into the bed" — va-ye'esof raglav el ha-mittah. His first recorded act as a man was va-yissa raglav, he lifted his feet and went to the east (29:1). His last is to draw them back in. And the verb of the gathering, asaf, is the same one in was gathered to his people in the same verse.

For your salvation I have waited, LORD.
Gad — a raiding band shall raid him, and he shall raid at their heel.
From Asher, his bread is rich, and he shall give a king's delicacies.
Naphtali is a doe let loose, giving words of beauty.
A fruitful son is Joseph, a fruitful son over a spring, branches striding over a wall.
And the archers embittered him and shot, and the masters of arrows hated him.
But his bow stayed firm, and the arms of his hands were made supple, from the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, from there, the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel.

From the God of your father — and may He help you — and with the Almighty — and may He bless you: blessings of the heavens above, blessings of the deep crouching beneath, blessings of breasts and womb.

The blessings of your father have prevailed over the blessings of my forebears, to the boundary of the everlasting hills. Let them be on the head of Joseph, on the crown of the one set apart from his brothers.
Benjamin is a wolf that tears. In the morning he eats the prey, and at evening he divides the spoil."
The Cave
All these are the tribes of Israel, twelve, and this is what their father spoke to them. And he blessed them — each man according to his blessing he blessed them.
And he commanded them and said to them, "I am being gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers, in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
in the cave that is in the field of Machpelah, which faces Mamre in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought, the field, from Ephron the Hittite, as a holding for burial.
There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife. And there I buried Leah.
The purchase of the field and the cave that is in it was from the sons of Heth."
And Jacob finished commanding his sons, and he gathered his feet into the bed, and expired, and was gathered to his people.

chapters.title: You Planned Evil Against Me; God Planned It for Good
chapters.html:
Genesis 50

1And Joseph fell on his father's face, and wept over him, and kissed him.

2And Joseph commanded his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father. And the physicians embalmed Israel.

3And forty days were filled for him, for so are the days of embalming filled. And Egypt wept for him seventy days.

4And the days of weeping for him passed, and Joseph spoke to the house of Pharaoh, saying, "If I have found favor in your eyes, speak, please, in Pharaoh's ears, saying,

5'My father made me swear, saying, Here, I am dying. In my grave that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan, there you shall bury me. And now let me go up, please, and bury my father, and I will return.'"

6And Pharaoh said, "Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear."

7And Joseph went up to bury his father, and all Pharaoh's servants went up with him — the elders of his house, and all the elders of the land of Egypt —

8and all of Joseph's house, and his brothers, and his father's house. Only their little ones and their flocks and their herds they left in the land of Goshen.

9And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen, and the camp was very heavy.

10And they came to the threshing floor of the Bramble, which is across the Jordan, and they wailed there a great and very heavy wailing. And he made mourning for his father seven days.

11And the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning at the threshing floor of the Bramble, and they said, "This is a heavy mourning for Egypt." Therefore its name was called Abel-mizraim, which is across the Jordan.

12And his sons did for him just as he had commanded them.

13And his sons carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham bought — the field — as a holding for burial, from Ephron the Hittite, facing Mamre.

14And Joseph returned to Egypt, he and his brothers and all who had gone up with him to bury his father, after he had buried his father.

What If Joseph Hates Us

15And Joseph's brothers saw that their father was dead, and they said, "What if Joseph hates us, and pays us back in full for all the evil we dealt him?"

16And they sent word to Joseph, saying, "Your father commanded before his death, saying,

17'So you shall say to Joseph: Please — lift the offense of your brothers and their sin, for they dealt you evil.' And now, lift, please, the offense of the servants of the God of your father." And Joseph wept when they spoke to him.

18And his brothers also went and fell before him and said, "Here we are, your slaves."

19And Joseph said to them, "Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?

20And you — you planned evil against me. God planned it for good, so as to do what is being done this day, to keep a great people alive.

21And now, do not be afraid. I myself will sustain you and your little ones." And he comforted them and spoke to their heart.

Carry My Bones Up From Here

22And Joseph dwelt in Egypt, he and his father's house. And Joseph lived a hundred and ten years.

23And Joseph saw Ephraim's sons to the third generation. Also the sons of Machir son of Manasseh were born on Joseph's knees.

24And Joseph said to his brothers, "I am dying. And God will surely visit you, and bring you up from this land to the land He swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob."

25And Joseph made the sons of Israel swear, saying, "God will surely visit you, and you shall carry my bones up from here."

26And Joseph died, a son of a hundred and ten years. And they embalmed him, and he was put in the coffin in Egypt.

Notes

  • vv2, 3, 26 "embalm" — chanat, and the word occurs four times in Genesis, all four in this chapter. Nowhere else in the Bible is a body treated this way. Israel buries; Egypt preserves. Jacob and Joseph are the only two people in Scripture embalmed, and both are embalmed in Egypt, and the book ends before either practice is ever repeated.

  • v3 "forty days... seventy days" — two numbers, two customs. Forty is the embalming; seventy is how long Egypt weeps. The country mourns the foreign shepherd's father for ten weeks, and the text gives the figure without remark.

  • v4 "speak, please, in Pharaoh's ears" — Joseph does not go himself. The man who stood before Pharaoh at thirty and was given the signet ring now asks the household to carry a message for him. The text gives the fact and no reason for it.

  • v5 "in my grave that I dug for myself" — kariti, and the verb is ordinarily to dig. But 49:30 says plainly that Abraham bought that cave from Ephron, and karah also carries the sense of acquiring by purchase elsewhere in the Bible. Either Jacob is claiming a digging the book never mentions, or he means he got it for himself. The word allows both and the chapter does not choose.

  • vv8, 9 what they take and what they leave — chariots and horsemen go up; the little ones and the flocks stay in Goshen. Nothing explains it here. In Exodus 10:24 Pharaoh will make the same division and get it backwards — only your flocks and your herds shall be left; your little ones may go too — and Moses refuses. The two verses are four hundred years and one book apart.

  • v10 "the threshing floor of the Bramble" — goren ha-atad. Atad is the thorn-bush, and a threshing floor is the flat open ground where grain is beaten out. It is an odd place name and an odd place to stop — a working floor, named for a thorn, on the far side of the Jordan, and the great mourning happens there rather than at the tomb.

  • v11 "Abel-mizraim" — the Canaanites watch, and what they see is Egypt: this is a heavy mourning for Egypt. The name they give the place, Avel Mitsrayim, turns on a sound — evel is mourning, and avel is a meadow — so the name reads as mourning of Egypt and as meadow of Egypt at once. Jacob is carried home by what looks from a distance like an Egyptian state funeral, and the locals name the ground after the wrong country.

  • v15 "What if Joseph hates us" — yistemenu, from satam, and it is the verb of 49:23, where Jacob's blessing said the masters of arrows hated him. Their father has been dead one verse. Seventeen years in Egypt under Joseph's protection have not convinced them, and the thing they have been waiting for is the funeral.

  • vv16–17 the message their father never sent — they claim Jacob left instructions before he died. Chapter 49 records his last words to all twelve sons in full, and this is not among them, and nothing anywhere in the book reports him saying it. They may be quoting something unrecorded. They may be inventing a dead man's wish to save their lives. The narrator supplies no verdict, and Joseph's only response to the message is to weep.

  • v17 "lift the offense" — sa na pesha, and the verb is nasa, to lift or carry. Hebrew's word for forgiving is picking a thing up and carrying it away, which means somebody is still holding it. Pesha is not an accident or a lapse; it is rebellion, a deliberate breach.

  • v18 "Here we are, your slaves" — hinnennu lekha la-avadim. This is the dream of 37:7 arriving in full: eleven brothers on the ground in front of him, saying the word out loud. They sold him into slavery for twenty pieces of silver and now offer themselves as the same thing. He refuses it in the next breath.

  • v19 "Am I in the place of God?" — ha-tachat Elohim ani, four words, and they are his father's words. Jacob said exactly this to Rachel in 30:2, shouting, when she demanded children: am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb? The son says the same sentence to refuse a power that is actually being handed to him.

  • v20 "you planned evil... God planned it for good" — chashavtem and chashavah, the same verb twice, from chashav, to reckon, devise, work something out. Not two events. One act, and two intentions running through it, and the text puts them in the same sentence in the same word without explaining how both can be true.

  • v21 "spoke to their heart" — va-yedabber al libbam, the idiom for reassuring speech. Its only other appearance in Genesis is 34:3, where Shechem spoke to the heart of Dinah after raping her. The book uses the phrase twice, and this is the second.

  • vv24–25 "God will surely visit you" — paqod yifqod, the verb doubled, and it becomes the password of the Exodus. Moses says it to the elders in Egypt; and Exodus 13:19 quotes this oath back word for word — Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for he had made the sons of Israel swear, saying, God will surely visit you, and you shall carry my bones up from here. Joshua 24:32 finishes it: the bones are buried at Shechem, in the field Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor for a hundred qesitah — which is Genesis 33:19. It takes four hundred years and two more books, and Joseph ends up in the one piece of ground his father paid for.

  • v26 "and he was put in the coffin in Egypt" — the last words of Genesis, and the last word is aron, a chest. It is the same word as the Ark of the Covenant, and it has appeared only once before in this book. Genesis opens with God making a world and closes with a box in Egypt, with a promise in it.
